domain:
    r: dim in [0, NR)
    q: dim in [0, NQ)
    p: dim in [0, NP)
    s: dim in [0, NP)

data:
    # 3D array A: A[r][q][p] in C code, row-major with p as fastest index
    A[r, q, p]: inout DATA_TYPE =
        (r, q, p) -> (r * NQ + q) * NP + p  # Row-major

    # 2D transform matrix C4: C4[s][p] in C code, row-major
    C4[s, p]: in DATA_TYPE =
        (s, p) -> s * NP + p                # Row-major, p-contiguous per fixed s

    # Per-(r,q) scratch vector used to hold the reduction result.
    # In the original C code this is a single NP-length array "sum" reused
    # across all (r,q). Here we model it conceptually as a local buffer
    # to enable parallel (r,q) execution; implementation uses one scratch
    # vector per thread.
    sum_local[p]: temp DATA_TYPE           # Size NP, kept in fast memory

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (compile-time or run-time)
    NR: int
    NQ: int
    NP: int

    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters
    RB: int  # tile size along r (outermost)
    QB: int  # tile size along q
    SB: int  # tile size along s (reduction dimension)
    PB: int  # tile size along p (output dimension)
    VEC: int # vector width for p-dimension SIMD (e.g., 4, 8, 16)
    UP: int  # unroll factor for inner p-loop
    US: int  # unroll factor for inner s-loop

computation:
    # Logical specification:
    # For each (r, q), the NP-length row A[r, q, *] is multiplied on the right
    # by the common NP×NP matrix C4. That is, for every output index p:
    #
    #   A_new[r, q, p] = sum_{s=0}^{NP-1} A_old[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    #
    # The implementation uses a temporary vector (sum_local) to avoid
    # overwriting A while it is still needed on the right-hand side.
    for r, q, p:
        A[r, q, p] = sum(s in [0, NP), A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p])

dependencies:
    # For each fixed (r, q), all outputs A[r, q, p] depend on the entire
    # original row A[r, q, *]. This creates a true flow dependence along p:
    #
    #   A[r, q, s] (old) -> A[r, q, p] (new)  for all p, s in [0, NP)
    #
    # Hence, a naive in-place update without a temporary would be incorrect.
    # A correct schedule must read all A[r, q, s] values from the pre-update
    # state and only then overwrite A[r, q, *].
    for r in [0, NR), q in [0, NQ), p in [0, NP), s in [0, NP):
        A[r, q, s] (read) -> A[r, q, p] (write)

optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Parallelize across independent (r, q) planes with outer tiling.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Each (r, q) pair is completely independent given read-only C4.
    # We therefore tile the (r, q) space and parallelize over r-tiles.
    block(r, R, RB)        # R: tile index along r, tile size RB
    block(q, Q, QB)        # Q: tile index along q, tile size QB
    hoist(R)               # Make R the outermost loop
    hoist(Q)               # Next outermost: process 2D tiles in (r, q)
    parallelize(R)         # Distribute r-tiles across threads

    # Implementation note: sum_local[p] is privatized per thread (or per
    # parallel (r, q) instance), so threads do not race on this buffer.
    # Memory overhead: O(#threads * NP * sizeof(DATA_TYPE)), which is
    # negligible compared to |A| and well below the 50% growth budget.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Exploit structure of the reduction for locality and reuse.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Starting from the mathematical reduction
    #   A[r, q, p] = sum_s A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    # we implement, for each fixed (r, q), the following GEMV-like kernel:
    #
    #   for p in [0, NP):               # initialize reduction buffer
    #       sum_local[p] = 0
    #   for s in [0, NP):               # reduction over s
    #       a_rqs = A[r, q, s]          # load once
    #       for p in [0, NP):           # accumulate along p
    #           sum_local[p] += a_rqs * C4[s, p]
    #   for p in [0, NP):               # write back
    #       A[r, q, p] = sum_local[p]
    #
    # Compared to the original C code (which loops p outer, then s),
    # this schedule:
    #   - Reads each A[r, q, s] exactly once and reuses it across all p.
    #   - Accesses C4[s, p] with p as the innermost index, which is
    #     contiguous in memory (row-major).
    #   - Performs the same floating-point work but reduces A-traffic
    #     and improves cache/TLB locality.
    #
    # This kernel is obtained by interchanging the order of (p, s)
    # in the reduction and hoisting the initialization of sum_local[p].
    interchange(p, s)      # in the reduction loop defining A[r, q, p]
    hoist(s)               # make s the outer loop inside each (r, q)

    # Optional local algebraic optimization:
    #   For each (r, q), rewrite the reduction as
    #     sum_local[p] = A[r, q, 0] * C4[0, p]
    #     for s in [1, NP): sum_local[p] += A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p]
    #   eliminating the explicit zero-initialization loop and one
    #   NP-length addition with zero. This preserves semantics and
    #   slightly reduces the number of adds and stores; modern compilers
    #   may perform this automatically.

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Block the (s, p) space for cache reuse on C4 and sum_local.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # C4 and sum_local are both NP-length along p; blocking improves
    # L1/L2 locality when NP is large and enables tuned micro-kernels.
    block(s, S, SB)        # S: tile index along s, tile size SB
    block(p, P, PB)        # P: tile index along p, tile size PB
    hoist(S)               # iterate S outermost inside each (r, q)
    # Resulting inner structure (within a tile of (r, q)):
    #   for S:
    #       for P:
    #           for s in tile S:
    #               a_rqs = A[r, q, s]
    #               for p in tile P:
    #                   sum_local[p] += a_rqs * C4[s, p]

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. SIMD vectorization and unrolling over the innermost p-dimension.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # The p-dimension is contiguous for both C4[s, p] and sum_local[p],
    # making it ideal for SIMD. We vectorize and unroll the innermost
    # loop over P (p within a tile).
    vectorize(P, VEC)      # generate SIMD over contiguous p
    unroll(P, UP)          # unroll inner p-loop for better ILP
    unroll(S, US)          # mild unrolling over s to hide FMA latency

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Memory-placement considerations.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    # - Keep sum_local in stack or thread-local storage to ensure it
    #   resides in L1/L2 cache and avoid false sharing.
    # - C4 is read-only; allow the compiler to place it in read-only
    #   segments and assume no aliasing with A.
    # - With the above blocking, the working set for each (r, q) tile
    #   (a slice of A plus the full C4 and sum_local) fits comfortably
    #   in the higher-cache levels on the target x64 system.
--- END OF MODEL: doitgen-04 ---

--- START OF MODEL: doitgen-05 ---
domain:
    r: dim in [0, NR)          # row index in first dimension of A
    q: dim in [0, NQ)          # row index in second dimension of A
    p: dim in [0, NP)          # output element index within A[r, q, :]
    s: dim in [0, NP)          # reduction index over input A[r, q, :]

data:
    # 3D tensor A, updated in-place.
    # Layout matches C's row-major: A[r][q][p] with p contiguous, then q, then r.
    A[r, q, p]: inout DATA_TYPE
        = (r, q, p) -> ((r * NQ + q) * NP + p)

    # 2D matrix C4, read-only in the kernel.
    # Standard row-major: C4[s][p] with p contiguous.
    C4[s, p]: in DATA_TYPE
        = (s, p) -> (s * NP + p)

    # The explicit 1D workspace `sum[p]` from the original C code is modeled
    # as a *local, per-(r,q) temporary vector* implementing the reduction;
    # it does not appear as a global data object here.
    # Implementation detail:
    #   for each (r, q), we allocate a local vector sum[0..NP-1].

parameters:
    # Problem sizes NR, NQ, NP are implicit in the domain bounds.

    # Tuning parameters for optimization (compile-time or launch-time constants).
    TR: int  # tile size for r, e.g., 8–32 depending on cache and NR
    TQ: int  # tile size for q, e.g., 8–32 depending on cache and NQ

    VEC_P: int  # SIMD width in elements along p (e.g., 4 or 8 for double, 8 or 16 for float)
    U_P:   int  # unroll factor for the innermost p loop inside each SIMD chunk
    U_S:   int  # unroll factor for the s loop (small, e.g., 2–4)

computation:
    # High-level mathematical semantics of `kernel_doitgen`:
    # For each (r, q, p), form a linear combination of the row A[r, q, :]
    # with the corresponding column of C4, and overwrite A in place.
    #
    # This matches the original C code:
    #   for (r, q):
    #     for (p): sum[p] = 0;
    #     for (p):
    #       for (s): sum[p] += A[r][q][s] * C4[s][p];
    #     for (p): A[r][q][p] = sum[p];
    #
    # which is equivalent to the reduction below.

    UPDATE_A:
      for r, q, p:
          A[r, q, p] = sum(s, A[r, q, s] * C4[s, p])

    # Notes:
    # - The reduction sum(s, ...) is over s in [0, NP).
    # - All reads of A on the right-hand side conceptually use the "old"
    #   values A_before; the write to A[r, q, p] occurs after the reduction
    #   has completed for that (r, q, p). An implementation uses a local
    #   temporary vector (sum[p]) for each (r, q) to avoid in-place hazards.
    # - Each (r, q) row of A is independent of all others.

dependencies:
    # True data dependencies:
    # - Within a fixed (r, q, p), UPDATE_A(r, q, p) depends on all A[r, q, s]
    #   for s in [0, NP) and on all C4[s, p].
    # - There are no cross-(r, q) dependencies in A or C4.
    #
    # This enables outer parallelism over (r, q) after privatizing the
    # reduction temporary.

    # Using a label for the update:
    for r in [0, NR), q in [0, NQ), p in [0, NP), s in [0, NP):
        A_read(r, q, s) -> UPDATE_A(r, q, p)

optimization:
    #------------------------------
    # 1. Loop reordering for locality and vectorization
    #------------------------------
    # The reduction in `computation` is symmetric in p and s, but the
    # memory layouts favor making p the innermost loop:
    #
    #   - A[r, q, s] is contiguous in s.
    #   - C4[s, p] is contiguous in p for fixed s.
    #
    # Implementation-level order used:
    #   for r, q:
    #     sum[p] = 0           (p innermost, contiguous)
    #     for s:
    #       a_rqs = A[r, q, s]   # scalar load
    #       for p:               # innermost loop
    #         sum[p] += a_rqs * C4[s, p]
    #     for p:
    #       A[r, q, p] = sum[p]
    #
    # The following interchange expresses this preference.

    interchange(p, s)
        # Interchange the logical roles of p and s in the reduction order
        # so that the innermost loops run along p (contiguous in C4) and
        # the outer reduction loop runs along s.

    #------------------------------
    # 2. Blocking over (r, q) for cache locality and parallel work
    #------------------------------
    # Tile the (r, q) plane. Each tile operates on a small block of
    # rows of A that can stay hot in caches while repeatedly streaming C4.

    block(r, Rb, TR)    # Rb indexes r-tiles of size TR
    block(q, Qb, TQ)    # Qb indexes q-tiles of size TQ
    hoist(Rb)           # Move tile loops to the outermost level
    hoist(Qb)

    # Conceptual loop nest after blocking (ignoring p/s for brevity):
    #
    # for Rb in [0, ceil(NR/TR)):
    #   for Qb in [0, ceil(NQ/TQ)):
    #     for r in tile Rb:
    #       for q in tile Qb:
    #         ... reduction over s and p for this (r, q) ...

    #------------------------------
    # 3. Parallelization across tiles (outer parallelism)
    #------------------------------
    # Since different (r, q) rows of A are independent, the outer tile
    # loop over Rb can be parallelized. The reduction temporary sum[p]
    # must be *privatized* per worker (e.g., per OpenMP thread).
    #
    # This does not change asymptotic memory usage: each worker allocates
    # one NP-element buffer for sum[p], and there was already a single
    # NP-element buffer in the sequential baseline.

    parallelize(Rb)
        # Parallelize the Rb loop with:
        # - sum[p] declared private to each worker
        # - A and C4 shared and read-only (except for the final writes to A)

    # Optionally, if NR is small and NQ is large, we could instead
    # parallelize Qb (or both Rb and Qb using a 2D decomposition).

    #------------------------------
    # 4. SIMD vectorization and unrolling on p
    #------------------------------
    # The innermost operations along p are simple FMA-like updates on
    # contiguous memory in sum[p] and C4[s, p]. These are ideal for SIMD.

    vectorize(p, VEC_P)
        # Generate SIMD code for the innermost p loop, with width VEC_P
        # elements (e.g., 4 or 8 for doubles, depending on ISA).

    unroll(p, U_P)
        # Unroll the (possibly SIMD) p loop by U_P to expose ILP and
        # reduce loop overhead. U_P is typically small (1–4).

    #------------------------------
    # 5. Unrolling over s and scalar replacement
    #------------------------------
    # Further improve ILP by unrolling the reduction loop over s and
    # keeping A[r, q, s] in a scalar register while iterating over p.

    unroll(s, U_S)
        # Unroll the reduction loop over s by a small factor U_S.

    scalar_replace(A[r, q, s])
        # Non-standard directive:
        #   Load A[r, q, s] into a scalar (e.g., a_rqs) once per (r, q, s)
        #   iteration and reuse it for all p in the innermost loop.
        # This reduces memory traffic by avoiding repeated loads of
        # A[r, q, s] inside the p loop.

    #------------------------------
    # 6. Implementation of the reduction with a local buffer
    #------------------------------
    # To avoid in-place update hazards and preserve the original semantics,
    # the reduction is implemented with a per-(r, q) local buffer sum[p]:
    #
    #   for each tile Rb, Qb (possibly in parallel over Rb):
    #     for each r in tile Rb:
    #       for each q in tile Qb:
    #         # initialize local accumulation vector
    #         for p in [0, NP):
    #             sum[p] = 0
    #         # main reduction, reordered for locality:
    #         for s in [0, NP):
    #             a_rqs = A[r, q, s]
    #             for p in [0, NP):          # vectorized over p
    #                 sum[p] += a_rqs * C4[s, p]
    #         # write-back
    #         for p in [0, NP):
    #             A[r, q, p] = sum[p]
    #
    # This algorithm is mathematically equivalent to the high-level
    # reduction in `computation` and respects the original kernel's
    # functionality.
--- END OF MODEL: doitgen-05 ---

/**

 *   Louis-Noel Pouchet <pouchet.ohio-state.edu>
 *   Tomofumi Yuki <tomofumi.yuki.fr>

/* durbin.c: this file is part of PolyBench/C */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Include polybench common header. */
#include <polybench.h>

/* Include benchmark-specific header. */
#include "durbin.h"


/* Array initialization. */
static
void init_array (int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(r,N,n))
{
  int i, j;

  for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    {
      r[i] = (n+1-i);
    }
}


/* DCE code. Must scan the entire live-out data.
   Can be used also to check the correctness of the output. */
static
void print_array(int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(y,N,n))

{
  int i;

  POLYBENCH_DUMP_START;
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_BEGIN("y");
  for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (i % 20 == 0) fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, "\n");
    fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, DATA_PRINTF_MODIFIER, y[i]);
  }
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_END("y");
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_FINISH;
}


/* Main computational kernel. The whole function will be timed,
   including the call and return. */
static
void kernel_durbin[[gnu::flatten, gnu::noinline]](int n,
		   DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(r,N,n),
		   DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(y,N,n))
{
 DATA_TYPE z[N];
 DATA_TYPE alpha;
 DATA_TYPE beta;
 DATA_TYPE sum;

 int i,k;

#pragma scop
 y[0] = -r[0];
 beta = SCALAR_VAL(1.0);
 alpha = -r[0];

 for (k = 1; k < _PB_N; k++) {
   beta = (1-alpha*alpha)*beta;
   sum = SCALAR_VAL(0.0);
   for (i=0; i<k; i++) {
      sum += r[k-i-1]*y[i];
   }
   alpha = - (r[k] + sum)/beta;

   for (i=0; i<k; i++) {
      z[i] = y[i] + alpha*y[k-i-1];
   }
   for (i=0; i<k; i++) {
     y[i] = z[i];
   }
   y[k] = alpha;
 }
#pragma endscop

}


int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
  /* Retrieve problem size. */
  int n = N;

  /* Variable declaration/allocation. */
  POLYBENCH_1D_ARRAY_DECL(r, DATA_TYPE, N, n);
  POLYBENCH_1D_ARRAY_DECL(y, DATA_TYPE, N, n);


  /* Initialize array(s). */
  init_array (n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(r));

  /* Start timer. */
  polybench_start_instruments;

  /* Run kernel. */
  kernel_durbin (n,
		 POLYBENCH_ARRAY(r),
		 POLYBENCH_ARRAY(y));

  /* Stop and print timer. */
  polybench_stop_instruments;
  polybench_print_instruments;

  /* Prevent dead-code elimination. All live-out data must be printed
     by the function call in argument. */
  polybench_prevent_dce(print_array(n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(y)));

  /* Be clean. */
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(r);
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(y);

  return 0;
}

    # Global problem-size upper bound from the C code.
    k: dim in [0, N)
    i: dim in [0, N)
    p: dim in [0, N/2)   # used for symmetric pair updates of y

data:
    # 1D contiguous arrays (row-major layout).
    r[i]: in    DATA_TYPE = i -> i        # input autocorrelation sequence
    y[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = i -> i        # solution / output sequence

    # Scalar state carried across k-iterations.
    alpha: inout DATA_TYPE
    beta:  inout DATA_TYPE

parameters:
    n: int, 1 <= n <= N        # actual problem size (_PB_N at run time)

    # Tuning parameters (can be compile-time constants or runtime knobs).
    U_SUM:    int > 0          # unroll factor for sum-reduction over i
    V_SUM:    int > 0          # vector width for sum-reduction over i
    U_UPDATE: int > 0          # unroll factor for y-update over p
    V_UPDATE: int > 0          # vector width for y-update over p
    P_THREADS: int >= 1        # max threads for inner parallelism (i/p dimensions)

computation:
    # Notation: "let x = expr" introduces a scalar temporary used only
    # in the following statements.

    # --- Initialization (k = 0) ---
    init_y0:
        y[0] = -r[0]
    init_beta:
        beta = 1.0
    init_alpha:
        alpha = -r[0]

    # --- Main Durbin recurrence ---
    # The outer loop over k is inherently sequential: alpha, beta and y
    # carry dependencies from k to k+1.
    for k in seq([1, n)):
        update_beta(k):
            beta = (1.0 - alpha * alpha) * beta

        # alpha_k = -(r[k] + sum_{i=0}^{k-1} r[k-1-i] * y[i]) / beta_k
        compute_alpha(k):
            alpha = -(r[k] + sum(i in [0, k), r[k-1-i] * y[i])) / beta

        # In-place symmetric update of y[0..k-1], replacing the original
        # two-loop scheme using a temporary array z[]:
        #   (original C)
        #     for i in 0..k-1: z[i] = y[i] + alpha * y[k-1-i];
        #     for i in 0..k-1: y[i] = z[i];
        #
        # Here we exploit the symmetry (i, j = k-1-i) and update pairs
        # (y[i], y[j]) using the OLD values of y[i], y[j] stored in
        # temporaries yi_old, yj_old. Each index in 0..k-1 participates
        # in exactly one pair, except an optional center index for odd k.
        update_y_pairs(k):
            for p in [0, k/2):
                let i = p
                let j = k - 1 - p
                let yi_old = y[i]
                let yj_old = y[j]
                y[i] = yi_old + alpha * yj_old
                y[j] = yj_old + alpha * yi_old

        update_y_center(k):
            # For odd k, there is a center index c = floor(k/2)
            # that in the original code satisfies:
            #   z[c] = y[c] + alpha * y[c]; y[c] = z[c]
            # which is equivalent to y[c] *= (1 + alpha).
            if (k % 2 == 1):
                let c = k / 2           # integer division
                y[c] = y[c] * (1.0 + alpha)

        set_yk(k):
            y[k] = alpha

dependencies:
    # The body at iteration k+1 depends on the fully updated
    # (alpha, beta, and y[0..k]) from iteration k.
    for k in [1, n-1):
        {update_beta(k), compute_alpha(k),
         update_y_pairs(k), update_y_center(k), set_yk(k)}
            -> {update_beta(k+1), compute_alpha(k+1),
                update_y_pairs(k+1), update_y_center(k+1), set_yk(k+1)}

optimization:
    # 1. Sum-reduction over i in compute_alpha(k).
    #    This is a purely data-parallel reduction for fixed k.
    vectorize(i, V_SUM)
    unroll(i, U_SUM)
    parallelize(i)   # with a reduction on the sum(i, ...) expression

    # 2. Symmetric in-place y-update over p in update_y_pairs(k).
    #    Each (i = p, j = k-1-p) pair touches disjoint y-indices, so
    #    iterations over p are independent and suitable for SIMD and
    #    thread parallelism.
    vectorize(p, V_UPDATE)
    unroll(p, U_UPDATE)
    parallelize(p)

    # 3. Keep k as the outermost sequential loop to preserve the
    #    recurrence structure in alpha, beta, and y.
    hoist(k)         # prevent any outer parallelization or tiling of k

    # 4. Eliminate the temporary array z[] used in the original C code.
    #    # new optimization kind:
    #    #   eliminate_temp(y, z):
    #    #       rewrite the two-step update
    #    #           z[i] = y[i] + alpha * y[k-1-i];
    #    #           y[i] = z[i];
    #    #       into the symmetric in-place pair update modeled by
    #    #       update_y_pairs(k) and update_y_center(k), using local
    #    #       temporaries yi_old, yj_old.
    #    #
    #    # This reduces memory footprint (no z[N] buffer) and halves
    #    # the number of passes over y while preserving the mathematical
    #    # result of the original algorithm.

domain:
    # Recurrence step (outer loop). Must remain sequential.
    k: dim in [0, N)

    # Index within the y / z / r vectors (inner loops).
    i: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # Input autocorrelation sequence r[0..N-1]
    r[i]: in DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i
        # 1D contiguous layout

    # Output vector y[0..N-1], updated in-place across k
    y[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i
        # 1D contiguous layout

    # Temporary buffer of length N used during each k-step
    z[i]: temp DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i
        # 1D contiguous layout
        # NOTE: This matches the original stack-allocated z[N] and does not
        #       increase the asymptotic memory footprint.

parameters:
    # Problem size
    N: int

    # Tunable micro-architecture parameters (for x64 with wide SIMD):
    VEC_WIDTH_I: int  # preferred SIMD width for i-loops, e.g., 8 for AVX2 doubles
    UNROLL_I:   int  # software-unroll factor for i-loops, e.g., 4

    # Scalar state of the Durbin recursion (carried across k-iterations)
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta:  DATA_TYPE

computation:
    # --- Initialization: k = 0 step ---
    init:
        y[0]   = -r[0]
        beta   = 1.0
        alpha  = -r[0]

    # --- Main Durbin recursion: k = 1..N-1, strictly sequential in k ---
    for k in seq([1, N)):

        # 1) Update beta using alpha from previous step
        update_beta(k):
            beta = (1.0 - alpha * alpha) * beta

        # 2) Compute sum_k = Σ_{i=0}^{k-1} r[k-i-1] * y[i]
        #    Expressed as an explicit reduction to expose parallelism and SIMD.
        compute_sum(k):
            sum_k = sum(i in [0, k)) r[k - i - 1] * y[i]

        # 3) Update reflection coefficient alpha_k
        update_alpha(k):
            alpha = -(r[k] + sum_k) / beta

        # 4) Compute new y[0..k-1] into temporary buffer z, using old y
        #    z[i] = y_old[i] + alpha_k * y_old[k-i-1]
        update_z(k):
            for i in [0, k):
                z[i] = y[i] + alpha * y[k - i - 1]

        # 5) Copy the updated prefix back into y
        copy_back(k):
            for i in [0, k):
                y[i] = z[i]

        # 6) Set the new element y[k] = alpha_k
        set_diagonal(k):
            y[k] = alpha

dependencies:
    # Enforce the recursive nature in k and intra-step ordering.
    for k in [1, N):
        init              -> update_beta(k)
        update_beta(k)    -> compute_sum(k)
        compute_sum(k)    -> update_alpha(k)
        update_alpha(k)   -> update_z(k)
        update_z(k)       -> copy_back(k)
        copy_back(k)      -> set_diagonal(k)

    # Successive k-steps are coupled through y, alpha, beta.
    for k in [2, N):
        set_diagonal(k-1) -> update_beta(k)

optimization:
    # --- High-level structure ---
    # Keep k as the outermost and strictly sequential loop because:
    #  - beta(k) depends on alpha(k-1) and beta(k-1),
    #  - alpha(k) depends on y(·, k-1), r, beta(k),
    #  - y(·, k) depends on y(·, k-1) and alpha(k).
    # Thus, no parallelize(k).

    # --- Inner-loop (i) optimizations ---

    # 1) Vectorize and unroll the reduction in compute_sum.
    #    The reduction form exposes that the order over i is not semantically
    #    important (floating-point associativity aside), allowing a tree-based
    #    parallel/SIMD reduction.
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH_I)   # use SIMD for r[k-i-1] * y[i] in compute_sum
    unroll(i, UNROLL_I)         # software-unroll i-loop for better ILP

    # 2) Parallelize the reduction in compute_sum over i using a reduction
    #    scheme (each worker accumulates a private partial sum_k, then a final
    #    merge). This exploits available cores without altering results beyond
    #    FP re-association effects.
    parallelize(i)              # in compute_sum only, as a parallel reduction

    # 3) Vectorize and unroll update_z and copy_back over i.
    #    - update_z has independent iterations in i for fixed k,
    #      so it is trivially vectorizable and parallelizable.
    #    - copy_back is a simple, contiguous copy; perfect for SIMD and
    #      bandwidth utilization.
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH_I)   # reuse same i-vectorization width
    unroll(i, UNROLL_I)

    # 4) Parallelize update_z and copy_back across i.
    #    For fixed k, each y[i] / z[i] pair is independent, so we can safely
    #    distribute work across threads.
    parallelize(i)              # for update_z and copy_back

    # NOTE: We intentionally DO NOT fuse update_z and copy_back into a single
    #       in-place update of y, because the expression
    #           y[i] = y[i] + alpha * y[k - i - 1]
    #       is not safely computable in-place in a simple forward or backward
    #       pass due to the dependence on both y[i] and y[k-i-1] from the
    #       previous step. The explicit temporary z buffer preserves the
    #       original Durbin semantics.

    # --- Memory / layout considerations ---
    # - r, y, and z are kept as 1D contiguous arrays; this already matches
    #   optimal layout for the purely 1D access patterns.
    # - Align r, y, and z to cache-line boundaries (e.g., 64 bytes) in the
    #   implementation to maximize SIMD efficiency and reduce cache-line
    #   splits. (Noted here as an implementation guideline.)

    # This model preserves the original numerical behavior while making
    # the reduction explicit and exposing i-dimension vectorization and
    # parallelism, which improves performance on a modern x64, multi-core,
    # SIMD-capable machine.
--- END OF MODEL: durbin-02 ---

--- START OF MODEL: durbin-03 ---
domain:
    k: dim in [0, N)          # recursion / time dimension
    i: dim in [0, N)          # index within a prefix [0, k)

data:
    # One-dimensional, contiguous arrays (row-major: index -> index)
    r[i]: in DATA_TYPE    = i      # input sequence, length N
    y[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = i      # output sequence, length N
    z[i]: temp DATA_TYPE  = i      # temporary buffer, length N (can be removed by optimization)

    # Scalar temporaries (0-D data)
    alpha: temp DATA_TYPE          # reflection coefficient at current k
    beta:  temp DATA_TYPE          # scaling coefficient at current k
    sum:   temp DATA_TYPE          # accumulator for inner product at current k

parameters:
    n: int                          # actual problem size, 1 <= n <= N

    # Tuning parameters (chosen per target machine)
    VEC_WIDTH:    int              # SIMD width in elements, e.g., 4 (double, AVX2) or 8 (float)
    I_UNROLL:     int = 4          # unroll factor for i-loops
    PAR_THRESHOLD:int              # minimal k for which parallelizing i-loops is beneficial

computation:
    # k = 0 initialization (matches: y[0] = -r[0]; beta = 1.0; alpha = -r[0];)
    INIT_Y0:
        y[0] = -r[0]
    INIT_BETA:
        beta = 1.0
    INIT_ALPHA:
        alpha = -r[0]

    # Durbin recursion for k = 1 .. n-1, strictly sequential in k
    K_LOOP: for k in seq([1, n)):

        # beta_k = (1 - alpha_{k-1}^2) * beta_{k-1}
        UPDATE_BETA(k):
            beta = (1.0 - alpha * alpha) * beta

        # sum = sum_{i=0}^{k-1} r[k-i-1] * y[i]
        SUM(k):
            sum = 0.0
            for i in [0, k):
                sum += r[k - i - 1] * y[i]

        # alpha_k = -(r[k] + sum) / beta_k
        UPDATE_ALPHA(k):
            alpha = -(r[k] + sum) / beta

        # z[i] = y[i] + alpha_k * y[k-i-1],  for i = 0 .. k-1
        Z_UPDATE(k):
            for i in [0, k):
                z[i] = y[i] + alpha * y[k - i - 1]

        # y[i] = z[i],  for i = 0 .. k-1
        Y_COPY(k):
            for i in [0, k):
                y[i] = z[i]

        # y[k] = alpha_k
        SET_DIAG(k):
            y[k] = alpha

optimization:
    # --- Ordering constraints / high-level structure ---
    # The Durbin recursion creates a true dependence chain along k:
    #   (alpha_k, beta_k, y[0..k]) depend on (alpha_{k-1}, beta_{k-1}, y[0..k-1]).
    # Therefore, the k-loop must remain outermost and sequential.
    hoist(k)        # keep k as the outermost loop
    # (No parallelize(k) is allowed.)

    # --- Vectorization and unrolling over i ---
    # All three i-loops (SUM, Z_UPDATE, Y_COPY) have regular, unit-stride
    # access in y and r (up to the index reversal in r). They are amenable
    # to SIMD vectorization and unrolling.
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH)
    unroll(i, I_UNROLL)

    # --- Parallelism over i within each fixed k ---
    # For each fixed k, iterations over i are independent in Z_UPDATE and
    # Y_COPY, and SUM is a reduction over i. We can exploit thread-level
    # parallelism over i once k is large enough to amortize synchronization.
    #
    # Logically:
    #   if k >= PAR_THRESHOLD:
    #       parallel for i in [0, k):    sum += r[k-i-1] * y[i]     (with reduction on sum)
    #       parallel for i in [0, k):    z[i] = y[i] + alpha*y[k-i-1]
    #       parallel for i in [0, k):    y[i] = z[i]
    #
    # Here we express this intent as:
    parallelize(i)  # apply to i-loops inside K_LOOP for k >= PAR_THRESHOLD (reduction for SUM)

    # --- Loop fusion to reduce memory traffic ---
    # The two i-loops Z_UPDATE and Y_COPY are back-to-back over the same
    # iteration space [0, k). They can be fused into a single loop that
    # computes z[i] and immediately stores it back to y[i] (z becomes an
    # SSA temporary whose lifetime is confined to the iteration).
    #
    # Conceptually:
    #   for i in [0, k):
    #       t    = y[i] + alpha*y[k-i-1]
    #       y[i] = t
    #
    # This fusion preserves the original semantics because z[i] is not
    # used outside Y_COPY(k).
    fuse(Z_UPDATE, Y_COPY)

    # --- Optional elimination of the temporary array z ---
    # We can further remove the z array entirely while preserving the
    # mathematical result of Z_UPDATE + Y_COPY, by performing pairwise
    # in-place updates on y that emulate a "simultaneous" update of all
    # entries.
    #
    # For a fixed k, Z_UPDATE + Y_COPY compute (for 0 <= i < k):
    #   y_new[i] = y_old[i] + alpha * y_old[k-1-i]
    #
    # This defines a symmetric pairwise transformation:
    #   Let j = k-1-i. Then for i < j we have the pair:
    #       y_new[i] = y_old[i] + alpha * y_old[j]
    #       y_new[j] = y_old[j] + alpha * y_old[i]
    #
    # Thus we can compute both y_new[i] and y_new[j] from the old values
    # y_old[i], y_old[j] without a temporary array:
    #
    #   for i from 0 to floor((k-1)/2):
    #       j  = k-1-i
    #       yi = y[i]
    #       yj = y[j]
    #       y[i] = yi + alpha * yj
    #       y[j] = yj + alpha * yi
    #
    # If k is odd, the middle index m = (k-1)/2 satisfies m = k-1-m, so:
    #       y[m] = y[m] + alpha * y[m] = (1 + alpha) * y[m]
    #
    # This exactly reproduces the effect of computing z[i] then copying
    # it back to y[i], but avoids:
    #   - the extra pass over z (Y_COPY),
    #   - all loads/stores to z[0..k-1],
    #   - the stack or heap footprint of z.
    #
    # We denote this transformation by a dedicated directive:
    pairwise_inplace_update(y, i, k)   # replaces Z_UPDATE + Y_COPY, removes need for z

    # After applying pairwise_inplace_update, implementations should:
    #   - drop z from the data section,
    #   - keep vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH), unroll(i, I_UNROLL), and parallelize(i)
    #     on the new pairwise i-loop (which now works over roughly k/2 iterations).
--- END OF MODEL: durbin-03 ---

--- START OF MODEL: durbin-04 ---
domain:
    # n = N is the problem size (length of r and y).
    k: dim in [0, N)          # outer Durbin recursion index
    i: dim in [0, N)          # inner index used inside each k-iteration

data:
    # 1D, contiguous (row-major) arrays, assumed non-aliasing.
    r[k]: in DATA_TYPE  = (k) -> k     # input reflection coefficients, length N
    y[k]: inout DATA_TYPE = (k) -> k   # output sequence, length N

    # Conceptual temporary from the original code.  It is eliminated by the
    # "eliminate_temp(z)" optimization (see below) via an in-place symmetric update.
    z[k]: temp DATA_TYPE = (k) -> k

    # Local scalars, kept in registers across the k-loop.
    alpha: local DATA_TYPE
    beta:  local DATA_TYPE
    sum:   local DATA_TYPE

    # Local temporaries used for the in-place y-update (to preserve correctness
    # when eliminating z); these never escape a single i-iteration.
    yi_tmp: local DATA_TYPE
    yj_tmp: local DATA_TYPE

parameters:
    N: int                    # problem size (macro N / _PB_N at runtime)

    # Tunable architecture-dependent constants:
    VLEN_SUM:    int          # SIMD width for SUM's inner loop (e.g., 8 for AVX2 double)
    VLEN_UPDATE: int          # SIMD width for UPDATE_Y
    I_PAR_MIN:   int          # minimum k to start parallelizing inner loops (e.g., 512)

computation:
    # Initialization corresponding to k = 0 in the original kernel.
    INIT:
        y[0] = -r[0]
        beta = 1.0
        alpha = -r[0]

    # Main Durbin recursion.
    LOOP_K:
        for k in seq([1, N)):

            UPDATE_BETA:
                beta = (1.0 - alpha * alpha) * beta

            SUM_INIT:
                sum = 0.0

            # Dot product: sum = Σ_{i=0}^{k-1} r[k - i - 1] * y[i]
            SUM:
                for i in [0, k):
                    sum += r[k - i - 1] * y[i]

            UPDATE_ALPHA:
                alpha = -(r[k] + sum) / beta

            # In the original code, the next two loops are:
            #   for i in [0, k): z[i] = y[i] + alpha * y[k - i - 1];
            #   for i in [0, k): y[i] = z[i];
            #
            # We replace that with an *equivalent in-place symmetric update* over y
            # that uses only two scalar temporaries per iteration and no z[.].
            # This preserves the mathematical effect of the z-buffer while halving
            # y-traffic and removing one full pass over [0, k).
            UPDATE_Y:
                for i in [0, k / 2):
                    yi_tmp = y[i]
                    yj_tmp = y[k - 1 - i]
                    y[i]        = yi_tmp + alpha * yj_tmp
                    y[k - 1 - i] = yj_tmp + alpha * yi_tmp

            # When k is odd, there is a "center" element c = (k - 1) / 2 that
            # is paired with itself in the original formula:
            #   z[c] = y[c] + alpha * y[k - c - 1] = y[c] + alpha * y[c].
            # We apply that update explicitly.
            CENTER:
                if (k % 2 == 1):
                    y[(k - 1) / 2] = y[(k - 1) / 2] + alpha * y[(k - 1) / 2]

            # Finally, set y[k] = alpha for this recursion step.
            SET_YK:
                y[k] = alpha

dependencies:
    # 1. Outer Durbin recursion is strictly sequential in k:
    #    iteration k depends on alpha, beta, and y[0..k-1] from iteration k-1.
    for k in [1, N):
        LOOP_K(k - 1) -> LOOP_K(k)

    # 2. SUM is a scalar reduction over i: each iteration updates "sum"
    #    but does not write to r or y.  All SUM(i) instances for a fixed k
    #    are related only through the associative+commutative reduction on "sum".
    for k in [1, N), i1 in [0, k), i2 in [0, k):
        SUM(i1) -> SUM(i2)    # reduction dependence on "sum" only

    # 3. UPDATE_Y performs pairwise updates on (i, k-1-i) with explicit
    #    scalar temporaries yi_tmp, yj_tmp, so there is no cross-iteration
    #    data dependence between distinct i-values once (i, k-1-i) is considered
    #    a single atomic update.  This makes UPDATE_Y.i parallelizable.

optimization:
    #---------------------------
    # Data layout and alignment
    #---------------------------
    # align(A, B) requests that A's base address be B-byte aligned in memory.
    align(r, 64)
    align(y, 64)

    # Mark r and y as non-aliasing to enable better vectorization and register
    # allocation (equivalent to "restrict" on the C pointers).
    # noalias(A) states that A does not alias any other top-level array.
    noalias(r)
    noalias(y)

    #--------------------------------------------------------------
    # Algorithmic optimization: eliminate the temporary buffer z[]
    #--------------------------------------------------------------
    # eliminate_temp(z) means: if z[.] is used only as an intermediate staging
    # buffer whose contents are immediately copied back into y[.], rewrite the
    # computation so that y[.] is updated directly using scalar temporaries,
    # preserving all data dependencies.  This is reflected in UPDATE_Y/CENTER.
    eliminate_temp(z)

    #--------------------------------------------------
    # SIMD vectorization and unrolling of inner loops
    #--------------------------------------------------
    # vectorize(DIM, FACTOR) requests SIMDization along DIM with width FACTOR.
    # unroll(DIM, FACTOR) requests loop unrolling by FACTOR along DIM.

    # Vectorize the dot-product SUM over i with a reduction on "sum".
    vectorize(SUM.i, VLEN_SUM)
    unroll(SUM.i, 4)

    # Vectorize the symmetric in-place UPDATE_Y over i.
    vectorize(UPDATE_Y.i, VLEN_UPDATE)
    unroll(UPDATE_Y.i, 4)

    #----------------------------------------------
    # Thread-level parallelism on inner dimensions
    #----------------------------------------------
    # parallelize(DIM) parallelizes the iterations of DIM, respecting the
    # declared dependencies.  For SUM, this is a reduction on "sum".
    # For UPDATE_Y, iterations are independent (after the symmetric pairing).
    # I_PAR_MIN is a cutoff to avoid parallel overhead for small k.
    parallelize(SUM.i)       # with reduction(+ : sum), only for k >= I_PAR_MIN
    parallelize(UPDATE_Y.i)  # only for k >= I_PAR_MIN

    #-----------------------------------------
    # Scalar optimizations / instruction use
    #-----------------------------------------
    # scalar_register(x) hints that x should be promoted to a register across
    # the k-loop (scalar replacement of loads/stores).
    scalar_register(alpha)
    scalar_register(beta)

    # use_fma(LABEL) requests generation of fused multiply-add instructions in
    # region LABEL where algebraically legal under the FP model.  Here that
    # mainly targets:
    #   - sum += r[...] * y[...] in SUM
    #   - y[i]  = yi_tmp + alpha * yj_tmp in UPDATE_Y
    #   - y[j]  = yj_tmp + alpha * yi_tmp in UPDATE_Y
    use_fma(SUM)
    use_fma(UPDATE_Y)
--- END OF MODEL: durbin-04 ---

# Optimized high-level model for PolyBench/C durbin

domain:
    k: dim in [0, N)         # outer Durbin recursion index
    i: dim in [0, N)         # inner index (used with k-dependent bounds)

data:
    # 1D, contiguous, row-major layouts
    r[i]: in    DATA_TYPE = i           # input reflection / Toeplitz coefficients
    y[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = i           # solution vector, updated in-place across k

    # Scalar temporaries local to kernel_durbin
    alpha: local DATA_TYPE
    beta:  local DATA_TYPE
    sum:   local DATA_TYPE

parameters:
    N: int                          # problem size (same as PolyBench N)

    # Tunable micro-architecture–dependent parameters
    VF_SUM: int                     # SIMD width for reduction over i
    UF_SUM: int                     # unroll factor for reduction over i
    VF_Y:   int                     # SIMD width for y update over i
    UF_Y:   int                     # unroll factor for y update over i

computation:
    # Initialization corresponds to the prefix of kernel_durbin.
    INIT:
        y[0] = -r[0]
        beta = 1.0
        alpha = -r[0]

    # Main Durbin recursion. The outer k loop is inherently sequential.
    K_LOOP:
        for k in seq([1, N)):

            UPDATE_BETA:
                # Same arithmetic as: beta = (1 - alpha*alpha) * beta;
                beta = (1.0 - alpha * alpha) * beta

            # --- Compute sum_k = sum_{i=0}^{k-1} r[k-i-1] * y[i]
            # Reindexed as r[i] * y[k-i-1] to make r access stride-1.
            REDUCE_SUM:
                sum = 0.0
                for i in [0, k):
                    sum += r[i] * y[k - i - 1]

            UPDATE_ALPHA:
                # Same as: alpha = -(r[k] + sum) / beta;
                alpha = -(r[k] + sum) / beta

            # --- Update y in-place using symmetric pairs (i, k-i-1)
            # Original code:
            #   for i in [0, k): z[i] = y[i] + alpha * y[k-i-1];
            #   for i in [0, k): y[i] = z[i];
            # We eliminate the temporary array z[ ] by computing both
            # new_y[i] and new_y[k-i-1] from the old y-values at once.
            PAIR_UPDATE_Y:
                for i in [0, k / 2):      # integer division, half-open interval
                    t0 = y[i]            # old y[i]
                    t1 = y[k - i - 1]    # old y[k-i-1]

                    y[i]         = t0 + alpha * t1
                    y[k - i - 1] = t1 + alpha * t0

            # For odd k, there is a center element mid = k/2 (integer div)
            # such that mid == k-mid-1. Its update is:
            #   new_y[mid] = old_y[mid] + alpha * old_y[mid]
            #               = (1 + alpha) * old_y[mid].
            CENTER_UPDATE_Y:
                if (k % 2 == 1):
                    mid = k / 2
                    y[mid] = y[mid] * (1.0 + alpha)

            # Append alpha at position k (same as original "y[k] = alpha;").
            SET_TAIL:
                y[k] = alpha

dependencies:
    # Outer recursion must remain sequential in k.
    for k in [1, N):
        # Everything for iteration k depends on completion of iteration k-1.
        SET_TAIL(k - 1) -> UPDATE_BETA(k)

    # Within a fixed k, preserve the original ordering of stages.
    for k in [1, N):
        UPDATE_BETA(k)    -> REDUCE_SUM(k)
        REDUCE_SUM(k)     -> UPDATE_ALPHA(k)
        UPDATE_ALPHA(k)   -> PAIR_UPDATE_Y(k)
        PAIR_UPDATE_Y(k)  -> CENTER_UPDATE_Y(k)
        CENTER_UPDATE_Y(k) -> SET_TAIL(k)

    # The PAIR_UPDATE_Y loop has no cross-iteration dependencies because
    #   iteration i writes exactly { i, k-i-1 },
    #   and for i in [0, k/2) these index sets are disjoint across i.
    # CENTER_UPDATE_Y writes the middle element only (for odd k), which is
    # excluded from the PAIR_UPDATE_Y domain, so there is no interference.

optimization:
    # --- Arithmetic / algorithmic optimizations ---------------------------
    # 1. Use the reindexed reduction:
    #       sum += r[i] * y[k-i-1]
    #    so that accesses to r are stride-1 and cache-friendly.
    # 2. Eliminate the temporary array z[ ] by symmetric in-place updates
    #    on (i, k-i-1) pairs, halving the number of passes over y and
    #    removing an O(N)-sized buffer.

    # --- Vectorization and unrolling -------------------------------------
    # Encourage SIMD for the reduction loop over i. The compiler should
    # implement sum as a vector reduction when k is large.
    vectorize(i, VF_SUM)  # in REDUCE_SUM
    unroll(i, UF_SUM)     # in REDUCE_SUM

    # The symmetric pair update has independent iterations over i, with
    # simple affine accesses, so we can SIMD-ize and unroll it as well.
    vectorize(i, VF_Y)    # in PAIR_UPDATE_Y
    unroll(i, UF_Y)       # in PAIR_UPDATE_Y

    # --- Parallelism ------------------------------------------------------
    # The Durbin recursion is inherently sequential in k, so we do NOT
    # parallelize over k.
    #
    # However, within each k, PAIR_UPDATE_Y has no cross-iteration
    # dependencies (see dependencies section), so it can be safely
    # parallelized across threads. CENTER_UPDATE_Y is scalar and remains
    # sequential.
    #
    # In practice, a runtime or code generator may:
    #   - parallelize(i) only for sufficiently large k to amortize
    #     threading overhead, and
    #   - use static scheduling for good load balance.
    parallelize(i)        # in PAIR_UPDATE_Y
--- END OF MODEL: durbin-05 ---

/* Array initialization. */
static
void init_array (int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(r,N,n))
{
  int i, j;

  for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    {
      r[i] = (n+1-i);
    }
}


/* DCE code. Must scan the entire live-out data.
   Can be used also to check the correctness of the output. */
static
void print_array(int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(y,N,n))

{
  int i;

  POLYBENCH_DUMP_START;
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_BEGIN("y");
  for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (i % 20 == 0) fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, "\n");
    fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, DATA_PRINTF_MODIFIER, y[i]);
  }
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_END("y");
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_FINISH;

/* Main computational kernel. The whole function will be timed,
   including the call and return. */
static
void kernel_durbin[[gnu::flatten, gnu::noinline]](int n,
		   DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(r,N,n),
		   DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(y,N,n))
{
 DATA_TYPE z[N];
 DATA_TYPE alpha;
 DATA_TYPE beta;
 DATA_TYPE sum;

 int i,k;

#pragma scop
 y[0] = -r[0];
 beta = SCALAR_VAL(1.0);
 alpha = -r[0];

 for (k = 1; k < _PB_N; k++) {
   beta = (1-alpha*alpha)*beta;
   sum = SCALAR_VAL(0.0);
   for (i=0; i<k; i++) {
      sum += r[k-i-1]*y[i];
   }
   alpha = - (r[k] + sum)/beta;

   for (i=0; i<k; i++) {
      z[i] = y[i] + alpha*y[k-i-1];
   }
   for (i=0; i<k; i++) {
     y[i] = z[i];
   }
   y[k] = alpha;
 }
#pragma endscop

}


int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
  /* Retrieve problem size. */
  int n = N;

  /* Variable declaration/allocation. */
  POLYBENCH_1D_ARRAY_DECL(r, DATA_TYPE, N, n);
  POLYBENCH_1D_ARRAY_DECL(y, DATA_TYPE, N, n);


  /* Initialize array(s). */
  init_array (n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(r));

  /* Start timer. */
  polybench_start_instruments;

  /* Run kernel. */
  kernel_durbin (n,
		 POLYBENCH_ARRAY(r),
		 POLYBENCH_ARRAY(y));

  /* Stop and print timer. */
  polybench_stop_instruments;
  polybench_print_instruments;

  /* Prevent dead-code elimination. All live-out data must be printed
     by the function call in argument. */
  polybench_prevent_dce(print_array(n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(y)));

  /* Be clean. */
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(r);
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(y);

  return 0;
}

        # 2) Compute sum_k = Σ_{i=0}^{k-1} r[k-i-1] * y[i]

domain:
    k: dim in [0, N)          # recursion / time dimension
    i: dim in [0, N)          # index within a prefix [0, k)

data:
    # One-dimensional, contiguous arrays (row-major: index -> index)
    r[i]: in DATA_TYPE    = i      # input sequence, length N
    y[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = i      # output sequence, length N
    z[i]: temp DATA_TYPE  = i      # temporary buffer, length N (can be removed by optimization)

    # Scalar temporaries (0-D data)
    alpha: temp DATA_TYPE          # reflection coefficient at current k
    beta:  temp DATA_TYPE          # scaling coefficient at current k
    sum:   temp DATA_TYPE          # accumulator for inner product at current k

parameters:
    n: int                          # actual problem size, 1 <= n <= N

    # Tuning parameters (chosen per target machine)
    VEC_WIDTH:    int              # SIMD width in elements, e.g., 4 (double, AVX2) or 8 (float)
    I_UNROLL:     int = 4          # unroll factor for i-loops
    PAR_THRESHOLD:int              # minimal k for which parallelizing i-loops is beneficial

computation:
    # k = 0 initialization (matches: y[0] = -r[0]; beta = 1.0; alpha = -r[0];)
    INIT_Y0:
        y[0] = -r[0]
    INIT_BETA:
        beta = 1.0
    INIT_ALPHA:
        alpha = -r[0]

    # Durbin recursion for k = 1 .. n-1, strictly sequential in k
    K_LOOP: for k in seq([1, n)):

        # beta_k = (1 - alpha_{k-1}^2) * beta_{k-1}
        UPDATE_BETA(k):
            beta = (1.0 - alpha * alpha) * beta

        # sum = sum_{i=0}^{k-1} r[k-i-1] * y[i]
        SUM(k):
            sum = 0.0
            for i in [0, k):
                sum += r[k - i - 1] * y[i]

        # alpha_k = -(r[k] + sum) / beta_k
        UPDATE_ALPHA(k):
            alpha = -(r[k] + sum) / beta

        # z[i] = y[i] + alpha_k * y[k-i-1],  for i = 0 .. k-1
        Z_UPDATE(k):
            for i in [0, k):
                z[i] = y[i] + alpha * y[k - i - 1]

        # y[i] = z[i],  for i = 0 .. k-1
        Y_COPY(k):
            for i in [0, k):
                y[i] = z[i]

        # y[k] = alpha_k
        SET_DIAG(k):
            y[k] = alpha

optimization:
    # --- Ordering constraints / high-level structure ---
    # The Durbin recursion creates a true dependence chain along k:
    #   (alpha_k, beta_k, y[0..k]) depend on (alpha_{k-1}, beta_{k-1}, y[0..k-1]).
    # Therefore, the k-loop must remain outermost and sequential.
    hoist(k)        # keep k as the outermost loop
    # (No parallelize(k) is allowed.)

    # --- Vectorization and unrolling over i ---
    # All three i-loops (SUM, Z_UPDATE, Y_COPY) have regular, unit-stride
    # access in y and r (up to the index reversal in r). They are amenable
    # to SIMD vectorization and unrolling.
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH)
    unroll(i, I_UNROLL)

    # --- Parallelism over i within each fixed k ---
    # For each fixed k, iterations over i are independent in Z_UPDATE and
    # Y_COPY, and SUM is a reduction over i. We can exploit thread-level
    # parallelism over i once k is large enough to amortize synchronization.
    #
    # Logically:
    #   if k >= PAR_THRESHOLD:
    #       parallel for i in [0, k):    sum += r[k-i-1] * y[i]     (with reduction on sum)
    #       parallel for i in [0, k):    z[i] = y[i] + alpha*y[k-i-1]
    #       parallel for i in [0, k):    y[i] = z[i]
    #
    # Here we express this intent as:
    parallelize(i)  # apply to i-loops inside K_LOOP for k >= PAR_THRESHOLD (reduction for SUM)

    # --- Loop fusion to reduce memory traffic ---
    # The two i-loops Z_UPDATE and Y_COPY are back-to-back over the same
    # iteration space [0, k). They can be fused into a single loop that
    # computes z[i] and immediately stores it back to y[i] (z becomes an
    # SSA temporary whose lifetime is confined to the iteration).
    #
    # Conceptually:
    #   for i in [0, k):
    #       t    = y[i] + alpha*y[k-i-1]
    #       y[i] = t
    #
    # This fusion preserves the original semantics because z[i] is not
    # used outside Y_COPY(k).
    fuse(Z_UPDATE, Y_COPY)

    # --- Optional elimination of the temporary array z ---
    # We can further remove the z array entirely while preserving the
    # mathematical result of Z_UPDATE + Y_COPY, by performing pairwise
    # in-place updates on y that emulate a "simultaneous" update of all
    # entries.
    #
    # For a fixed k, Z_UPDATE + Y_COPY compute (for 0 <= i < k):
    #   y_new[i] = y_old[i] + alpha * y_old[k-1-i]
    #
    # This defines a symmetric pairwise transformation:
    #   Let j = k-1-i. Then for i < j we have the pair:
    #       y_new[i] = y_old[i] + alpha * y_old[j]
    #       y_new[j] = y_old[j] + alpha * y_old[i]
    #
    # Thus we can compute both y_new[i] and y_new[j] from the old values
    # y_old[i], y_old[j] without a temporary array:
    #
    #   for i from 0 to floor((k-1)/2):
    #       j  = k-1-i
    #       yi = y[i]
    #       yj = y[j]
    #       y[i] = yi + alpha * yj
    #       y[j] = yj + alpha * yi
    #
    # If k is odd, the middle index m = (k-1)/2 satisfies m = k-1-m, so:
    #       y[m] = y[m] + alpha * y[m] = (1 + alpha) * y[m]
    #
    # This exactly reproduces the effect of computing z[i] then copying
    # it back to y[i], but avoids:
    #   - the extra pass over z (Y_COPY),
    #   - all loads/stores to z[0..k-1],
    #   - the stack or heap footprint of z.
    #
    # We denote this transformation by a dedicated directive:
    pairwise_inplace_update(y, i, k)   # replaces Z_UPDATE + Y_COPY, removes need for z

    # After applying pairwise_inplace_update, implementations should:
    #   - drop z from the data section,
    #   - keep vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH), unroll(i, I_UNROLL), and parallelize(i)
    #     on the new pairwise i-loop (which now works over roughly k/2 iterations).

    alpha: local DATA_TYPE
    beta:  local DATA_TYPE

    yi_tmp: local DATA_TYPE
    yj_tmp: local DATA_TYPE

parameters:
    N: int                    # problem size (macro N / _PB_N at runtime)

    VLEN_SUM:    int          # SIMD width for SUM's inner loop (e.g., 8 for AVX2 double)
    VLEN_UPDATE: int          # SIMD width for UPDATE_Y
    I_PAR_MIN:   int          # minimum k to start parallelizing inner loops (e.g., 512)

computation:
    # Initialization corresponding to k = 0 in the original kernel.
    INIT:
        y[0] = -r[0]
        beta = 1.0
        alpha = -r[0]

    # Main Durbin recursion.
    LOOP_K:
        for k in seq([1, N)):

            UPDATE_BETA:
                beta = (1.0 - alpha * alpha) * beta

            SUM_INIT:
                sum = 0.0

            # Dot product: sum = Σ_{i=0}^{k-1} r[k - i - 1] * y[i]
            SUM:
                for i in [0, k):
                    sum += r[k - i - 1] * y[i]

            UPDATE_ALPHA:
                alpha = -(r[k] + sum) / beta

            # In the original code, the next two loops are:
            #   for i in [0, k): z[i] = y[i] + alpha * y[k - i - 1];
            #   for i in [0, k): y[i] = z[i];
            #
            # We replace that with an *equivalent in-place symmetric update* over y
            # that uses only two scalar temporaries per iteration and no z[.].
            # This preserves the mathematical effect of the z-buffer while halving
            # y-traffic and removing one full pass over [0, k).
            UPDATE_Y:
                for i in [0, k / 2):
                    yi_tmp = y[i]
                    yj_tmp = y[k - 1 - i]
                    y[i]        = yi_tmp + alpha * yj_tmp
                    y[k - 1 - i] = yj_tmp + alpha * yi_tmp

            # When k is odd, there is a "center" element c = (k - 1) / 2 that
            # is paired with itself in the original formula:
            #   z[c] = y[c] + alpha * y[k - c - 1] = y[c] + alpha * y[c].
            # We apply that update explicitly.
            CENTER:
                if (k % 2 == 1):
                    y[(k - 1) / 2] = y[(k - 1) / 2] + alpha * y[(k - 1) / 2]

            # Finally, set y[k] = alpha for this recursion step.
            SET_YK:
                y[k] = alpha

    # 1. Outer Durbin recursion is strictly sequential in k:
    #    iteration k depends on alpha, beta, and y[0..k-1] from iteration k-1.
    for k in [1, N):

    #    but does not write to r or y.  All SUM(i) instances for a fixed k
    #    are related only through the associative+commutative reduction on "sum".
    for k in [1, N), i1 in [0, k), i2 in [0, k):

    align(r, 64)

    noalias(r)
    noalias(y)

    # Algorithmic optimization: eliminate the temporary buffer z[]
    #--------------------------------------------------------------
    # eliminate_temp(z) means: if z[.] is used only as an intermediate staging
    # buffer whose contents are immediately copied back into y[.], rewrite the
    # computation so that y[.] is updated directly using scalar temporaries,
    # preserving all data dependencies.  This is reflected in UPDATE_Y/CENTER.
    eliminate_temp(z)

    # SIMD vectorization and unrolling of inner loops
    #--------------------------------------------------
    # vectorize(DIM, FACTOR) requests SIMDization along DIM with width FACTOR.
    # unroll(DIM, FACTOR) requests loop unrolling by FACTOR along DIM.

    # Vectorize the dot-product SUM over i with a reduction on "sum".
    vectorize(SUM.i, VLEN_SUM)
    unroll(SUM.i, 4)

    # Vectorize the symmetric in-place UPDATE_Y over i.
    vectorize(UPDATE_Y.i, VLEN_UPDATE)
    unroll(UPDATE_Y.i, 4)

    #----------------------------------------------
    # Thread-level parallelism on inner dimensions
    #----------------------------------------------
    # parallelize(DIM) parallelizes the iterations of DIM, respecting the
    # declared dependencies.  For SUM, this is a reduction on "sum".
    # For UPDATE_Y, iterations are independent (after the symmetric pairing).
    # I_PAR_MIN is a cutoff to avoid parallel overhead for small k.
    parallelize(SUM.i)       # with reduction(+ : sum), only for k >= I_PAR_MIN
    parallelize(UPDATE_Y.i)  # only for k >= I_PAR_MIN

    #-----------------------------------------
    # Scalar optimizations / instruction use
    #-----------------------------------------
    # scalar_register(x) hints that x should be promoted to a register across
    # the k-loop (scalar replacement of loads/stores).
    scalar_register(alpha)
    scalar_register(beta)

    # region LABEL where algebraically legal under the FP model.  Here that
    # mainly targets:
    #   - sum += r[...] * y[...] in SUM
    #   - y[i]  = yi_tmp + alpha * yj_tmp in UPDATE_Y
    #   - y[j]  = yj_tmp + alpha * yi_tmp in UPDATE_Y
    use_fma(SUM)
    use_fma(UPDATE_Y)

# Optimized high-level model for PolyBench/C durbin

domain:
    k: dim in [0, N)         # outer Durbin recursion index
    i: dim in [0, N)         # inner index (used with k-dependent bounds)

data:
    # 1D, contiguous, row-major layouts
    r[i]: in    DATA_TYPE = i           # input reflection / Toeplitz coefficients
    y[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = i           # solution vector, updated in-place across k

    # Scalar temporaries local to kernel_durbin
    alpha: local DATA_TYPE
    beta:  local DATA_TYPE
    sum:   local DATA_TYPE

parameters:
    N: int                          # problem size (same as PolyBench N)

    # Tunable micro-architecture–dependent parameters
    VF_SUM: int                     # SIMD width for reduction over i
    UF_SUM: int                     # unroll factor for reduction over i
    VF_Y:   int                     # SIMD width for y update over i
    UF_Y:   int                     # unroll factor for y update over i

computation:
    # Initialization corresponds to the prefix of kernel_durbin.
    INIT:
        y[0] = -r[0]
        beta = 1.0
        alpha = -r[0]

    # Main Durbin recursion. The outer k loop is inherently sequential.
    K_LOOP:
        for k in seq([1, N)):

            UPDATE_BETA:
                # Same arithmetic as: beta = (1 - alpha*alpha) * beta;
                beta = (1.0 - alpha * alpha) * beta

            # --- Compute sum_k = sum_{i=0}^{k-1} r[k-i-1] * y[i]
            # Reindexed as r[i] * y[k-i-1] to make r access stride-1.
            REDUCE_SUM:
                sum = 0.0
                for i in [0, k):
                    sum += r[i] * y[k - i - 1]

            UPDATE_ALPHA:
                # Same as: alpha = -(r[k] + sum) / beta;
                alpha = -(r[k] + sum) / beta

            # --- Update y in-place using symmetric pairs (i, k-i-1)
            # Original code:
            #   for i in [0, k): z[i] = y[i] + alpha * y[k-i-1];
            #   for i in [0, k): y[i] = z[i];
            # We eliminate the temporary array z[ ] by computing both
            # new_y[i] and new_y[k-i-1] from the old y-values at once.
            PAIR_UPDATE_Y:
                for i in [0, k / 2):      # integer division, half-open interval
                    t0 = y[i]            # old y[i]
                    t1 = y[k - i - 1]    # old y[k-i-1]

                    y[i]         = t0 + alpha * t1
                    y[k - i - 1] = t1 + alpha * t0

            # For odd k, there is a center element mid = k/2 (integer div)
            # such that mid == k-mid-1. Its update is:
            #   new_y[mid] = old_y[mid] + alpha * old_y[mid]
            #               = (1 + alpha) * old_y[mid].
            CENTER_UPDATE_Y:
                if (k % 2 == 1):
                    mid = k / 2
                    y[mid] = y[mid] * (1.0 + alpha)

            # Append alpha at position k (same as original "y[k] = alpha;").
            SET_TAIL:
                y[k] = alpha

dependencies:
    # Outer recursion must remain sequential in k.
    for k in [1, N):
        # Everything for iteration k depends on completion of iteration k-1.
        SET_TAIL(k - 1) -> UPDATE_BETA(k)

    # Within a fixed k, preserve the original ordering of stages.
    for k in [1, N):
        UPDATE_BETA(k)    -> REDUCE_SUM(k)
        REDUCE_SUM(k)     -> UPDATE_ALPHA(k)
        UPDATE_ALPHA(k)   -> PAIR_UPDATE_Y(k)
        PAIR_UPDATE_Y(k)  -> CENTER_UPDATE_Y(k)
        CENTER_UPDATE_Y(k) -> SET_TAIL(k)

    # The PAIR_UPDATE_Y loop has no cross-iteration dependencies because
    #   iteration i writes exactly { i, k-i-1 },
    #   and for i in [0, k/2) these index sets are disjoint across i.
    # CENTER_UPDATE_Y writes the middle element only (for odd k), which is
    # excluded from the PAIR_UPDATE_Y domain, so there is no interference.

optimization:
    # --- Arithmetic / algorithmic optimizations ---------------------------
    # 1. Use the reindexed reduction:
    #       sum += r[i] * y[k-i-1]
    #    so that accesses to r are stride-1 and cache-friendly.
    # 2. Eliminate the temporary array z[ ] by symmetric in-place updates
    #    on (i, k-i-1) pairs, halving the number of passes over y and
    #    removing an O(N)-sized buffer.

    # --- Vectorization and unrolling -------------------------------------
    # Encourage SIMD for the reduction loop over i. The compiler should
    # implement sum as a vector reduction when k is large.
    vectorize(i, VF_SUM)  # in REDUCE_SUM
    unroll(i, UF_SUM)     # in REDUCE_SUM

    # The symmetric pair update has independent iterations over i, with
    # simple affine accesses, so we can SIMD-ize and unroll it as well.
    vectorize(i, VF_Y)    # in PAIR_UPDATE_Y
    unroll(i, UF_Y)       # in PAIR_UPDATE_Y

    # --- Parallelism ------------------------------------------------------
    # The Durbin recursion is inherently sequential in k, so we do NOT
    # parallelize over k.
    #
    # However, within each k, PAIR_UPDATE_Y has no cross-iteration
    # dependencies (see dependencies section), so it can be safely
    # parallelized across threads. CENTER_UPDATE_Y is scalar and remains
    # sequential.
    #
    # In practice, a runtime or code generator may:
    #   - parallelize(i) only for sufficiently large k to amortize
    #     threading overhead, and
    #   - use static scheduling for good load balance.
    parallelize(i)        # in PAIR_UPDATE_Y

/* durbin.c: this file is part of PolyBench/C */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Include polybench common header. */
#include <polybench.h>

/* Include benchmark-specific header. */
#include "durbin.h"


/* Array initialization. */
static
void init_array (int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(r,N,n))
{
  int i, j;

  for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    {
      r[i] = (n+1-i);
    }
}


/* DCE code. Must scan the entire live-out data.
   Can be used also to check the correctness of the output. */
static
void print_array(int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(y,N,n))

{
  int i;

  POLYBENCH_DUMP_START;
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_BEGIN("y");
  for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (i % 20 == 0) fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, "\n");
    fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, DATA_PRINTF_MODIFIER, y[i]);
  }
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_END("y");
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_FINISH;
}


/* Main computational kernel. The whole function will be timed,
   including the call and return. */
static
void kernel_durbin[[gnu::flatten, gnu::noinline]](int n,
		   DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(r,N,n),
		   DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(y,N,n))
{
 DATA_TYPE z[N];
 DATA_TYPE alpha;
 DATA_TYPE beta;
 DATA_TYPE sum;

 int i,k;

#pragma scop
 y[0] = -r[0];
 beta = SCALAR_VAL(1.0);
 alpha = -r[0];

 for (k = 1; k < _PB_N; k++) {
   beta = (1-alpha*alpha)*beta;
   sum = SCALAR_VAL(0.0);
   for (i=0; i<k; i++) {
      sum += r[k-i-1]*y[i];
   }
   alpha = - (r[k] + sum)/beta;

   for (i=0; i<k; i++) {
      z[i] = y[i] + alpha*y[k-i-1];
   }
   for (i=0; i<k; i++) {
     y[i] = z[i];
   }
   y[k] = alpha;
 }
#pragma endscop

}


int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
  /* Retrieve problem size. */
  int n = N;

  /* Variable declaration/allocation. */
  POLYBENCH_1D_ARRAY_DECL(r, DATA_TYPE, N, n);
  POLYBENCH_1D_ARRAY_DECL(y, DATA_TYPE, N, n);


  /* Initialize array(s). */
  init_array (n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(r));

  /* Start timer. */
  polybench_start_instruments;

  /* Run kernel. */
  kernel_durbin (n,
		 POLYBENCH_ARRAY(r),
		 POLYBENCH_ARRAY(y));

  /* Stop and print timer. */
  polybench_stop_instruments;
  polybench_print_instruments;

  /* Prevent dead-code elimination. All live-out data must be printed
     by the function call in argument. */
  polybench_prevent_dce(print_array(n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(y)));

  /* Be clean. */
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(r);
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(y);

  return 0;
}

                let j = k - 1 - p
                let yi_old = y[i]
                let yj_old = y[j]

                y[j] = yj_old + alpha * yi_old

domain:
    # Recurrence step (outer loop). Must remain sequential.
    k: dim in [0, N)

    # Index within the y / z / r vectors (inner loops).
    i: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # Input autocorrelation sequence r[0..N-1]
    r[i]: in DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i
        # 1D contiguous layout

    # Output vector y[0..N-1], updated in-place across k
    y[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i
        # 1D contiguous layout

    # Temporary buffer of length N used during each k-step
    z[i]: temp DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i
        # 1D contiguous layout
        # NOTE: This matches the original stack-allocated z[N] and does not
        #       increase the asymptotic memory footprint.

parameters:
    # Problem size
    N: int

    # Tunable micro-architecture parameters (for x64 with wide SIMD):
    VEC_WIDTH_I: int  # preferred SIMD width for i-loops, e.g., 8 for AVX2 doubles
    UNROLL_I:   int  # software-unroll factor for i-loops, e.g., 4

    # Scalar state of the Durbin recursion (carried across k-iterations)
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta:  DATA_TYPE

computation:
    # --- Initialization: k = 0 step ---
    init:
        y[0]   = -r[0]
        beta   = 1.0
        alpha  = -r[0]

    # --- Main Durbin recursion: k = 1..N-1, strictly sequential in k ---
    for k in seq([1, N)):

        # 1) Update beta using alpha from previous step
        update_beta(k):
            beta = (1.0 - alpha * alpha) * beta

        # 2) Compute sum_k = Σ_{i=0}^{k-1} r[k-i-1] * y[i]
        #    Expressed as an explicit reduction to expose parallelism and SIMD.
        compute_sum(k):
            sum_k = sum(i in [0, k)) r[k - i - 1] * y[i]

        # 3) Update reflection coefficient alpha_k
        update_alpha(k):
            alpha = -(r[k] + sum_k) / beta

        # 4) Compute new y[0..k-1] into temporary buffer z, using old y
        #    z[i] = y_old[i] + alpha_k * y_old[k-i-1]
        update_z(k):
            for i in [0, k):
                z[i] = y[i] + alpha * y[k - i - 1]

        # 5) Copy the updated prefix back into y
        copy_back(k):
            for i in [0, k):
                y[i] = z[i]

        # 6) Set the new element y[k] = alpha_k
        set_diagonal(k):
            y[k] = alpha

dependencies:
    # Enforce the recursive nature in k and intra-step ordering.
    for k in [1, N):
        init              -> update_beta(k)
        update_beta(k)    -> compute_sum(k)
        compute_sum(k)    -> update_alpha(k)
        update_alpha(k)   -> update_z(k)
        update_z(k)       -> copy_back(k)
        copy_back(k)      -> set_diagonal(k)

    # Successive k-steps are coupled through y, alpha, beta.
    for k in [2, N):
        set_diagonal(k-1) -> update_beta(k)

optimization:
    # --- High-level structure ---
    # Keep k as the outermost and strictly sequential loop because:
    #  - beta(k) depends on alpha(k-1) and beta(k-1),
    #  - alpha(k) depends on y(·, k-1), r, beta(k),
    #  - y(·, k) depends on y(·, k-1) and alpha(k).
    # Thus, no parallelize(k).

    # --- Inner-loop (i) optimizations ---

    # 1) Vectorize and unroll the reduction in compute_sum.
    #    The reduction form exposes that the order over i is not semantically
    #    important (floating-point associativity aside), allowing a tree-based
    #    parallel/SIMD reduction.
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH_I)   # use SIMD for r[k-i-1] * y[i] in compute_sum
    unroll(i, UNROLL_I)         # software-unroll i-loop for better ILP

    #      so it is trivially vectorizable and parallelizable.
    #    - copy_back is a simple, contiguous copy; perfect for SIMD and
    #      bandwidth utilization.
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH_I)   # reuse same i-vectorization width
    unroll(i, UNROLL_I)

    #    For fixed k, each y[i] / z[i] pair is independent, so we can safely
    #    distribute work across threads.
    parallelize(i)              # for update_z and copy_back

    #       pass due to the dependence on both y[i] and y[k-i-1] from the
    #       previous step. The explicit temporary z buffer preserves the
    #       original Durbin semantics.

    # --- Memory / layout considerations ---
    # - r, y, and z are kept as 1D contiguous arrays; this already matches
    #   optimal layout for the purely 1D access patterns.
    # - Align r, y, and z to cache-line boundaries (e.g., 64 bytes) in the
    #   implementation to maximize SIMD efficiency and reduce cache-line

    # This model preserves the original numerical behavior while making
    # the reduction explicit and exposing i-dimension vectorization and
    # parallelism, which improves performance on a modern x64, multi-core,
    # SIMD-capable machine.
--- END OF MODEL: durbin-02 ---

domain:

    i: dim in [0, N)          # index within a prefix [0, k)

data:
    # One-dimensional, contiguous arrays (row-major: index -> index)
    r[i]: in DATA_TYPE    = i      # input sequence, length N
    y[i]: inout DATA_TYPE = i      # output sequence, length N
    z[i]: temp DATA_TYPE  = i      # temporary buffer, length N (can be removed by optimization)

    # Scalar temporaries (0-D data)
    alpha: temp DATA_TYPE          # reflection coefficient at current k
    beta:  temp DATA_TYPE          # scaling coefficient at current k
    sum:   temp DATA_TYPE          # accumulator for inner product at current k

parameters:
    n: int                          # actual problem size, 1 <= n <= N

    # Tuning parameters (chosen per target machine)
    VEC_WIDTH:    int              # SIMD width in elements, e.g., 4 (double, AVX2) or 8 (float)
    I_UNROLL:     int = 4          # unroll factor for i-loops
    PAR_THRESHOLD:int              # minimal k for which parallelizing i-loops is beneficial

computation:
    # k = 0 initialization (matches: y[0] = -r[0]; beta = 1.0; alpha = -r[0];)
    INIT_Y0:
        y[0] = -r[0]
    INIT_BETA:
        beta = 1.0
    INIT_ALPHA:
        alpha = -r[0]

    # Durbin recursion for k = 1 .. n-1, strictly sequential in k
    K_LOOP: for k in seq([1, n)):

        # beta_k = (1 - alpha_{k-1}^2) * beta_{k-1}
        UPDATE_BETA(k):
            beta = (1.0 - alpha * alpha) * beta

        # sum = sum_{i=0}^{k-1} r[k-i-1] * y[i]
        SUM(k):
            sum = 0.0
            for i in [0, k):
                sum += r[k - i - 1] * y[i]

        # alpha_k = -(r[k] + sum) / beta_k
        UPDATE_ALPHA(k):
            alpha = -(r[k] + sum) / beta

        # z[i] = y[i] + alpha_k * y[k-i-1],  for i = 0 .. k-1
        Z_UPDATE(k):
            for i in [0, k):
                z[i] = y[i] + alpha * y[k - i - 1]

        # y[i] = z[i],  for i = 0 .. k-1
        Y_COPY(k):
            for i in [0, k):
                y[i] = z[i]

        # y[k] = alpha_k
        SET_DIAG(k):
            y[k] = alpha

optimization:
    # --- Ordering constraints / high-level structure ---
    # The Durbin recursion creates a true dependence chain along k:
    #   (alpha_k, beta_k, y[0..k]) depend on (alpha_{k-1}, beta_{k-1}, y[0..k-1]).
    # Therefore, the k-loop must remain outermost and sequential.
    hoist(k)        # keep k as the outermost loop
    # (No parallelize(k) is allowed.)

    # --- Vectorization and unrolling over i ---
    # All three i-loops (SUM, Z_UPDATE, Y_COPY) have regular, unit-stride
    # access in y and r (up to the index reversal in r). They are amenable
    # to SIMD vectorization and unrolling.
    vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH)
    unroll(i, I_UNROLL)

    # --- Parallelism over i within each fixed k ---
    # For each fixed k, iterations over i are independent in Z_UPDATE and
    # Y_COPY, and SUM is a reduction over i. We can exploit thread-level
    # parallelism over i once k is large enough to amortize synchronization.
    #
    # Logically:
    #   if k >= PAR_THRESHOLD:
    #       parallel for i in [0, k):    sum += r[k-i-1] * y[i]     (with reduction on sum)
    #       parallel for i in [0, k):    z[i] = y[i] + alpha*y[k-i-1]
    #       parallel for i in [0, k):    y[i] = z[i]
    #
    # Here we express this intent as:
    parallelize(i)  # apply to i-loops inside K_LOOP for k >= PAR_THRESHOLD (reduction for SUM)

    # --- Loop fusion to reduce memory traffic ---
    # The two i-loops Z_UPDATE and Y_COPY are back-to-back over the same
    # iteration space [0, k). They can be fused into a single loop that
    # computes z[i] and immediately stores it back to y[i] (z becomes an
    # SSA temporary whose lifetime is confined to the iteration).
    #
    # Conceptually:
    #   for i in [0, k):
    #       t    = y[i] + alpha*y[k-i-1]
    #       y[i] = t
    #
    # This fusion preserves the original semantics because z[i] is not
    # used outside Y_COPY(k).
    fuse(Z_UPDATE, Y_COPY)

    # --- Optional elimination of the temporary array z ---
    # We can further remove the z array entirely while preserving the
    # mathematical result of Z_UPDATE + Y_COPY, by performing pairwise
    # in-place updates on y that emulate a "simultaneous" update of all
    # entries.
    #
    # For a fixed k, Z_UPDATE + Y_COPY compute (for 0 <= i < k):
    #   y_new[i] = y_old[i] + alpha * y_old[k-1-i]
    #
    # This defines a symmetric pairwise transformation:
    #   Let j = k-1-i. Then for i < j we have the pair:
    #       y_new[i] = y_old[i] + alpha * y_old[j]
    #       y_new[j] = y_old[j] + alpha * y_old[i]
    #
    # Thus we can compute both y_new[i] and y_new[j] from the old values
    # y_old[i], y_old[j] without a temporary array:
    #
    #   for i from 0 to floor((k-1)/2):
    #       j  = k-1-i
    #       yi = y[i]
    #       yj = y[j]
    #       y[i] = yi + alpha * yj
    #       y[j] = yj + alpha * yi
    #
    # If k is odd, the middle index m = (k-1)/2 satisfies m = k-1-m, so:
    #       y[m] = y[m] + alpha * y[m] = (1 + alpha) * y[m]
    #
    # This exactly reproduces the effect of computing z[i] then copying
    # it back to y[i], but avoids:
    #   - the extra pass over z (Y_COPY),
    #   - all loads/stores to z[0..k-1],
    #   - the stack or heap footprint of z.
    #
    # We denote this transformation by a dedicated directive:
    pairwise_inplace_update(y, i, k)   # replaces Z_UPDATE + Y_COPY, removes need for z

    # After applying pairwise_inplace_update, implementations should:
    #   - drop z from the data section,
    #   - keep vectorize(i, VEC_WIDTH), unroll(i, I_UNROLL), and parallelize(i)
    #     on the new pairwise i-loop (which now works over roughly k/2 iterations).
--- END OF MODEL: durbin-03 ---

domain:
    # n = N is the problem size (length of r and y).
    k: dim in [0, N)          # outer Durbin recursion index

    # 1D, contiguous (row-major) arrays, assumed non-aliasing.
    r[k]: in DATA_TYPE  = (k) -> k     # input reflection coefficients, length N
    y[k]: inout DATA_TYPE = (k) -> k   # output sequence, length N

    # "eliminate_temp(z)" optimization (see below) via an in-place symmetric update.
    z[k]: temp DATA_TYPE = (k) -> k

    alpha: local DATA_TYPE
    beta:  local DATA_TYPE
    sum:   local DATA_TYPE

    # Local temporaries used for the in-place y-update (to preserve correctness
    # when eliminating z); these never escape a single i-iteration.
    yi_tmp: local DATA_TYPE
    yj_tmp: local DATA_TYPE

    N: int                    # problem size (macro N / _PB_N at runtime)

    # Tunable architecture-dependent constants:
    VLEN_SUM:    int          # SIMD width for SUM's inner loop (e.g., 8 for AVX2 double)
    VLEN_UPDATE: int          # SIMD width for UPDATE_Y
    I_PAR_MIN:   int          # minimum k to start parallelizing inner loops (e.g., 512)
