domain:
    # Time and space dimensions
    t: dim in [0, TMAX)
    i: dim in [0, NX)
    j: dim in [0, NY)

data:
    # All 2D fields are stored row-major as in the C code: a[i][j] -> i * NY + j.
    ex[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j   # electric field component Ex
    ey[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j   # electric field component Ey
    hz[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j   # magnetic field component Hz

    # Fictitious source term, 1D in time, contiguous
    _fict_[t]: in DATA_TYPE = (t) -> t

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (match NX, NY, TMAX in C)
    NX: int
    NY: int
    TMAX: int

    # Numeric constants (factored out to enable reuse and FMA)
    c_e:  DATA_TYPE  # typically SCALAR_VAL(0.5)
    c_h:  DATA_TYPE  # typically SCALAR_VAL(0.7)

    # Tunable blocking / vectorization parameters (chosen per hardware)
    Ti: int  # tile size in i (e.g., 32 or 64)
    Tj: int  # tile size in j (e.g., 256 or 512)
    Vj: int  # SIMD width along j (e.g., 4 for AVX2 double, 8 for AVX2 float)
    Uj: int  # unroll factor along j (e.g., 4 or 8)

computation:
    # Time-stepping loop; strictly sequential due to dependence across t.
    for t in seq[0, TMAX):
        # 1) Ey boundary condition at i = 0
        ey_boundary(t):
            for j in [0, NY):
                ey[0, j] = _fict_[t]

        # 2) Ey update for i >= 1
        ey_update(t):
            for i in [1, NX), j in [0, NY):
                ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - c_e * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])

        # 3) Ex update for j >= 1
        ex_update(t):
            for i in [0, NX), j in [1, NY):
                ex[i, j] = ex[i, j] - c_e * (hz[i, j] - hz[i, j - 1])

        # 4) Hz update on interior points (i < NX-1, j < NY-1)
        hz_update(t):
            for i in [0, NX - 1), j in [0, NY - 1):
                hz[i, j] = hz[i, j] - c_h * (
                    (ex[i, j + 1] - ex[i, j]) +
                    (ey[i + 1, j] - ey[i, j])
                )

dependencies:
    # Time is strictly ordered; each step t+1 uses fields updated at t.
    for t in [0, TMAX - 1]:
        ey_boundary(t) -> ey_boundary(t + 1)
        ey_update(t)   -> ey_update(t + 1)
        ex_update(t)   -> ex_update(t + 1)
        hz_update(t)   -> hz_update(t + 1)

        # Within a given time step t:
        # Hz(t) must see the Ey and Ex values updated at time t.
        ey_boundary(t) -> hz_update(t)
        ey_update(t)   -> hz_update(t)
        ex_update(t)   -> hz_update(t)

    # Within each spatial loop at fixed t, different (i, j) iterations are independent:
    # - ey updates use only hz (read-only in this step) and ey[i,j] itself.
    # - ex updates use only hz (read-only) and ex[i,j] itself.
    # - hz updates use only hz[i,j] itself and Ex/Ey (read-only in this step).
    # This permits parallelization and vectorization over i and j.

optimization:
    # --- Parallelization -----------------------------------------------------
    # Exploit spatial parallelism; keep t sequential.
    parallelize(i)   # distribute rows across threads
    parallelize(j)   # allow 2D decomposition or parallelization of j-only loops

    # --- Spatial blocking (tiling) for cache locality -----------------------
    # Tile the 2D spatial domain so that tiles of ex/ey/hz fit into fast caches.
    block(i, I, Ti)  # i = I * Ti + i_inner
    block(j, J, Tj)  # j = J * Tj + j_inner

    # Reorder inner loops to get 2D tiles with unit-stride access in j:
    # Resulting order per time step: for I, for J, for i, for j.
    interchange(J, i)

    # --- Vectorization and unrolling along j (unit-stride dimension) --------
    # j is contiguous in memory; vectorize and unroll inner j loops.
    vectorize(j, Vj)
    unroll(j, Uj)

    # --- Loop fusion for reduced memory traffic ------------------------------
    # Fuse the two Ey passes (boundary and interior) into one i-j loop:
    # This reduces the number of sweeps over ey and improves cache behavior,
    # while preserving semantics (ey(0, *) set from _fict_[t], others updated).
    #
    # for i in [0, NX), j in [0, NY):
    #     if i == 0:
    #         ey[0, j] = _fict_[t]
    #     else:
    #         ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - c_e * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])
    #
    # We express this as a suggested transformation:
    fuse(ey_boundary, ey_update)  # # fuse loops labeled ey_boundary and ey_update

    # --- Arithmetic and load-use optimizations (conceptual) ------------------
    # # Use FMAs where available:
    #   ex[i,j] = fma(-c_e, (hz[i,j] - hz[i,j-1]), ex[i,j])
    #   ey[i,j] = fma(-c_e, (hz[i,j] - hz[i-1,j]), ey[i,j])
    #   hz[i,j] = fma(-c_h, ( (ex[i,j+1]-ex[i,j]) + (ey[i+1,j]-ey[i,j]) ), hz[i,j])
    #
    # # Scalar replacement of common loads inside j-loops:
    #   - Keep hz[i,j] and neighboring ex/ey values in registers as j advances
    #     to avoid reloading them from memory.
    # These are local code-generation choices that preserve the above semantics
    # and require no additional large buffers (only scalars), keeping extra
    # memory usage well below the allowed 50% overhead.
--- END OF MODEL: fdtd-2d-02 ---

--- START OF MODEL: fdtd-2d-03 ---
domain:
    # Problem sizes (compile-time constants or runtime parameters)
    t: dim in [0, TMAX)        # time steps
    i: dim in [0, NX)          # spatial x-dimension (rows)
    j: dim in [0, NY)          # spatial y-dimension (columns)

data:
    # All 2D fields are stored in row-major order: [i][j] -> i * NY + j
    ex[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j
    ey[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j
    hz[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j

    # Time-dependent boundary-driving signal
    _fict_[t]: in DATA_TYPE = (t) -> t

parameters:
    # Physical/algorithmic constants (compile-time or runtime tunables)
    cey:  DATA_TYPE = 0.5      # factor used in ex/ey updates
    chz:  DATA_TYPE = 0.7      # factor used in hz update

    # Tuning parameters for performance (chosen based on hardware)
    TI:   int                  # tile size in i (e.g., 32 or 64)
    TJ:   int                  # tile size in j (e.g., 64 or 128)
    V:    int                  # SIMD vector width in elements (e.g., 8 for AVX2 double)
    UJ:   int                  # unroll factor for inner j loops (e.g., 4)

computation:
    # Time stepping is strictly sequential because each step depends
    # on the fields produced by the previous step.
    for t in seq([0, TMAX)):

        # 1. Boundary condition on ey at i = 0 (first row).
        ey_boundary:
            let bc = _fict_[t]
            for j in [0, NY):
                ey[0, j] = bc

        # 2. Update ey for interior rows: finite difference in i, using hz.
        #    Reads:  ey[i, j] (old), hz[i, j], hz[i-1, j]
        #    Writes: ey[i, j] (new)
        ey_update:
            for i in [1, NX):
                for j in [0, NY):
                    ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - cey * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])

        # 3. Update ex for interior columns: finite difference in j, using hz.
        #    Reads:  ex[i, j] (old), hz[i, j], hz[i, j-1]
        #    Writes: ex[i, j] (new)
        ex_update:
            for i in [0, NX):
                for j in [1, NY):
                    ex[i, j] = ex[i, j] - cey * (hz[i, j] - hz[i, j - 1])

        # 4. Update hz in the interior: curl of (ex, ey).
        #    Uses newly updated ex and ey, and previous hz value.
        #    Reads:  hz[i, j] (old),
        #            ex[i, j], ex[i, j+1],
        #            ey[i, j], ey[i+1, j]
        #    Writes: hz[i, j] (new)
        hz_update:
            for i in [0, NX - 1):
                for j in [0, NY - 1):
                    hz[i, j] = hz[i, j]
                               - chz * ( (ex[i, j + 1] - ex[i, j])
                                       + (ey[i + 1, j] - ey[i, j]) )

dependencies:
    # Intra-time-step:
    #   - ey_boundary produces ey[0, *] used by hz_update at i = 0.
    #   - ey_update produces ey[i, *] used by hz_update at i and i-1.
    #   - ex_update produces ex[i, *] used by hz_update at j and j-1.
    # These are already enforced by the lexical order of the labeled
    # regions within each time step.
    for t in [0, TMAX), i in [0, NX), j in [0, NY):
        ey_boundary(t, j) -> hz_update(t, 0, j)           # where 0 ≤ j < NY-1
        ey_update(t, i, j) -> hz_update(t, i, j)          # where 0 ≤ i < NX-1, 0 ≤ j < NY-1
        ey_update(t, i, j) -> hz_update(t, i - 1, j)      # where 1 ≤ i < NX-1, 0 ≤ j < NY-1
        ex_update(t, i, j) -> hz_update(t, i, j)          # where 0 ≤ i < NX-1, 0 ≤ j < NY-1
        ex_update(t, i, j) -> hz_update(t, i, j - 1)      # where 0 ≤ i < NX-1, 1 ≤ j < NY-1

    # Inter-time-step:
    # The full state (ex, ey, hz) produced by time step t is used as input
    # to time step t+1. This enforces sequential execution along t and
    # prevents time-parallelization without more advanced wavefront schemes.
    for t in [0, TMAX - 1):
        hz_update(t, i, j) -> ey_boundary(t + 1, j)   # all i, j (conceptually: step t finishes before step t+1)

optimization:
    # 1. Spatial tiling (blocking) in i and j for better cache locality.
    #    Applies to the large 2D loops ey_update, ex_update, hz_update.
    #    TI and TJ should be chosen so that 3 * TI * TJ * sizeof(DATA_TYPE)
    #    comfortably fits into L1/L2 cache per core.
    block(i, iB, TI)      # tile i into outer tile index iB and inner i
    block(j, jB, TJ)      # tile j into outer tile index jB and inner j

    # Hoist tile loops (iB, jB) to be outermost among spatial loops
    # inside a fixed time step, so each tile is processed contiguously.
    hoist(iB)
    hoist(jB)

    # 2. Parallelization across space:
    #    There are no loop-carried dependencies along i or j within
    #    a given stage, so we can parallelize over outer spatial tiles.
    #    Time loop t remains sequential because of inter-step dependencies.
    parallelize(iB)       # distribute tiles (rows) across threads

    # 3. Vectorization and unrolling in the innermost j dimension:
    #    Arrays are row-major, so j varies over contiguous memory.
    #    Vectorizing j exploits SIMD units efficiently.
    vectorize(j, V)       # e.g., V = 8 for AVX2 double, 16 for AVX2 float
    unroll(j, UJ)         # small unroll (e.g., 4) to reduce loop overhead

    # 4. Scalar hoisting within each time step:
    #    The boundary-driving value _fict_[t] is invariant over j.
    #    We already expressed this as a local variable 'bc' in
    #    ey_boundary; this corresponds to load hoisting into a register.
    # (Implicit from the 'let bc = _fict_[t]' in computation.)

    # 5. No extra large temporaries:
    #    The computation updates ex, ey, hz in-place as in the original
    #    code. No additional 2D buffers are introduced, keeping the
    #    memory footprint within the original size (well under +50%).
--- END OF MODEL: fdtd-2d-03 ---

--- START OF MODEL: fdtd-2d-04 ---
domain:
    # Time and 2D space dimensions
    t: dim in [0, TMAX)       # physical time steps
    i: dim in [0, NX)         # x-direction
    j: dim in [0, NY)         # y-direction

data:
    # All 2D fields are stored row-major: inner dimension j is contiguous in memory.
    ex[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j   # electric field component Ex
    ey[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j   # electric field component Ey
    hz[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j   # magnetic field component Hz

    _fict_[t]: in DATA_TYPE = (t) -> t                 # boundary-driving waveform

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (match PolyBench macros / runtime values)
    TMAX: int   # number of time steps
    NX:   int   # grid size in x
    NY:   int   # grid size in y

    # Pre-scaled constants (SCALAR_VAL(0.5) and SCALAR_VAL(0.7))
    c_e: DATA_TYPE = SCALAR_VAL(0.5)   # scaling for E-field updates
    c_h: DATA_TYPE = SCALAR_VAL(0.7)   # scaling for H-field update

    # Tunable optimization parameters (chosen empirically for the target machine)
    BI:   int   # tile size in i (e.g., 32 or 64)
    BJ:   int   # tile size in j (e.g., 64 or 128)
    VEC:  int   # SIMD width in j (e.g., 8 for AVX2 double, 16 for AVX512 single)

computation:
    # Time stepping: must remain sequential in t due to dependence hz(t) -> hz(t+1)
    for t in seq [0, TMAX):

        # 1. Boundary condition on Ey at i = 0 (top row).
        E_BNDY:
            for j in [0, NY):
                ey[0, j] = _fict_[t]

        # 2. Ex update on row i = 0 (uses hz[0, j] - hz[0, j-1]).
        #    This is separated so that interior (i >= 1) Ex and Ey can be fused.
        EX_ROW0:
            for j in [1, NY):
                ex[0, j] = ex[0, j] - c_e * (hz[0, j] - hz[0, j - 1])

        # 3. Fused interior E-field update for i >= 1.
        #    - Updates Ey(i, j) using vertical difference of Hz: hz[i, j] - hz[i-1, j]
        #    - Updates Ex(i, j) using horizontal difference of Hz: hz[i, j] - hz[i, j-1]
        #    This fusion reduces the number of loads of hz[i, j] from 2 to 1 per cell
        #    compared to two separate passes, while preserving semantics.
        E_INTERIOR:
            for i in [1, NX):
                # j = 0 column: only Ey is updated here
                ey[i, 0] = ey[i, 0] - c_e * (hz[i, 0] - hz[i - 1, 0])

                # j >= 1: update both Ey and Ex, reusing hz[i, j]
                for j in [1, NY):
                    ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - c_e * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])
                    ex[i, j] = ex[i, j] - c_e * (hz[i, j] - hz[i, j - 1])

        # 4. Hz update over the interior stencil domain.
        #    Note the use of updated Ex and Ey from this time step, and old Hz.
        H_UPDATE:
            for i in [0, NX - 1):        # equivalent to 0 <= i < NX-1
                for j in [0, NY - 1):    # equivalent to 0 <= j < NY-1
                    # Precompute local differences to expose reuse and simplify codegen.
                    d_ex = ex[i, j + 1] - ex[i, j]
                    d_ey = ey[i + 1, j] - ey[i, j]
                    hz[i, j] = hz[i, j] - c_h * (d_ex + d_ey)

dependencies:
    # Within each time step t, the stages must execute in order:
    for t in [0, TMAX):
        E_BNDY(t)    -> EX_ROW0(t)
        EX_ROW0(t)   -> E_INTERIOR(t)
        E_INTERIOR(t)-> H_UPDATE(t)

    # Time dependence: Hz at step t+1 depends on Hz, Ex, Ey at step t.
    for t in [0, TMAX - 1):
        H_UPDATE(t)  -> E_BNDY(t + 1)

optimization:
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Spatial blocking to improve cache locality
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Block the i and j dimensions so that tiles of ex, ey, hz
    # for one time step fit well in L2/L3 cache.  Each tile of size
    # BI x BJ touches 3 fields (ex, ey, hz) and their neighbors.
    block(i, I, BI)
    block(j, J, BJ)

    # Hoist tile loops I, J outside the inner j loops so that
    # the computation iterates over tiles in (I, J) order, and
    # within each tile, over the inner i, j.
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelization
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelize over spatial tiles I for each time step t.
    # t remains sequential due to the temporal dependency chain.
    # All per-tile updates (E_BNDY, EX_ROW0, E_INTERIOR, H_UPDATE)
    # are pointwise in space and have no write-write conflicts.
    parallelize(I)

    # Optionally, for very large NY and moderate NX, we can also
    # parallelize over J tiles or use a 2D decomposition:
    # parallelize((I, J))

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Vectorization and unrolling
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # j is the innermost index and corresponds to contiguous memory;
    # it is the natural candidate for SIMD vectorization.
    vectorize(j, VEC)

    # Slight unrolling of j improves ILP and reduces loop control overhead.
    # The compiler can tune the exact factor; 4 is a reasonable default.
    unroll(j, 4)

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Arithmetic simplifications
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # c_e and c_h are hoisted scalars; all loops reuse them from registers.
    # The fused E_INTERIOR loop already computes the central value hz[i, j]
    # once and reuses it for both vertical and horizontal differences.
    #
    # No further algebraic rearrangement is applied, to preserve the
    # original floating-point roundoff behavior as closely as possible.
--- END OF MODEL: fdtd-2d-04 ---

--- START OF MODEL: fdtd-2d-05 ---
domain:
    t: dim in [0, TMAX)
    i: dim in [0, NX)
    j: dim in [0, NY)

data:
    # All 2D fields are stored row-major: inner dimension j is unit-stride.
    ex[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j
    ey[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j
    hz[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j

    # Fictitious boundary values are a 1D array, contiguous in memory.
    _fict_[t]: in DATA_TYPE = (t) -> t

    # Scalar temporary, used to hoist _fict_[t] out of the inner loop.
    ft: tmp DATA_TYPE

parameters:
    # Physical/scalar parameters (match SCALAR_VAL constants in the C code).
    cey: DATA_TYPE   # = 0.5
    chz: DATA_TYPE   # = 0.7

    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters.
    I_TILE: int      # typical values: 64–256, tuned to L2/L3 cache
    J_TILE: int      # typical values: 64–256, tuned to cache line / page size
    VEC_WIDTH: int   # SIMD width in elements (e.g., 4 for double AVX2, 8 for float AVX2)

computation:
    # Time stepping is inherently sequential: each step t reads fields updated at step t-1.
    for t in seq(0, TMAX):

        # Hoist the boundary value _fict_[t] into a scalar to avoid reloading it per j.
        FT_LOAD:
            ft = _fict_[t]

        # 1) Impose boundary condition on ey at i = 0:
        #    ey(0, j) = _fict_[t] for all j.
        for j in [0, NY):
            EY_BC:
                ey[0, j] = ft

        # 2) Update ey for i in [1, NX):
        #    ey(i, j) <- ey(i, j) - 0.5 * (hz(i, j) - hz(i-1, j)).
        #    Reads only old hz; no cross-(i,j) dependencies in ey, fully data-parallel.
        for i in [1, NX), j in [0, NY):
            EY_UPDATE:
                ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - cey * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])

        # 3) Update ex for j in [1, NY):
        #    ex(i, j) <- ex(i, j) - 0.5 * (hz(i, j) - hz(i, j-1)).
        #    Reads only old hz; again no cross-(i,j) dependencies in ex.
        for i in [0, NX), j in [1, NY):
            EX_UPDATE:
                ex[i, j] = ex[i, j] - cey * (hz[i, j] - hz[i, j - 1])

        # 4) Update hz on the interior [0, NX-1) × [0, NY-1):
        #    hz(i, j) <- hz(i, j) - 0.7 * [(ex(i, j+1) - ex(i, j))
        #                                  + (ey(i+1, j) - ey(i, j))].
        #    Uses the *new* ex and ey from steps (2) and (3).
        for i in [0, NX - 1), j in [0, NY - 1):
            HZ_UPDATE:
                hz[i, j] = hz[i, j] - chz * (
                               (ex[i, j + 1] - ex[i, j]) +
                               (ey[i + 1, j] - ey[i, j])
                           )

optimization:
    # --- Spatial blocking (tiling) ---
    # Split the spatial dimensions into tiles to improve cache locality for each sweep.
    # This keeps smaller i×j blocks of ex/ey/hz in cache while streaming through them.
    block(i, ii, I_TILE)   # ii: tile index in x-direction, i: intra-tile index
    block(j, jj, J_TILE)   # jj: tile index in y-direction, j: intra-tile index

    # --- Parallelism ---
    # Time dimension t stays sequential due to true dependences across time steps.
    # Within a single time step, tiles in ii are independent for all three updates,
    # so we parallelize over ii (outer tile) to exploit multicore hardware.
    parallelize(ii)

    # --- SIMD vectorization ---
    # The inner j-dimension is unit-stride in memory (row-major layout), which is ideal
    # for SIMD. Vectorize j in all sweeps and in the ey boundary initialization.
    vectorize(j, VEC_WIDTH)

    # --- Loop unrolling ---
    # Unroll j inside tiles to increase ILP and reduce loop overhead; this works in
    # addition to vectorization (the compiler can generate wider/unrolled SIMD loops).
    unroll(j, 4)

    # Notes:
    #  - The ordering of phases within each time step (EY_BC → EY_UPDATE → EX_UPDATE
    #    → HZ_UPDATE) is preserved exactly, ensuring functional equivalence with the
    #    original C code.
    #  - Parallelization is applied only to spatial tiles (ii), which are provably
    #    independent because each (i, j) point is written exactly once per phase and
    #    there are no intra-phase neighbor dependences in the written arrays.
    #  - Blocking(i, j) is per-sweep; more aggressive cross-sweep fusion/tiling
    #    (to reuse ex/ey tiles immediately when updating hz) is possible but not
    #    modeled here to keep the schedule simple and explicit.
--- END OF MODEL: fdtd-2d-05 ---

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Include polybench common header. */
#include <polybench.h>

/* Include benchmark-specific header. */
#include "fdtd-2d.h"


/* Array initialization. */
static
void init_array (int tmax,
		 int nx,
		 int ny,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(ex,NX,NY,nx,ny),
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(ey,NX,NY,nx,ny),
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(hz,NX,NY,nx,ny),
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(_fict_,TMAX,tmax))
{
  int i, j;

  for (i = 0; i < tmax; i++)
    _fict_[i] = (DATA_TYPE) i;
  for (i = 0; i < nx; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < ny; j++)
      {
	ex[i][j] = ((DATA_TYPE) i*(j+1)) / nx;
	ey[i][j] = ((DATA_TYPE) i*(j+2)) / ny;
	hz[i][j] = ((DATA_TYPE) i*(j+3)) / nx;
      }
}


/* DCE code. Must scan the entire live-out data.
   Can be used also to check the correctness of the output. */
static
void print_array(int nx,
		 int ny,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(ex,NX,NY,nx,ny),
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(ey,NX,NY,nx,ny),
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(hz,NX,NY,nx,ny))
{
  int i, j;

  POLYBENCH_DUMP_START;
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_BEGIN("ex");
  for (i = 0; i < nx; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < ny; j++) {
      if ((i * nx + j) % 20 == 0) fprintf(POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, "\n");
      fprintf(POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, DATA_PRINTF_MODIFIER, ex[i][j]);
    }
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_END("ex");
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_FINISH;

  POLYBENCH_DUMP_BEGIN("ey");
  for (i = 0; i < nx; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < ny; j++) {
      if ((i * nx + j) % 20 == 0) fprintf(POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, "\n");
      fprintf(POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, DATA_PRINTF_MODIFIER, ey[i][j]);
    }
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_END("ey");

  POLYBENCH_DUMP_BEGIN("hz");
  for (i = 0; i < nx; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < ny; j++) {
      if ((i * nx + j) % 20 == 0) fprintf(POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, "\n");
      fprintf(POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, DATA_PRINTF_MODIFIER, hz[i][j]);
    }
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_END("hz");
}


/* Main computational kernel. The whole function will be timed,
   including the call and return. */
static
void kernel_fdtd_2d[[gnu::flatten, gnu::noinline]](int tmax,
		    int nx,
		    int ny,
		    DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(ex,NX,NY,nx,ny),
		    DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(ey,NX,NY,nx,ny),
		    DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(hz,NX,NY,nx,ny),
		    DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_1D(_fict_,TMAX,tmax))
{
  int t, i, j;

#pragma scop

  for(t = 0; t < _PB_TMAX; t++)
    {
      for (j = 0; j < _PB_NY; j++)
	ey[0][j] = _fict_[t];
      for (i = 1; i < _PB_NX; i++)
	for (j = 0; j < _PB_NY; j++)
	  ey[i][j] = ey[i][j] - SCALAR_VAL(0.5)*(hz[i][j]-hz[i-1][j]);
      for (i = 0; i < _PB_NX; i++)
	for (j = 1; j < _PB_NY; j++)
	  ex[i][j] = ex[i][j] - SCALAR_VAL(0.5)*(hz[i][j]-hz[i][j-1]);
      for (i = 0; i < _PB_NX - 1; i++)
	for (j = 0; j < _PB_NY - 1; j++)
	  hz[i][j] = hz[i][j] - SCALAR_VAL(0.7)*  (ex[i][j+1] - ex[i][j] +
				       ey[i+1][j] - ey[i][j]);
    }

#pragma endscop
}


int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
  /* Retrieve problem size. */
  int tmax = TMAX;
  int nx = NX;
  int ny = NY;

    hz[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j   # magnetic field component Hz

    _fict_[t]: in DATA_TYPE = (t) -> t

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (match NX, NY, TMAX in C)
    NX: int
    NY: int
    TMAX: int

    c_e:  DATA_TYPE  # typically SCALAR_VAL(0.5)
    c_h:  DATA_TYPE  # typically SCALAR_VAL(0.7)

    # Tunable blocking / vectorization parameters (chosen per hardware)
    Ti: int  # tile size in i (e.g., 32 or 64)
    Tj: int  # tile size in j (e.g., 256 or 512)
    Vj: int  # SIMD width along j (e.g., 4 for AVX2 double, 8 for AVX2 float)
    Uj: int  # unroll factor along j (e.g., 4 or 8)

computation:
    # Time-stepping loop; strictly sequential due to dependence across t.
    for t in seq[0, TMAX):
        # 1) Ey boundary condition at i = 0
        ey_boundary(t):
            for j in [0, NY):
                ey[0, j] = _fict_[t]

        # 2) Ey update for i >= 1
        ey_update(t):
            for i in [1, NX), j in [0, NY):
                ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - c_e * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])

        # 3) Ex update for j >= 1
        ex_update(t):
            for i in [0, NX), j in [1, NY):
                ex[i, j] = ex[i, j] - c_e * (hz[i, j] - hz[i, j - 1])

        # 4) Hz update on interior points (i < NX-1, j < NY-1)
        hz_update(t):
            for i in [0, NX - 1), j in [0, NY - 1):
                hz[i, j] = hz[i, j] - c_h * (
                    (ex[i, j + 1] - ex[i, j]) +
                    (ey[i + 1, j] - ey[i, j])
                )

dependencies:
    # Time is strictly ordered; each step t+1 uses fields updated at t.
    for t in [0, TMAX - 1]:
        ey_boundary(t) -> ey_boundary(t + 1)
        ey_update(t)   -> ey_update(t + 1)
        ex_update(t)   -> ex_update(t + 1)
        hz_update(t)   -> hz_update(t + 1)

        # Within a given time step t:
        # Hz(t) must see the Ey and Ex values updated at time t.
        ey_boundary(t) -> hz_update(t)
        ey_update(t)   -> hz_update(t)
        ex_update(t)   -> hz_update(t)

    # Within each spatial loop at fixed t, different (i, j) iterations are independent:
    # - ey updates use only hz (read-only in this step) and ey[i,j] itself.
    # - ex updates use only hz (read-only) and ex[i,j] itself.
    # - hz updates use only hz[i,j] itself and Ex/Ey (read-only in this step).

    block(j, J, Tj)  # j = J * Tj + j_inner

    # j is contiguous in memory; vectorize and unroll inner j loops.
    vectorize(j, Vj)
    unroll(j, Uj)

    # Fuse the two Ey passes (boundary and interior) into one i-j loop:
    # This reduces the number of sweeps over ey and improves cache behavior,
    # while preserving semantics (ey(0, *) set from _fict_[t], others updated).

    #     else:
    #         ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - c_e * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])
    #
    # We express this as a suggested transformation:

    # # Use FMAs where available:
    #   ex[i,j] = fma(-c_e, (hz[i,j] - hz[i,j-1]), ex[i,j])
    #   ey[i,j] = fma(-c_e, (hz[i,j] - hz[i-1,j]), ey[i,j])
    #   hz[i,j] = fma(-c_h, ( (ex[i,j+1]-ex[i,j]) + (ey[i+1,j]-ey[i,j]) ), hz[i,j])

    #     to avoid reloading them from memory.
    # These are local code-generation choices that preserve the above semantics
    # and require no additional large buffers (only scalars), keeping extra
    # memory usage well below the allowed 50% overhead.

domain:
    # Problem sizes (compile-time constants or runtime parameters)
    t: dim in [0, TMAX)        # time steps
    i: dim in [0, NX)          # spatial x-dimension (rows)
    j: dim in [0, NY)          # spatial y-dimension (columns)

data:
    # All 2D fields are stored in row-major order: [i][j] -> i * NY + j
    ex[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j
    ey[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j
    hz[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j

    # Time-dependent boundary-driving signal
    _fict_[t]: in DATA_TYPE = (t) -> t

parameters:
    # Physical/algorithmic constants (compile-time or runtime tunables)
    cey:  DATA_TYPE = 0.5      # factor used in ex/ey updates
    chz:  DATA_TYPE = 0.7      # factor used in hz update

    # Tuning parameters for performance (chosen based on hardware)
    TI:   int                  # tile size in i (e.g., 32 or 64)
    TJ:   int                  # tile size in j (e.g., 64 or 128)
    V:    int                  # SIMD vector width in elements (e.g., 8 for AVX2 double)
    UJ:   int                  # unroll factor for inner j loops (e.g., 4)

computation:
    # Time stepping is strictly sequential because each step depends
    # on the fields produced by the previous step.
    for t in seq([0, TMAX)):

        # 1. Boundary condition on ey at i = 0 (first row).
        ey_boundary:
            let bc = _fict_[t]
            for j in [0, NY):
                ey[0, j] = bc

        # 2. Update ey for interior rows: finite difference in i, using hz.
        #    Reads:  ey[i, j] (old), hz[i, j], hz[i-1, j]
        #    Writes: ey[i, j] (new)
        ey_update:
            for i in [1, NX):
                for j in [0, NY):
                    ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - cey * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])

        # 3. Update ex for interior columns: finite difference in j, using hz.
        #    Reads:  ex[i, j] (old), hz[i, j], hz[i, j-1]
        #    Writes: ex[i, j] (new)
        ex_update:
            for i in [0, NX):
                for j in [1, NY):
                    ex[i, j] = ex[i, j] - cey * (hz[i, j] - hz[i, j - 1])

        # 4. Update hz in the interior: curl of (ex, ey).
        #    Uses newly updated ex and ey, and previous hz value.
        #    Reads:  hz[i, j] (old),
        #            ex[i, j], ex[i, j+1],
        #            ey[i, j], ey[i+1, j]
        #    Writes: hz[i, j] (new)
        hz_update:
            for i in [0, NX - 1):
                for j in [0, NY - 1):
                    hz[i, j] = hz[i, j]
                               - chz * ( (ex[i, j + 1] - ex[i, j])
                                       + (ey[i + 1, j] - ey[i, j]) )

dependencies:
    # Intra-time-step:
    #   - ey_boundary produces ey[0, *] used by hz_update at i = 0.
    #   - ey_update produces ey[i, *] used by hz_update at i and i-1.
    #   - ex_update produces ex[i, *] used by hz_update at j and j-1.
    # These are already enforced by the lexical order of the labeled
    # regions within each time step.
    for t in [0, TMAX), i in [0, NX), j in [0, NY):
        ey_boundary(t, j) -> hz_update(t, 0, j)           # where 0 ≤ j < NY-1
        ey_update(t, i, j) -> hz_update(t, i, j)          # where 0 ≤ i < NX-1, 0 ≤ j < NY-1
        ey_update(t, i, j) -> hz_update(t, i - 1, j)      # where 1 ≤ i < NX-1, 0 ≤ j < NY-1
        ex_update(t, i, j) -> hz_update(t, i, j)          # where 0 ≤ i < NX-1, 0 ≤ j < NY-1
        ex_update(t, i, j) -> hz_update(t, i, j - 1)      # where 0 ≤ i < NX-1, 1 ≤ j < NY-1

    # Inter-time-step:
    # The full state (ex, ey, hz) produced by time step t is used as input
    # to time step t+1. This enforces sequential execution along t and
    # prevents time-parallelization without more advanced wavefront schemes.
    for t in [0, TMAX - 1):
        hz_update(t, i, j) -> ey_boundary(t + 1, j)   # all i, j (conceptually: step t finishes before step t+1)

optimization:
    # 1. Spatial tiling (blocking) in i and j for better cache locality.
    #    Applies to the large 2D loops ey_update, ex_update, hz_update.
    #    TI and TJ should be chosen so that 3 * TI * TJ * sizeof(DATA_TYPE)
    #    comfortably fits into L1/L2 cache per core.
    block(i, iB, TI)      # tile i into outer tile index iB and inner i
    block(j, jB, TJ)      # tile j into outer tile index jB and inner j

    # Hoist tile loops (iB, jB) to be outermost among spatial loops
    # inside a fixed time step, so each tile is processed contiguously.
    hoist(iB)
    hoist(jB)

    # 2. Parallelization across space:
    #    There are no loop-carried dependencies along i or j within
    #    a given stage, so we can parallelize over outer spatial tiles.
    #    Time loop t remains sequential because of inter-step dependencies.
    parallelize(iB)       # distribute tiles (rows) across threads

    # 3. Vectorization and unrolling in the innermost j dimension:
    #    Arrays are row-major, so j varies over contiguous memory.
    #    Vectorizing j exploits SIMD units efficiently.
    vectorize(j, V)       # e.g., V = 8 for AVX2 double, 16 for AVX2 float
    unroll(j, UJ)         # small unroll (e.g., 4) to reduce loop overhead

    # 4. Scalar hoisting within each time step:
    #    The boundary-driving value _fict_[t] is invariant over j.
    #    We already expressed this as a local variable 'bc' in
    #    ey_boundary; this corresponds to load hoisting into a register.
    # (Implicit from the 'let bc = _fict_[t]' in computation.)

    # 5. No extra large temporaries:
    #    The computation updates ex, ey, hz in-place as in the original
    #    code. No additional 2D buffers are introduced, keeping the
    #    memory footprint within the original size (well under +50%).
--- END OF MODEL: fdtd-2d-03 ---

--- START OF MODEL: fdtd-2d-04 ---
domain:
    # Time and 2D space dimensions
    t: dim in [0, TMAX)       # physical time steps
    i: dim in [0, NX)         # x-direction
    j: dim in [0, NY)         # y-direction

data:
    # All 2D fields are stored row-major: inner dimension j is contiguous in memory.
    ex[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j   # electric field component Ex
    ey[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j   # electric field component Ey
    hz[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * NY + j   # magnetic field component Hz

    _fict_[t]: in DATA_TYPE = (t) -> t                 # boundary-driving waveform

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (match PolyBench macros / runtime values)
    TMAX: int   # number of time steps
    NX:   int   # grid size in x
    NY:   int   # grid size in y

    # Pre-scaled constants (SCALAR_VAL(0.5) and SCALAR_VAL(0.7))
    c_e: DATA_TYPE = SCALAR_VAL(0.5)   # scaling for E-field updates
    c_h: DATA_TYPE = SCALAR_VAL(0.7)   # scaling for H-field update

    # Tunable optimization parameters (chosen empirically for the target machine)
    BI:   int   # tile size in i (e.g., 32 or 64)
    BJ:   int   # tile size in j (e.g., 64 or 128)
    VEC:  int   # SIMD width in j (e.g., 8 for AVX2 double, 16 for AVX512 single)

computation:
    # Time stepping: must remain sequential in t due to dependence hz(t) -> hz(t+1)
    for t in seq [0, TMAX):

        # 1. Boundary condition on Ey at i = 0 (top row).
        E_BNDY:
            for j in [0, NY):
                ey[0, j] = _fict_[t]

        # 2. Ex update on row i = 0 (uses hz[0, j] - hz[0, j-1]).
        #    This is separated so that interior (i >= 1) Ex and Ey can be fused.
        EX_ROW0:
            for j in [1, NY):
                ex[0, j] = ex[0, j] - c_e * (hz[0, j] - hz[0, j - 1])

        # 3. Fused interior E-field update for i >= 1.
        #    - Updates Ey(i, j) using vertical difference of Hz: hz[i, j] - hz[i-1, j]
        #    - Updates Ex(i, j) using horizontal difference of Hz: hz[i, j] - hz[i, j-1]
        #    This fusion reduces the number of loads of hz[i, j] from 2 to 1 per cell
        #    compared to two separate passes, while preserving semantics.
        E_INTERIOR:
            for i in [1, NX):
                # j = 0 column: only Ey is updated here
                ey[i, 0] = ey[i, 0] - c_e * (hz[i, 0] - hz[i - 1, 0])

                # j >= 1: update both Ey and Ex, reusing hz[i, j]
                for j in [1, NY):
                    ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - c_e * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])
                    ex[i, j] = ex[i, j] - c_e * (hz[i, j] - hz[i, j - 1])

        # 4. Hz update over the interior stencil domain.
        #    Note the use of updated Ex and Ey from this time step, and old Hz.
        H_UPDATE:
            for i in [0, NX - 1):        # equivalent to 0 <= i < NX-1
                for j in [0, NY - 1):    # equivalent to 0 <= j < NY-1
                    # Precompute local differences to expose reuse and simplify codegen.
                    d_ex = ex[i, j + 1] - ex[i, j]
                    d_ey = ey[i + 1, j] - ey[i, j]
                    hz[i, j] = hz[i, j] - c_h * (d_ex + d_ey)

dependencies:
    # Within each time step t, the stages must execute in order:
    for t in [0, TMAX):
        E_BNDY(t)    -> EX_ROW0(t)
        EX_ROW0(t)   -> E_INTERIOR(t)
        E_INTERIOR(t)-> H_UPDATE(t)

    # Time dependence: Hz at step t+1 depends on Hz, Ex, Ey at step t.
    for t in [0, TMAX - 1):
        H_UPDATE(t)  -> E_BNDY(t + 1)

optimization:
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Spatial blocking to improve cache locality
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Block the i and j dimensions so that tiles of ex, ey, hz
    # for one time step fit well in L2/L3 cache.  Each tile of size
    # BI x BJ touches 3 fields (ex, ey, hz) and their neighbors.
    block(i, I, BI)
    block(j, J, BJ)

    # Hoist tile loops I, J outside the inner j loops so that
    # the computation iterates over tiles in (I, J) order, and
    # within each tile, over the inner i, j.
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelization
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelize over spatial tiles I for each time step t.
    # t remains sequential due to the temporal dependency chain.
    # All per-tile updates (E_BNDY, EX_ROW0, E_INTERIOR, H_UPDATE)
    # are pointwise in space and have no write-write conflicts.
    parallelize(I)

    # Optionally, for very large NY and moderate NX, we can also
    # parallelize over J tiles or use a 2D decomposition:
    # parallelize((I, J))

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Vectorization and unrolling
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # j is the innermost index and corresponds to contiguous memory;
    # it is the natural candidate for SIMD vectorization.
    vectorize(j, VEC)

    # Slight unrolling of j improves ILP and reduces loop control overhead.
    # The compiler can tune the exact factor; 4 is a reasonable default.
    unroll(j, 4)

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Arithmetic simplifications
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # c_e and c_h are hoisted scalars; all loops reuse them from registers.
    # The fused E_INTERIOR loop already computes the central value hz[i, j]
    # once and reuses it for both vertical and horizontal differences.
    #
    # No further algebraic rearrangement is applied, to preserve the
    # original floating-point roundoff behavior as closely as possible.
--- END OF MODEL: fdtd-2d-04 ---

    _fict_[t]: in DATA_TYPE = (t) -> t

    # Scalar temporary, used to hoist _fict_[t] out of the inner loop.
    ft: tmp DATA_TYPE

parameters:
    # Physical/scalar parameters (match SCALAR_VAL constants in the C code).
    cey: DATA_TYPE   # = 0.5
    chz: DATA_TYPE   # = 0.7

    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters.
    I_TILE: int      # typical values: 64–256, tuned to L2/L3 cache
    J_TILE: int      # typical values: 64–256, tuned to cache line / page size
    VEC_WIDTH: int   # SIMD width in elements (e.g., 4 for double AVX2, 8 for float AVX2)

computation:
    # Time stepping is inherently sequential: each step t reads fields updated at step t-1.
    for t in seq(0, TMAX):

        # Hoist the boundary value _fict_[t] into a scalar to avoid reloading it per j.
        FT_LOAD:
            ft = _fict_[t]

        # 1) Impose boundary condition on ey at i = 0:
        #    ey(0, j) = _fict_[t] for all j.
        for j in [0, NY):
            EY_BC:
                ey[0, j] = ft

        # 2) Update ey for i in [1, NX):
        #    ey(i, j) <- ey(i, j) - 0.5 * (hz(i, j) - hz(i-1, j)).
        #    Reads only old hz; no cross-(i,j) dependencies in ey, fully data-parallel.
        for i in [1, NX), j in [0, NY):
            EY_UPDATE:
                ey[i, j] = ey[i, j] - cey * (hz[i, j] - hz[i - 1, j])

        # 3) Update ex for j in [1, NY):
        #    ex(i, j) <- ex(i, j) - 0.5 * (hz(i, j) - hz(i, j-1)).
        #    Reads only old hz; again no cross-(i,j) dependencies in ex.
        for i in [0, NX), j in [1, NY):
            EX_UPDATE:
                ex[i, j] = ex[i, j] - cey * (hz[i, j] - hz[i, j - 1])

        # 4) Update hz on the interior [0, NX-1) × [0, NY-1):
        #    hz(i, j) <- hz(i, j) - 0.7 * [(ex(i, j+1) - ex(i, j))
        #                                  + (ey(i+1, j) - ey(i, j))].
        #    Uses the *new* ex and ey from steps (2) and (3).
        for i in [0, NX - 1), j in [0, NY - 1):
            HZ_UPDATE:
                hz[i, j] = hz[i, j] - chz * (
                               (ex[i, j + 1] - ex[i, j]) +
                               (ey[i + 1, j] - ey[i, j])
                           )

optimization:
    # --- Spatial blocking (tiling) ---
    # Split the spatial dimensions into tiles to improve cache locality for each sweep.
    # This keeps smaller i×j blocks of ex/ey/hz in cache while streaming through them.
    block(i, ii, I_TILE)   # ii: tile index in x-direction, i: intra-tile index
    block(j, jj, J_TILE)   # jj: tile index in y-direction, j: intra-tile index

    # --- Parallelism ---
    # Time dimension t stays sequential due to true dependences across time steps.
    # Within a single time step, tiles in ii are independent for all three updates,
    # so we parallelize over ii (outer tile) to exploit multicore hardware.
    parallelize(ii)

    # --- SIMD vectorization ---
    # The inner j-dimension is unit-stride in memory (row-major layout), which is ideal
    # for SIMD. Vectorize j in all sweeps and in the ey boundary initialization.
    vectorize(j, VEC_WIDTH)

    # --- Loop unrolling ---
    # Unroll j inside tiles to increase ILP and reduce loop overhead; this works in
    # addition to vectorization (the compiler can generate wider/unrolled SIMD loops).
    unroll(j, 4)

    # Notes:
    #  - The ordering of phases within each time step (EY_BC → EY_UPDATE → EX_UPDATE
    #    → HZ_UPDATE) is preserved exactly, ensuring functional equivalence with the
    #    original C code.
    #  - Parallelization is applied only to spatial tiles (ii), which are provably
    #    independent because each (i, j) point is written exactly once per phase and
    #    there are no intra-phase neighbor dependences in the written arrays.
    #  - Blocking(i, j) is per-sweep; more aggressive cross-sweep fusion/tiling
    #    (to reuse ex/ey tiles immediately when updating hz) is possible but not
    #    modeled here to keep the schedule simple and explicit.
--- END OF MODEL: fdtd-2d-05 ---

/* floyd-warshall.c: this file is part of PolyBench/C */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Include polybench common header. */
#include <polybench.h>

/* Include benchmark-specific header. */
#include "floyd-warshall.h"


/* Array initialization. */
static
void init_array (int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(path,N,N,n,n))
{
  int i, j;

  for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++) {
      path[i][j] = i*j%7+1;
      if ((i+j)%13 == 0 || (i+j)%7==0 || (i+j)%11 == 0)
         path[i][j] = 999;
    }
}


/* DCE code. Must scan the entire live-out data.
   Can be used also to check the correctness of the output. */
static
void print_array(int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(path,N,N,n,n))

{
  int i, j;

  POLYBENCH_DUMP_START;
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_BEGIN("path");
  for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++) {
      if ((i * n + j) % 20 == 0) fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, "\n");
      fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, DATA_PRINTF_MODIFIER, path[i][j]);
    }
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_END("path");
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_FINISH;
}


/* Main computational kernel. The whole function will be timed,
   including the call and return. */
static
void kernel_floyd_warshall[[gnu::flatten, gnu::noinline]](int n,
			   DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(path,N,N,n,n))
{
  int i, j, k;

#pragma scop
  for (k = 0; k < _PB_N; k++)
    {
      for(i = 0; i < _PB_N; i++)
	for (j = 0; j < _PB_N; j++)
	  path[i][j] = path[i][j] < path[i][k] + path[k][j] ?
	    path[i][j] : path[i][k] + path[k][j];
    }
#pragma endscop

}


int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
  /* Retrieve problem size. */
  int n = N;

  /* Variable declaration/allocation. */
  POLYBENCH_2D_ARRAY_DECL(path, DATA_TYPE, N, N, n, n);


  /* Initialize array(s). */
  init_array (n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(path));

  /* Start timer. */
  polybench_start_instruments;

  /* Run kernel. */
  kernel_floyd_warshall (n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(path));

  /* Stop and print timer. */
  polybench_stop_instruments;
  polybench_print_instruments;

  /* Prevent dead-code elimination. All live-out data must be printed
     by the function call in argument. */
  polybench_prevent_dce(print_array(n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(path)));

  /* Be clean. */
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(path);

  return 0;
}

parameters:

    TJ: int  # tile size along j (e.g., 64)
    TK: int  # tile size along k (e.g., 16 or 32)

    UJ: int  # unroll factor for the innermost j loop (multiple of VJ, e.g., 2 or 4)

computation:
    # Floyd–Warshall all-pairs shortest paths.
    # Semantics: for each intermediate vertex k in sequence, relax all pairs (i, j).
    FW_UPDATE:
      for k in seq([0, N)):      # k must be executed sequentially
        for i, j:               # (i, j) for a fixed k can be done in any order
          if path[i, k] + path[k, j] < path[i, j]:
            path[i, j] = path[i, k] + path[k, j]

dependencies:
    # Dynamic-programming dependence across k:
    #   All updates for step k must observe the results of all updates from step k-1.
    for k in [1, N), i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        FW_UPDATE(k-1, *, *) -> FW_UPDATE(k, i, j)

    # No dependences between different (i, j) at the same k in this high-level model,
    # so the (i, j) space at fixed k may be freely reordered and parallelized.

optimization:
    # ---------------- Cache blocking / tiling ----------------
    # Tile the spatial (i, j) dimensions so that a TI x TJ tile of path
    # fits into L1/L2 cache while sweeping over a small block of k values.
    block(i, I, TI)   # i = I * TI + ii, where ii is the new inner i
    block(j, J, TJ)   # j = J * TJ + jj

    # Tile the k loop into blocks as well, but keep the overall k dimension
    # strictly sequential to preserve the DP order.
    block(k, K, TK)   # k = K * TK + kk

    # Hoist tile loops to form a six-deep, cache-friendly nest:
    #   for K  in seq([0, ceil(N/TK))):
    #     for I in     [0, ceil(N/TI))):
    #       for J in   [0, ceil(N/TJ))):
    #         for kk in seq([0, TK)):
    #           for ii in [0, TI):
    #             for jj in [0, TJ):
    #               ... FW update on (i = I*TI+ii, j = J*TJ+jj, k = K*TK+kk) ...
    hoist(K)
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    # This preserves the original sequential order in k but improves temporal
    # locality for tiles of path[i, j] and the k-th row/column accessed within
    # each (K, I, J) tile.

    # ---------------- Parallelism ----------------
    # At fixed k (and thus fixed K, kk), all (i, j) updates are independent
    # in this model, so we can parallelize over tiles of i (and optionally j).
    parallelize(I)
    # Optionally, if the runtime and hardware support nested parallelism well:
    # parallelize(J)

    # ---------------- Vectorization & unrolling ----------------
    # Vectorize and unroll along the innermost j dimension, which is
    # contiguous in memory due to row-major layout.
    vectorize(j, VJ)
    unroll(j, UJ)

    # ---------------- Scalar replacement / register promotion ----------------
    # For fixed (k, i), the value path[i, k] is invariant across all j in the
    # inner tile. Load it once into a scalar register and reuse it, instead of
    # reloading from memory for every j.
    #
    # New optimization directive (explained by this comment):
    #   scalar_replace(EXPR):
    #       Replace repeated loads of EXPR that is invariant in an inner
    #       dimension by a single scalar variable, live across that dimension.
    #
    scalar_replace(path[i, k])

    # ---------------- Additional low-level considerations (conceptual) ----------------
    # - Ensure 'path' is aligned (e.g., to 64 bytes) to maximize SIMD efficiency.

    #   kk, ii, jj tiles hot in cache.
    # - Do NOT parallelize or reorder across K/kk beyond simple tiling; k remains
    #   sequential to respect the dynamic-programming dependence across k.

domain:
    # Problem size: single parameter N defining an N×N graph.
    i: dim in [0, N)
    j: dim in [0, N)
    k: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # Distance / adjacency matrix (initialized by init_array, updated in-place).
    path[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
        # Row-major layout: path[i][j] is contiguous in j.

    # Scratch buffers reused for every k-iteration.
    # They hold a snapshot of row k and column k from path at the *start* of iteration k.
    row_k[j]: temp DATA_TYPE = j -> j
        # Length-N buffer: row_k[j] ≈ path[k][j] at the beginning of the current k-step.
    col_k[i]: temp DATA_TYPE = i -> i
        # Length-N buffer: col_k[i] ≈ path[i][k] at the beginning of the current k-step.

parameters:
    N: int                     # Number of vertices

computation:
    # Floyd–Warshall all-pairs shortest paths.
    #
    # We adopt the standard dynamic-programming formulation:
    #   D^(k)[i, j] = min( D^(k-1)[i, j],
    #                     D^(k-1)[i, k] + D^(k-1)[k, j] )
    # and implement it using per-k snapshots of row k and column k.
    # This removes intra-k loop-carried dependences and exposes parallelism,
    # while remaining equivalent to the original kernel for all inputs.

    for k in seq[0, N):    # k must remain sequential (DP over increasing set of intermediates)
        # 1. Snapshot row k and column k of path at the beginning of iteration k.
        #    These are read-only during the UPDATE phase.
        SNAPSHOT_ROW:
        for j in seq[0, N):
            row_k[j] = path[k, j]
        SNAPSHOT_COL:
        for i in seq[0, N):
            col_k[i] = path[i, k]

        # 2. Relax all pairs (i, j) using the snapshots.
        #    Once row_k[] and col_k[] are materialized, each (i, j) update is independent:
        #      path[i, j] ← min( path[i, j], col_k[i] + row_k[j] )
        #    so the (i, j) space can be tiled, reordered and parallelized freely.
        UPDATE:
        for i in [0, N):
            col_i: DATA_TYPE = col_k[i]     # Hoist col_k[i] out of inner loop to reduce repeated loads
            for j in [0, N):
                new_dist: DATA_TYPE = col_i + row_k[j]
                path[i, j] = path[i, j] < new_dist ? path[i, j] : new_dist


dependencies:
    # 1. Dynamic programming dependence along k:
    #    iteration k consumes the result of iteration k-1.
    for k in [1, N), i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        UPDATE(k-1, i, j) -> SNAPSHOT_ROW(k)
        UPDATE(k-1, i, j) -> SNAPSHOT_COL(k)

    # 2. Within a fixed k:
    #    SNAPSHOT_ROW(k) and SNAPSHOT_COL(k) must complete before UPDATE(k, i, j) starts.
    for k in [0, N), i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        SNAPSHOT_ROW(k) -> UPDATE(k, i, j)
        SNAPSHOT_COL(k) -> UPDATE(k, i, j)

    # 3. After snapshots are taken, all UPDATE(k, i, j) are independent for fixed k.
    #    There are no dependencies between distinct (i, j) at the same k in UPDATE.


optimization:
    # ---------- Memory-access and locality optimizations ----------

    # Keep k outermost and sequential; all other transformations apply inside each k.
    # This preserves the Floyd–Warshall DP structure.

    # Block the (i, j) iteration space in UPDATE to improve cache locality and create
    # coarser parallel tasks. This does *not* change the global (k, i, j) ordering,
    # only decomposes i and j into tiles.
    #
    # BI, BJ are tuning parameters (e.g., 32–128) chosen so that:
    #   BI * BJ * sizeof(DATA_TYPE) fits comfortably into L1/L2.
    block(i, I, BI)      # Split i into tile index I and intra-tile i
    block(j, J, BJ)      # Split j into tile index J and intra-tile j

    # Row-major layout makes j the stride-1 dimension; keep j innermost in UPDATE
    # so that path[i, j] and row_k[j] are accessed contiguously, enabling SIMD loads/stores.

    # ---------- Parallelism ----------

    # After SNAPSHOT_ROW and SNAPSHOT_COL are done at a given k, UPDATE(k, i, j) has
    # no cross-(i, j) dependences. We can parallelize the outer tile dimension I
    # (or i directly) to exploit multi-core hardware.
    #
    # Parallelization is per-k: each k-step runs UPDATE in parallel, but different
    # k-steps remain sequential due to DP dependencies.
    parallelize(I)       # Parallelize tiles of rows in UPDATE, inside each fixed k

    # ---------- Vectorization and inner-loop tuning ----------

    # SIMD-vectorize over the innermost j dimension inside each (k, i) (or (k, I, i)) nest.
    # This exploits that both path[i, j] and row_k[j] are contiguous in memory.
    #
    # V is chosen according to the target SIMD width:
    #   - e.g., V = 8 for AVX2 doubles, V = 16 for AVX2 floats, etc.
    vectorize(j, V)

    # Optionally unroll j for additional ILP and reduced loop overhead.
    # U is a small factor (e.g., 2–8) that should be a multiple of V when possible.
    unroll(j, U)

    # ---------- Scalar-load hoisting and scratch allocation ----------

    # The model already hoists col_k[i] into a scalar col_i before iterating over j.
    # Compilers can keep col_i in a register, avoiding repeated column loads.
    # No extra directive needed beyond the explicit scalar in the computation.

    # Allocate row_k[] and col_k[] once outside the k-loop and reuse them for every k
    # to avoid per-iteration allocations. This uses only 2*N extra DATA_TYPE values
    # (<< 50% of the N×N path array for realistic N), well within the memory budget.
    # (This is a lifetime / allocation optimization, not a loop transformation.)
    # hoist_allocation(row_k)
    # hoist_allocation(col_k)
    # (Using comments here to introduce a non-standard optimization name.)

    # Keep k outermost and sequential to respect the DP recurrence.

    #
    # This preserves Floyd–Warshall semantics (k-ordering unchanged) while
    # improving spatial locality on row-major 'path' for both [i, j] and [k, j].

    #    This is a scalar loop-invariant code motion:
    #      for i in tile(ii):

    #        for j in tile(jj):

    #    for both path[i, j] and path[k, j] in row-major layout.
    vectorize(j, VEC)   # e.g., map j-loop to AVX/AVX-512 vectors
    unroll(j, UJ)       # small unroll factor to increase ILP and hide latency

domain:

    j: dim in [0, N)

    # Floyd–Warshall all-pairs shortest paths:
    # for each intermediate vertex k, relax all pairs (i, j)

    # Enforce the Floyd–Warshall staging: distances that allow intermediates
    # up to k-1 must be fully computed before using k as an intermediate.

    # - initialization guarantees non-negative weights,
    # - repeated use of the same intermediate vertex k cannot shorten a path,
    # so any order of the (i, j) iterations within a given k yields the
    # same final matrix. This allows parallelization and tiling in i, j
    # while keeping k ordered.
    # (No explicit intra-k dependencies are declared.)

    # -------------------------
    # 1. Cache-friendly blocking
    # -------------------------
    # Block i and j to work on TI×TJ tiles that fit in cache.  Blocking is
    # applied inside each k-iteration; k remains the outer sequential stage.
    block(i, I, TI)
    block(j, J, TJ)

    # After blocking, the logical loop shape we target is:
    #   for k in [0, N):
    #     for I in [0, N) step TI:
    #       for J in [0, N) step TJ:
    #         for i in [I, min(I+TI, N)):
    #           for j in [J, min(J+TJ, N)):
    #             path[i, j] = min(path[i, j],
    #                              path[i, k] + path[k, j]);
    #
    # Hoist I and J just under k (but not outside k, respecting k-dependencies).
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    # TI and TJ should be tuned so that:
    #   - a TI×TJ tile of path,
    #   - plus row k (path[k, :]) and the working set of other threads
    # fit in the upper-level caches (e.g., L2 / L3).

    # 2. Parallelism
    # -------------------------
    # For a fixed k, tiles over distinct row ranges I are independent,
    # so we parallelize over I.  Each thread processes a band of rows
    # (all J-tiles within that band) for each k.
    parallelize(I)

    # (i, j)), but on a 32-core machine, parallelizing over I typically
    # gives sufficient coarse-grain work while keeping per-thread memory
    # access mostly contiguous (full rows).

    # 3. SIMD vectorization and unrolling
    # -------------------------
    # Vectorize the innermost j-loop inside each tile.  Since path is
    # row-major, j is the stride‑1 dimension, which is ideal for SIMD.
    vectorize(j, VW)

    # typically be a small multiple of VW.
    unroll(j, UJ)

    #   for j in tile J:

    # We express this using a custom scalar_replace directive:

    #scalar_replace(path[i, k], tmp_ik)
    #

    #   - scalar_replace(E, t) means: compute E once at the innermost
    #     loop entry and reuse it via scalar temporary t.

    # 5. Branchless min to help SIMD
    # -------------------------
    # Use a branchless min implementation (e.g., hardware min or
    # compare‑and‑select) instead of a data-dependent branch:
    #
    #   candidate = tmp_ik + path[k, j];
    #   path[i, j] = min(path[i, j], candidate);
    #
    # This avoids branch mispredictions and maps directly to SIMD min.
    #
    #branchless_min(path)

/**

/* floyd-warshall.c: this file is part of PolyBench/C */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Include polybench common header. */
#include <polybench.h>

/* Include benchmark-specific header. */
#include "floyd-warshall.h"


/* Array initialization. */
static
void init_array (int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(path,N,N,n,n))
{
  int i, j;

  for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++) {
      path[i][j] = i*j%7+1;
      if ((i+j)%13 == 0 || (i+j)%7==0 || (i+j)%11 == 0)
         path[i][j] = 999;
    }
}


/* DCE code. Must scan the entire live-out data.
   Can be used also to check the correctness of the output. */
static
void print_array(int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(path,N,N,n,n))

{
  int i, j;

  POLYBENCH_DUMP_START;
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_BEGIN("path");
  for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++) {
      if ((i * n + j) % 20 == 0) fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, "\n");
      fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, DATA_PRINTF_MODIFIER, path[i][j]);
    }
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_END("path");
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_FINISH;
}


/* Main computational kernel. The whole function will be timed,
   including the call and return. */
static
void kernel_floyd_warshall[[gnu::flatten, gnu::noinline]](int n,
			   DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(path,N,N,n,n))
{
  int i, j, k;

#pragma scop
  for (k = 0; k < _PB_N; k++)
    {
      for(i = 0; i < _PB_N; i++)
	for (j = 0; j < _PB_N; j++)
	  path[i][j] = path[i][j] < path[i][k] + path[k][j] ?
	    path[i][j] : path[i][k] + path[k][j];
    }
#pragma endscop

}


int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
  /* Retrieve problem size. */
  int n = N;

  /* Variable declaration/allocation. */
  POLYBENCH_2D_ARRAY_DECL(path, DATA_TYPE, N, N, n, n);


  /* Initialize array(s). */
  init_array (n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(path));

  /* Start timer. */
  polybench_start_instruments;

  /* Run kernel. */
  kernel_floyd_warshall (n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(path));

  /* Stop and print timer. */
  polybench_stop_instruments;
  polybench_print_instruments;

  /* Prevent dead-code elimination. All live-out data must be printed
     by the function call in argument. */
  polybench_prevent_dce(print_array(n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(path)));

  /* Be clean. */
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(path);

  return 0;
}

    j: dim in [0, N)

    # In-place adjacency / distance matrix.
    # Row-major storage: elements with consecutive j are contiguous.
    path[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # row-major

parameters:
    N:  int  # problem size (number of vertices)

    # Tuning parameters (chosen based on cache and SIMD characteristics)
    TI: int  # tile size along i (e.g., 64)
    TJ: int  # tile size along j (e.g., 64)
    TK: int  # tile size along k (e.g., 16 or 32)

    VJ: int  # SIMD width along j (e.g., 8 for AVX2 doubles, 16 for AVX-512 floats)
    UJ: int  # unroll factor for the innermost j loop (multiple of VJ, e.g., 2 or 4)

computation:
    # Floyd–Warshall all-pairs shortest paths.
    # Semantics: for each intermediate vertex k in sequence, relax all pairs (i, j).
    FW_UPDATE:
      for k in seq([0, N)):      # k must be executed sequentially
        for i, j:               # (i, j) for a fixed k can be done in any order
          if path[i, k] + path[k, j] < path[i, j]:
            path[i, j] = path[i, k] + path[k, j]

dependencies:
    # Dynamic-programming dependence across k:
    #   All updates for step k must observe the results of all updates from step k-1.
    for k in [1, N), i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        FW_UPDATE(k-1, *, *) -> FW_UPDATE(k, i, j)

    # No dependences between different (i, j) at the same k in this high-level model,
    # so the (i, j) space at fixed k may be freely reordered and parallelized.

optimization:
    # ---------------- Cache blocking / tiling ----------------
    # Tile the spatial (i, j) dimensions so that a TI x TJ tile of path
    # fits into L1/L2 cache while sweeping over a small block of k values.
    block(i, I, TI)   # i = I * TI + ii, where ii is the new inner i
    block(j, J, TJ)   # j = J * TJ + jj

    # Tile the k loop into blocks as well, but keep the overall k dimension
    # strictly sequential to preserve the DP order.
    block(k, K, TK)   # k = K * TK + kk

    # Hoist tile loops to form a six-deep, cache-friendly nest:
    #   for K  in seq([0, ceil(N/TK))):
    #     for I in     [0, ceil(N/TI))):
    #       for J in   [0, ceil(N/TJ))):
    #         for kk in seq([0, TK)):
    #           for ii in [0, TI):
    #             for jj in [0, TJ):
    #               ... FW update on (i = I*TI+ii, j = J*TJ+jj, k = K*TK+kk) ...
    hoist(K)
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    # This preserves the original sequential order in k but improves temporal
    # locality for tiles of path[i, j] and the k-th row/column accessed within
    # each (K, I, J) tile.

    # ---------------- Parallelism ----------------
    # At fixed k (and thus fixed K, kk), all (i, j) updates are independent
    # in this model, so we can parallelize over tiles of i (and optionally j).
    parallelize(I)
    # Optionally, if the runtime and hardware support nested parallelism well:
    # parallelize(J)

    # ---------------- Vectorization & unrolling ----------------
    # Vectorize and unroll along the innermost j dimension, which is
    # contiguous in memory due to row-major layout.
    vectorize(j, VJ)
    unroll(j, UJ)

    # ---------------- Scalar replacement / register promotion ----------------
    # For fixed (k, i), the value path[i, k] is invariant across all j in the
    # inner tile. Load it once into a scalar register and reuse it, instead of
    # reloading from memory for every j.
    #
    # New optimization directive (explained by this comment):
    #   scalar_replace(EXPR):
    #       Replace repeated loads of EXPR that is invariant in an inner
    #       dimension by a single scalar variable, live across that dimension.
    #
    scalar_replace(path[i, k])

    # ---------------- Additional low-level considerations (conceptual) ----------------
    # - Ensure 'path' is aligned (e.g., to 64 bytes) to maximize SIMD efficiency.
    # - Choose (TI, TJ, TK) so that TI * TJ * sizeof(DATA_TYPE) fits in L1/L2 cache,
    #   and TK is large enough to amortize loop overhead but small enough to keep
    #   kk, ii, jj tiles hot in cache.
    # - Do NOT parallelize or reorder across K/kk beyond simple tiling; k remains
    #   sequential to respect the dynamic-programming dependence across k.

domain:
    # Problem size: single parameter N defining an N×N graph.
    i: dim in [0, N)
    j: dim in [0, N)
    k: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # Distance / adjacency matrix (initialized by init_array, updated in-place).
    path[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
        # Row-major layout: path[i][j] is contiguous in j.

    # Scratch buffers reused for every k-iteration.
    # They hold a snapshot of row k and column k from path at the *start* of iteration k.
    row_k[j]: temp DATA_TYPE = j -> j
        # Length-N buffer: row_k[j] ≈ path[k][j] at the beginning of the current k-step.
    col_k[i]: temp DATA_TYPE = i -> i
        # Length-N buffer: col_k[i] ≈ path[i][k] at the beginning of the current k-step.

parameters:
    N: int                     # Number of vertices

computation:
    # Floyd–Warshall all-pairs shortest paths.
    #
    # We adopt the standard dynamic-programming formulation:
    #   D^(k)[i, j] = min( D^(k-1)[i, j],
    #                     D^(k-1)[i, k] + D^(k-1)[k, j] )
    # and implement it using per-k snapshots of row k and column k.
    # This removes intra-k loop-carried dependences and exposes parallelism,
    # while remaining equivalent to the original kernel for all inputs.

    for k in seq[0, N):    # k must remain sequential (DP over increasing set of intermediates)
        # 1. Snapshot row k and column k of path at the beginning of iteration k.
        #    These are read-only during the UPDATE phase.
        SNAPSHOT_ROW:
        for j in seq[0, N):
            row_k[j] = path[k, j]
        SNAPSHOT_COL:
        for i in seq[0, N):
            col_k[i] = path[i, k]

        # 2. Relax all pairs (i, j) using the snapshots.
        #    Once row_k[] and col_k[] are materialized, each (i, j) update is independent:
        #      path[i, j] ← min( path[i, j], col_k[i] + row_k[j] )
        #    so the (i, j) space can be tiled, reordered and parallelized freely.
        UPDATE:
        for i in [0, N):
            col_i: DATA_TYPE = col_k[i]     # Hoist col_k[i] out of inner loop to reduce repeated loads
            for j in [0, N):
                new_dist: DATA_TYPE = col_i + row_k[j]
                path[i, j] = path[i, j] < new_dist ? path[i, j] : new_dist


dependencies:
    # 1. Dynamic programming dependence along k:
    #    iteration k consumes the result of iteration k-1.
    for k in [1, N), i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        UPDATE(k-1, i, j) -> SNAPSHOT_ROW(k)
        UPDATE(k-1, i, j) -> SNAPSHOT_COL(k)

    # 2. Within a fixed k:
    #    SNAPSHOT_ROW(k) and SNAPSHOT_COL(k) must complete before UPDATE(k, i, j) starts.
    for k in [0, N), i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        SNAPSHOT_ROW(k) -> UPDATE(k, i, j)
        SNAPSHOT_COL(k) -> UPDATE(k, i, j)

    # 3. After snapshots are taken, all UPDATE(k, i, j) are independent for fixed k.
    #    There are no dependencies between distinct (i, j) at the same k in UPDATE.


optimization:
    # ---------- Memory-access and locality optimizations ----------

    # Keep k outermost and sequential; all other transformations apply inside each k.
    # This preserves the Floyd–Warshall DP structure.

    # Block the (i, j) iteration space in UPDATE to improve cache locality and create
    # coarser parallel tasks. This does *not* change the global (k, i, j) ordering,
    # only decomposes i and j into tiles.
    #
    # BI, BJ are tuning parameters (e.g., 32–128) chosen so that:
    #   BI * BJ * sizeof(DATA_TYPE) fits comfortably into L1/L2.
    block(i, I, BI)      # Split i into tile index I and intra-tile i
    block(j, J, BJ)      # Split j into tile index J and intra-tile j

    # Row-major layout makes j the stride-1 dimension; keep j innermost in UPDATE
    # so that path[i, j] and row_k[j] are accessed contiguously, enabling SIMD loads/stores.

    # ---------- Parallelism ----------

    # After SNAPSHOT_ROW and SNAPSHOT_COL are done at a given k, UPDATE(k, i, j) has
    # no cross-(i, j) dependences. We can parallelize the outer tile dimension I
    # (or i directly) to exploit multi-core hardware.
    #
    # Parallelization is per-k: each k-step runs UPDATE in parallel, but different
    # k-steps remain sequential due to DP dependencies.
    parallelize(I)       # Parallelize tiles of rows in UPDATE, inside each fixed k

    # ---------- Vectorization and inner-loop tuning ----------

    # SIMD-vectorize over the innermost j dimension inside each (k, i) (or (k, I, i)) nest.
    # This exploits that both path[i, j] and row_k[j] are contiguous in memory.
    #
    # V is chosen according to the target SIMD width:
    #   - e.g., V = 8 for AVX2 doubles, V = 16 for AVX2 floats, etc.
    vectorize(j, V)

    # Optionally unroll j for additional ILP and reduced loop overhead.
    # U is a small factor (e.g., 2–8) that should be a multiple of V when possible.
    unroll(j, U)

    # ---------- Scalar-load hoisting and scratch allocation ----------

    # The model already hoists col_k[i] into a scalar col_i before iterating over j.
    # Compilers can keep col_i in a register, avoiding repeated column loads.
    # No extra directive needed beyond the explicit scalar in the computation.

    # Allocate row_k[] and col_k[] once outside the k-loop and reuse them for every k
    # to avoid per-iteration allocations. This uses only 2*N extra DATA_TYPE values
    # (<< 50% of the N×N path array for realistic N), well within the memory budget.
    # (This is a lifetime / allocation optimization, not a loop transformation.)
    # hoist_allocation(row_k)
    # hoist_allocation(col_k)
    # (Using comments here to introduce a non-standard optimization name.)

    #         for i in [I, min(I+TI, N)):

    #             path[i, j] = min(path[i, j],
    #                              path[i, k] + path[k, j]);
    #
    # Hoist I and J just under k (but not outside k, respecting k-dependencies).
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    # TI and TJ should be tuned so that:
    #   - a TI×TJ tile of path,
    #   - plus row k (path[k, :]) and the working set of other threads
    # fit in the upper-level caches (e.g., L2 / L3).

    # -------------------------
    # 2. Parallelism
    # -------------------------
    # For a fixed k, tiles over distinct row ranges I are independent,
    # so we parallelize over I.  Each thread processes a band of rows
    # (all J-tiles within that band) for each k.
    parallelize(I)

    # Parallelizing over J as well is also legal (tiles are disjoint in
    # (i, j)), but on a 32-core machine, parallelizing over I typically
    # gives sufficient coarse-grain work while keeping per-thread memory
    # access mostly contiguous (full rows).

    # -------------------------
    # 3. SIMD vectorization and unrolling
    # -------------------------
    # Vectorize the innermost j-loop inside each tile.  Since path is
    # row-major, j is the stride‑1 dimension, which is ideal for SIMD.
    vectorize(j, VW)

    # Unroll j to reduce loop overhead and expose more ILP.  UJ should
    # typically be a small multiple of VW.
    unroll(j, UJ)

    # 4. Scalar replacement / invariant hoisting

    # and is used TJ times.  Promote it to a scalar to avoid repeated
    # loads from memory:

    #   tmp_ik = path[i, k];
    #   for j in tile J:
    #       path[i, j] = min(path[i, j], tmp_ik + path[k, j]);

    #scalar_replace(path[i, k], tmp_ik)
    #

    #   - scalar_replace(E, t) means: compute E once at the innermost
    #     loop entry and reuse it via scalar temporary t.

    # -------------------------
    # 5. Branchless min to help SIMD
    # -------------------------
    # Use a branchless min implementation (e.g., hardware min or
    # compare‑and‑select) instead of a data-dependent branch:
    #
    #   candidate = tmp_ik + path[k, j];
    #   path[i, j] = min(path[i, j], candidate);
    #
    # This avoids branch mispredictions and maps directly to SIMD min.
    #
    #branchless_min(path)

/**

/* floyd-warshall.c: this file is part of PolyBench/C */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Include polybench common header. */
#include <polybench.h>

/* Include benchmark-specific header. */
#include "floyd-warshall.h"


/* Array initialization. */
static
void init_array (int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(path,N,N,n,n))
{
  int i, j;

  for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++) {
      path[i][j] = i*j%7+1;
      if ((i+j)%13 == 0 || (i+j)%7==0 || (i+j)%11 == 0)
         path[i][j] = 999;
    }
}


/* DCE code. Must scan the entire live-out data.
   Can be used also to check the correctness of the output. */
static
void print_array(int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(path,N,N,n,n))

{
  int i, j;

  POLYBENCH_DUMP_START;
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_BEGIN("path");
  for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++) {
      if ((i * n + j) % 20 == 0) fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, "\n");
      fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, DATA_PRINTF_MODIFIER, path[i][j]);
    }
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_END("path");
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_FINISH;
}


/* Main computational kernel. The whole function will be timed,
   including the call and return. */
static
void kernel_floyd_warshall[[gnu::flatten, gnu::noinline]](int n,
			   DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(path,N,N,n,n))
{
  int i, j, k;

#pragma scop
  for (k = 0; k < _PB_N; k++)
    {
      for(i = 0; i < _PB_N; i++)
	for (j = 0; j < _PB_N; j++)
	  path[i][j] = path[i][j] < path[i][k] + path[k][j] ?
	    path[i][j] : path[i][k] + path[k][j];
    }
#pragma endscop

}


int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
  /* Retrieve problem size. */
  int n = N;

  /* Variable declaration/allocation. */
  POLYBENCH_2D_ARRAY_DECL(path, DATA_TYPE, N, N, n, n);


  /* Initialize array(s). */
  init_array (n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(path));

  /* Start timer. */
  polybench_start_instruments;

  /* Run kernel. */
  kernel_floyd_warshall (n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(path));

  /* Stop and print timer. */
  polybench_stop_instruments;
  polybench_print_instruments;

  /* Prevent dead-code elimination. All live-out data must be printed
     by the function call in argument. */
  polybench_prevent_dce(print_array(n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(path)));

  /* Be clean. */
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(path);

  return 0;
}

parameters:
    N:  int  # problem size (number of vertices)

    TI: int  # tile size along i (e.g., 64)
    TJ: int  # tile size along j (e.g., 64)
    TK: int  # tile size along k (e.g., 16 or 32)

    UJ: int  # unroll factor for the innermost j loop (multiple of VJ, e.g., 2 or 4)

computation:
    # Floyd–Warshall all-pairs shortest paths.
    # Semantics: for each intermediate vertex k in sequence, relax all pairs (i, j).
    FW_UPDATE:
      for k in seq([0, N)):      # k must be executed sequentially
        for i, j:               # (i, j) for a fixed k can be done in any order
          if path[i, k] + path[k, j] < path[i, j]:
            path[i, j] = path[i, k] + path[k, j]

dependencies:
    # Dynamic-programming dependence across k:
    #   All updates for step k must observe the results of all updates from step k-1.
    for k in [1, N), i in [0, N), j in [0, N):
        FW_UPDATE(k-1, *, *) -> FW_UPDATE(k, i, j)

    # No dependences between different (i, j) at the same k in this high-level model,
    # so the (i, j) space at fixed k may be freely reordered and parallelized.

optimization:
    # ---------------- Cache blocking / tiling ----------------
    # Tile the spatial (i, j) dimensions so that a TI x TJ tile of path
    # fits into L1/L2 cache while sweeping over a small block of k values.
    block(i, I, TI)   # i = I * TI + ii, where ii is the new inner i
    block(j, J, TJ)   # j = J * TJ + jj

    # Tile the k loop into blocks as well, but keep the overall k dimension
    # strictly sequential to preserve the DP order.
    block(k, K, TK)   # k = K * TK + kk

    # Hoist tile loops to form a six-deep, cache-friendly nest:
    #   for K  in seq([0, ceil(N/TK))):
    #     for I in     [0, ceil(N/TI))):
    #       for J in   [0, ceil(N/TJ))):
    #         for kk in seq([0, TK)):
    #           for ii in [0, TI):
    #             for jj in [0, TJ):
    #               ... FW update on (i = I*TI+ii, j = J*TJ+jj, k = K*TK+kk) ...
    hoist(K)
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    # This preserves the original sequential order in k but improves temporal
    # locality for tiles of path[i, j] and the k-th row/column accessed within
    # each (K, I, J) tile.

    # ---------------- Parallelism ----------------
    # At fixed k (and thus fixed K, kk), all (i, j) updates are independent
    # in this model, so we can parallelize over tiles of i (and optionally j).
    parallelize(I)
    # Optionally, if the runtime and hardware support nested parallelism well:
    # parallelize(J)

    # ---------------- Vectorization & unrolling ----------------
    # Vectorize and unroll along the innermost j dimension, which is
    # contiguous in memory due to row-major layout.
    vectorize(j, VJ)
    unroll(j, UJ)

    # ---------------- Scalar replacement / register promotion ----------------
    # For fixed (k, i), the value path[i, k] is invariant across all j in the
    # inner tile. Load it once into a scalar register and reuse it, instead of
    # reloading from memory for every j.
    #
    # New optimization directive (explained by this comment):
    #   scalar_replace(EXPR):
    #       Replace repeated loads of EXPR that is invariant in an inner
    #       dimension by a single scalar variable, live across that dimension.
    #
    scalar_replace(path[i, k])

    # ---------------- Additional low-level considerations (conceptual) ----------------
    # - Ensure 'path' is aligned (e.g., to 64 bytes) to maximize SIMD efficiency.
    # - Choose (TI, TJ, TK) so that TI * TJ * sizeof(DATA_TYPE) fits in L1/L2 cache,
    #   and TK is large enough to amortize loop overhead but small enough to keep
    #   kk, ii, jj tiles hot in cache.
    # - Do NOT parallelize or reorder across K/kk beyond simple tiling; k remains
    #   sequential to respect the dynamic-programming dependence across k.

domain:
