domain:
    # Time dimension: tsteps outer loop is strictly sequential
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)

    # Space dimensions: N x N grid
    i: dim in [0, N)
    j: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # Row-major 2D arrays: contiguous in j
    # index(i, j) = i * N + j
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
    B[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Only interior points [1, N-1) x [1, N-1) are updated.
    # Boundary values A[0,*], A[N-1,*], A[* ,0], A[* ,N-1] remain as initialized
    # and are read as fixed Dirichlet boundaries throughout the computation.

parameters:
    N: int                  # grid size in each dimension
    TSTEPS: int             # number of outer iterations
    w: DATA_TYPE            # Jacobi weight, w = SCALAR_VAL(0.2) in code

    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters
    TI: int                 # spatial tile size in i (rows), e.g., 32–128
    TJ: int                 # spatial tile size in j (cols), e.g., 32–256
    VEC: int                # vector width for j (e.g., 4 or 8 for doubles)

computation:
    # For each time step, perform two Jacobi sweeps:
    #  1. B <- stencil(A)
    #  2. A <- stencil(B)
    #
    # Time is strictly sequential to match original semantics and FP behavior.
    for t in seq([0, TSTEPS)):

        # First sweep: compute B from A at time t
        # Matches:
        #   B[i][j] = 0.2 * (A[i][j] + A[i][j-1] + A[i][j+1]
        #                    + A[i+1][j] + A[i-1][j]);
        for i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
            S1_B_from_A(t, i, j):
                B[i, j] =
                    w * ( A[i,   j  ] +
                          A[i,   j-1] +
                          A[i,   j+1] +
                          A[i+1, j  ] +
                          A[i-1, j  ] )

        # Second sweep: compute A from B at the same time step
        # Matches:
        #   A[i][j] = 0.2 * (B[i][j] + B[i][j-1] + B[i][j+1]
        #                    + B[i+1][j] + B[i-1][j]);
        for i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
            S2_A_from_B(t, i, j):
                A[i, j] =
                    w * ( B[i,   j  ] +
                          B[i,   j-1] +
                          B[i,   j+1] +
                          B[i+1, j  ] +
                          B[i-1, j  ] )

dependencies:
    # Within a given time step t, each A-update depends on the corresponding
    # B-updates of the same step.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS), i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
        S1_B_from_A(t, i, j) -> S2_A_from_B(t, i, j)

    # Across time steps, A at step t is the input state for computing B at t+1.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS-1), i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
        S2_A_from_B(t, i, j) -> S1_B_from_A(t+1, i, j)

optimization:
    # ---- Spatial blocking (tiling) for cache locality ----
    # We tile i and j so that sub-blocks of A and B fit better into caches.
    # This preserves semantics because tiles are processed in a way that
    # respects the original order within each full sweep.
    block(i, ii, TI)     # i = ii * TI + i_in_tile
    block(j, jj, TJ)     # j = jj * TJ + j_in_tile

    # Keep time dimension outermost; sweeps remain ordered as in original code.
    hoist(t)

    # Apply tiling separately to both sweeps inside each time step:
    #   for t:
    #     for ii, jj: tile of B-from-A
    #     for ii, jj: tile of A-from-B
    #
    # B tiles for a given time step are fully computed (global barrier implied)
    # before any A tiles of that step are used, preserving:
    #   "finish all B updates at t before any A update at t".
    hoist(ii)
    hoist(jj)

    # ---- Parallelization ----
    # Each (i, j) update within a sweep depends only on neighbor values
    # from the *input* grid of that sweep, which is read-only in that phase.
    # Therefore, the spatial loops are safe to parallelize.
    #
    # We parallelize at the outer tile level to:
    #  - amortize thread-management overhead,
    #  - avoid false sharing on adjacent rows/cols,
    #  - map well onto a 32-core CPU (many tiles in flight).
    parallelize(ii)      # distribute tiles of rows across threads
    # Optionally also:
    # parallelize(jj)    # if many cores and large N, 2D tile parallelism

    # Time loop t remains sequential: there are true dependencies between
    # successive timesteps and between S1 and S2 at a given t.

    # ---- Vectorization along j ----
    # j is contiguous in memory (row-major layout), and the stencil
    # in j-direction has unit stride. This is ideal for SIMD.
    vectorize(j, VEC)

    # ---- Loop unrolling ----
    # Unroll the innermost j loop to:
    #  - expose more ILP,
    #  - reduce loop-control overhead,
    #  - help the compiler schedule loads of neighboring points.
    unroll(j, 4)

    # Optional: mild unrolling in time to increase ILP while respecting
    # sequential time semantics (compiler will emit code for two t-steps
    # inlined, but still ordered).
    unroll(t, 2)

    # ---- Arithmetic hoisting ----
    # The scalar weight w = 0.2 is invariant across all loops.
    # Ensure it is loaded once into a register and reused:
    hoist(w)
    # (This corresponds to computing SCALAR_VAL(0.2) once before
    #  entering the time-stepping loops.)

    # ---- Notes on correctness ----
    # - Boundaries (i = 0 or N-1, j = 0 or N-1) are never written,
    #   exactly as in the original code; they are read as fixed values.
    # - No change is made to the stencil formula or to the ordering
    #   between:
    #       B <- A   and   A <- B
    #   within each time step.
    # - All time steps t are executed in order; no reordering across t.
    # - Parallelization and vectorization affect only independent
    #   (i, j) iterations within each sweep, preserving semantics.
--- END OF MODEL: jacobi-2d-04 ---

domain:
    # Interior grid points only; boundary rows/cols 0 and N-1 remain unchanged.
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)
    i: dim in [1, N-1)
    j: dim in [1, N-1)

data:
    # Full N×N grids stored in row-major order.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j   # Row-major, includes boundaries at indices 0 and N-1
    B[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j   # Row-major, used as a ping-pong buffer

parameters:
    N: int                  # Grid size (both dimensions)
    TSTEPS: int             # Number of outer loop iterations in the original code
    w: DATA_TYPE            # Relaxation weight; in the given code w = SCALAR_VAL(0.2)
    TI: int                 # Tunable tile size in the i (row) dimension
    TJ: int                 # Tunable tile size in the j (column) dimension
    VEC_WIDTH: int          # Target vector width (elements) for vectorization over j
    UNROLL_J: int           # Unroll factor for inner j loop

computation:
    # Jacobi 2D stencil with two sweeps per outer time iteration:
    #   1) B = J(A)
    #   2) A = J(B)
    # Boundaries of A and B (i=0 or i=N-1 or j=0 or j=N-1) are never updated.

    for t in seq([0, TSTEPS)):
        # Sweep 1: read from A, write to B.
        A_to_B:
            for i, j:
                B[i, j] = w * (
                              A[i,   j  ] +
                              A[i,   j-1] +
                              A[i,   j+1] +
                              A[i-1, j  ] +
                              A[i+1, j  ]
                          )

        # Sweep 2: read from B, write to A.
        B_to_A:
            for i, j:
                A[i, j] = w * (
                              B[i,   j  ] +
                              B[i,   j-1] +
                              B[i,   j+1] +
                              B[i-1, j  ] +
                              B[i+1, j  ]
                          )

optimization:
    # --- Scalar and aliasing assumptions ------------------------------------
    hoist(w)
    # hoist(S): treat scalar S as loop-invariant and hoist its load/definition
    # outside all loops that use it. Here, w = 0.2 is a constant; ensure it is
    # computed/loaded once, not per iteration.

    assume_no_alias(A, B)
    # assume_no_alias(X, Y): X and Y do not alias in memory. This matches the
    # benchmark intent and enables better vectorization and reordering.

    # --- Spatial blocking for cache locality --------------------------------
    # Tile the 2D interior domain (i, j) to improve cache reuse within each
    # sweep. Each tile operates on a small sub-block of the grid.
    block(i, ii, TI)
    block(j, jj, TJ)
    # block(d, D, S): replace loop over dimension d by an outer tile loop D and
    # an inner loop over d with tile size S. For example:
    #   for i in [1, N-1)  -->
    #     for ii in [1, N-1) step TI:
    #       for i in [ii, min(ii+TI, N-1))
    #
    # TI, TJ should be tuned so that a tile of A and B plus its 1-cell halo
    # fits comfortably in L1/L2 cache.

    # --- Parallelization -----------------------------------------------------
    parallelize(ii)
    # parallelize(D): iterations along tile dimension D can be executed in
    # parallel (e.g., via OpenMP). Each time-step t is sequential, but within
    # a time-step, tiles in ii are independent in a Jacobi sweep, so they can
    # be distributed across cores on the 32-core machine.

    # To increase parallelism further for very large N, one can also
    # parallelize over jj in addition to ii, as long as the runtime partitions
    # tiles to avoid excessive synchronization:
    # parallelize(jj)

    # --- Vectorization and unrolling ----------------------------------------
    vectorize(j, VEC_WIDTH)
    # vectorize(d, W): enforce SIMD vectorization along dimension d with width W.
    # Here, inner j is contiguous in row-major layout, so vector loads/stores
    # for A[i, j±1] and B[i, j±1] are naturally aligned and efficient.

    unroll(j, UNROLL_J)
    # unroll(d, F): unroll loop d by factor F to reduce loop overhead and allow
    # the compiler to better schedule loads, adds, and the final multiply by w.

    # --- Loop ordering -------------------------------------------------------
    # Preserve the original nesting order (t outer, then i, then j) to ensure
    # correctness of the time-dependent stencil and to keep j innermost for
    # vectorization and unit-stride memory access:
    #   t (sequential) -> ii (parallel tiles) -> jj -> i -> j (vectorized)
    #
    # No interchange of t with spatial dimensions is allowed because each
    # time-step depends on the previous one.

    # --- Optional: time-iteration unrolling (purely local) -------------------
    # The outer time loop can be unrolled by a small factor (e.g., 2) to expose
    # more ILP, without changing the number of stencil applications:
    # unroll(t, 2)
    # This preserves semantics because iterations of t are strictly sequential
    # but can still be mechanically unrolled by the compiler.
--- END OF MODEL: jacobi-2d-05 ---

/**

/* jacobi-2d.c: this file is part of PolyBench/C */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Include polybench common header. */
#include <polybench.h>

/* Include benchmark-specific header. */
#include "jacobi-2d.h"


/* Array initialization. */
static
void init_array (int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(A,N,N,n,n),
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(B,N,N,n,n))
{
  int i, j;

  for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++)
      {
	A[i][j] = ((DATA_TYPE) i*(j+2) + 2) / n;
	B[i][j] = ((DATA_TYPE) i*(j+3) + 3) / n;
      }
}


/* DCE code. Must scan the entire live-out data.
   Can be used also to check the correctness of the output. */
static
void print_array(int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(A,N,N,n,n))

{
  int i, j;

  POLYBENCH_DUMP_START;
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_BEGIN("A");
  for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++) {
      if ((i * n + j) % 20 == 0) fprintf(POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, "\n");
      fprintf(POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, DATA_PRINTF_MODIFIER, A[i][j]);
    }
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_END("A");
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_FINISH;
}


/* Main computational kernel. The whole function will be timed,
   including the call and return. */
static
void kernel_jacobi_2d[[gnu::flatten, gnu::noinline]](int tsteps,
			    int n,
			    DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(A,N,N,n,n),
			    DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(B,N,N,n,n))
{
  int t, i, j;

#pragma scop
  for (t = 0; t < _PB_TSTEPS; t++)
    {
      for (i = 1; i < _PB_N - 1; i++)
	for (j = 1; j < _PB_N - 1; j++)
	  B[i][j] = SCALAR_VAL(0.2) * (A[i][j] + A[i][j-1] + A[i][1+j] + A[1+i][j] + A[i-1][j]);
      for (i = 1; i < _PB_N - 1; i++)
	for (j = 1; j < _PB_N - 1; j++)
	  A[i][j] = SCALAR_VAL(0.2) * (B[i][j] + B[i][j-1] + B[i][1+j] + B[1+i][j] + B[i-1][j]);
    }
#pragma endscop

}


int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
  /* Retrieve problem size. */
  int n = N;
  int tsteps = TSTEPS;

  /* Variable declaration/allocation. */
  POLYBENCH_2D_ARRAY_DECL(A, DATA_TYPE, N, N, n, n);
  POLYBENCH_2D_ARRAY_DECL(B, DATA_TYPE, N, N, n, n);


  /* Initialize array(s). */
  init_array (n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(A), POLYBENCH_ARRAY(B));

  /* Start timer. */
  polybench_start_instruments;

  /* Run kernel. */
  kernel_jacobi_2d(tsteps, n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(A), POLYBENCH_ARRAY(B));

  /* Stop and print timer. */
  polybench_stop_instruments;
  polybench_print_instruments;

  /* Prevent dead-code elimination. All live-out data must be printed
     by the function call in argument. */
  polybench_prevent_dce(print_array(n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(A)));

  /* Be clean. */
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(A);
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(B);

  return 0;
}

domain:
    # Global problem sizes
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)        # time iteration (each iteration = 2 Jacobi sweeps)
    i: dim in [0, N)             # space, row index
    j: dim in [0, N)             # space, column index

    # Interior region where the stencil is applied
    ii: dim in [1, N-1)          # interior rows
    jj: dim in [1, N-1)          # interior columns

data:
    # 2D grids, row-major layout
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
        # A is both input and output:
        # - boundaries i ∈ {0, N-1} or j ∈ {0, N-1} are initialized once and never updated
        # - interior ii, jj is updated at every time step
    B[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
        # B is a temporary ping-pong buffer:
        # - boundaries same as for A: initialized and never updated
        # - interior holds intermediate Jacobi values between the two sweeps in each t

parameters:
    N:       int                  # grid size (same in both dimensions)
    TSTEPS:  int                  # number of outer iterations in the original code
    w:       DATA_TYPE            # stencil weight, w = SCALAR_VAL(0.2)

    # Tunable performance parameters (no effect on numerical semantics):
    TI:      int                  # tile size in i (rows), e.g., 32 or 64
    TJ:      int                  # tile size in j (cols), e.g., 64 or 128
    VJ:      int                  # vector width (elements processed per SIMD op), e.g., 4, 8
    UJ:      int                  # unroll factor for j, e.g., 2, 4

computation:
    # Precompute scalar weight once, outside time loop
    C0: w = w

    # Time loop is strictly sequential: each t depends on t-1 via A
    for t in seq([0, TSTEPS)):
        #------------------------------------------
        # Sweep 1: Jacobi update from A^t to B^t
        #   B[i,j] = w * ( A[i,j] + A[i,j-1] + A[i,j+1] + A[i-1,j] + A[i+1,j] )
        #------------------------------------------
        S1:
            for ii in [1, N-1), jj in [1, N-1):
                B[ii, jj] =
                    C0 * ( A[ii,   jj  ] +
                           A[ii,   jj-1] +
                           A[ii,   jj+1] +
                           A[ii-1, jj  ] +
                           A[ii+1, jj  ] )

        #------------------------------------------
        # Sweep 2: Jacobi update from B^t to A^(t+1)
        #   A[i,j] = w * ( B[i,j] + B[i,j-1] + B[i,j+1] + B[i-1,j] + B[i+1,j] )
        #------------------------------------------
        S2:
            for ii in [1, N-1), jj in [1, N-1):
                A[ii, jj] =
                    C0 * ( B[ii,   jj  ] +
                           B[ii,   jj-1] +
                           B[ii,   jj+1] +
                           B[ii-1, jj  ] +
                           B[ii+1, jj  ] )

dependencies:
    # 1. Within a given time step t, all S1 updates must complete before any S2 update:
    #    (matches the two separate for-loops in the original C code)
    for t in [0, TSTEPS):
        for ii in [1, N-1), jj in [1, N-1):
            S1(t, ii, jj) -> S2(t, *, *)

    # 2. Across time steps, new A produced by S2 at time t is the input A for S1 at time t+1:
    for t in [0, TSTEPS-1):
        S2(t, *, *) -> S1(t+1, *, *)

    # 3. There are no loop-carried dependencies along ii or jj *within* a sweep:
    #    each point only reads from the previous array (A for S1, B for S2),
    #    and writes to a distinct element in the target array.
    #    This allows full parallelization in the spatial dimensions per sweep.

optimization:
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Spatial blocking (tiling) to improve cache reuse
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Tile the 2D spatial domain for both sweeps:
    #   - I and J are tile indices
    #   - ii and jj (interior indices) become intra-tile indices
    block(ii, I, TI)      # ii = I * TI + local_ii, tiles of TI rows
    block(jj, J, TJ)      # jj = J * TJ + local_jj, tiles of TJ cols

    # Hoist tile loops to just inside the time loop, so entire tiles are
    # processed for S1, then entire tiles for S2, preserving S1->S2 ordering.
    hoist(I)              # place I as the outermost spatial loop (after t)
    hoist(J)              # place J as next outer spatial loop

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelization
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Each (I, J) tile in a given sweep and time step is independent:
    # we can process tiles in parallel both in S1 and S2.
    # On a 32-core x64 machine, TI×TJ is chosen so that one or a few tiles
    # fit comfortably into L2 / L3 per core.
    parallelize(I)        # distribute tiles across threads
    # (J remains inside I; larger TJ gives good work per tile and contiguous memory)

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # SIMD vectorization along the innermost dimension
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # jj indexes contiguous memory (row-major), so we vectorize along jj.
    # VJ should match the hardware SIMD width, e.g., 4 for AVX2 float, 8 for AVX2 double.
    vectorize(jj, VJ)     # emit vector loads/stores and fused adds for stencil in j

    # Optional loop unrolling in j to reduce loop overhead and expose ILP
    unroll(jj, UJ)

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Arithmetic and scalar optimizations
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    #  - The constant weight 0.2 (C0) is hoisted out of all loops.
    #  - Compilers can fuse additions and multiplication into FMA instructions
    #    where available, especially under -O3.
    #  - No change to the mathematical stencil; only the evaluation order within
    #    each sum may change, causing at most benign floating-point roundoff differences.
    hoist(C0)             # ensure 'w' is computed/loaded once outside the time-space loops

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Layout and memory access
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # We *keep* row-major layout for both A and B; the innermost jj loop traverses
    # contiguous elements, yielding:
    #   - unit-stride loads/stores for A[ii,*] and B[ii,*]
    #   - regular strided accesses for neighbors in i (ii-1, ii+1)
    #
    # Changing to column-major would harm the primary access pattern in jj,
    # so we explicitly preserve row-major layout and rely on spatial blocking
    # plus caches to amortize the strided accesses in ii.

domain:
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)   # time steps
    i: dim in [0, N)        # space, row index
    j: dim in [0, N)        # space, column index

data:
    # Row-major 2D arrays matching C layout: A[i][j] and B[i][j]
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # live-in and live-out
    B[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # used as ping-pong buffer; initial contents unused

parameters:
    N: int                  # grid dimension
    TSTEPS: int             # number of Jacobi time steps
    omega: DATA_TYPE        # relaxation coefficient, = SCALAR_VAL(0.2)

    # Tunable performance parameters (chosen w.r.t. cache / SIMD of the target)
    TI: int                 # tile size in i (e.g., 32–256)
    TJ: int                 # tile size in j (e.g., 64–512, multiple of VEC_J)
    VEC_J: int              # SIMD vector width along j (elements)
    UNROLL_J: int           # unroll factor for inner j-loop

computation:
    # 2D Jacobi with 5-point stencil, double-buffered in A and B.
    # Boundary points (i==0, i==N-1, j==0, j==N-1) are never updated.
    for t in seq([0, TSTEPS)):      # time loop must remain sequential
        # Phase 1: B := Jacobi(A)
        for i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
            S1: B[i, j] =
                    omega * ( A[i,   j  ] +
                              A[i,   j-1] +
                              A[i,   j+1] +
                              A[i-1, j  ] +
                              A[i+1, j  ] )

        # Phase 2: A := Jacobi(B)
        for i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
            S2: A[i, j] =
                    omega * ( B[i,   j  ] +
                              B[i,   j-1] +
                              B[i,   j+1] +
                              B[i-1, j  ] +
                              B[i+1, j  ] )

optimization:
    # Assumptions:
    # - A and B are distinct, non-aliasing row-major buffers.
    # - N is large so the interior dominates.
    # - N, TSTEPS, omega and tile / SIMD parameters are invariant inside the kernel.

    # 1. Spatial blocking (tiling) over i and j to improve cache locality.
    #    Applied identically to both S1 and S2; boundaries are handled by
    #    clipping tile ranges to [1, N-1).
    block(i, II, TI)        # split i into outer tile index II and inner i
    block(j, JJ, TJ)        # split j into outer tile index JJ and inner j

    # Resulting per-time-step structure (conceptually):
    #   for II                          # tiles of rows
    #     for JJ                        # tiles of columns
    #       for i in tile(II) ∩ [1,N-1)
    #         for j in tile(JJ) ∩ [1,N-1)

    # 2. Loop ordering:
    #    - Keep t outermost and sequential.
    #    - Within each time step, iterate over tiles first (II, JJ),
    #      then intra-tile i, then intra-tile j (unit-stride).
    hoist(t)                # t already outermost; make this explicit
    hoist(II)               # tile rows outside tile columns
    hoist(JJ)               # tile columns outside intra-tile loops

    # 3. Parallelization:
    #    - Within a fixed (t, phase), all (i,j) updates are independent.
    #    - Parallelize on the outer row tiles to reduce scheduling overhead
    #      and balance work across cores.
    parallelize(II)         # distribute II-tiles across threads for S1 and S2

    # 4. Vectorization and unrolling:
    #    - j is the innermost loop and contiguous in memory (row-major),
    #      so vectorize along j.
    #    - Choose TJ as a multiple of VEC_J to minimize scalar remainder work.
    vectorize(j, VEC_J)     # map inner j loop to SIMD lanes
    unroll(j, UNROLL_J)     # unroll j loop within each vectorized chunk

    # 5. Scalar / arithmetic hoisting:
    #    - Keep omega in a register at the innermost level.
    #    - Allow the compiler to use fused multiply-add for omega * sum5.
    hoist(omega)            # load omega once per (t, II, JJ) region (or wider)
--- END OF MODEL: jacobi-2d-02 ---

--- START OF MODEL: jacobi-2d-03 ---
domain:
    # Time dimension (Jacobi iterations; each iteration performs two 5-point sweeps)
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)

    # Spatial dimensions restricted to the interior points actually updated
    # (grid is N x N, but i=0, i=N-1, j=0, j=N-1 are fixed boundary values)
    i: dim in [1, N-1)
    j: dim in [1, N-1)

data:
    # 2D grids stored in row-major order (C layout)
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
    B[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Note: memory for A and B is actually allocated for i,j in [0, N),
    # but only interior indices [1, N-1) are written in the kernel.
    # Boundary rows/columns (i=0, i=N-1, j=0, j=N-1) remain at their
    # initialized values and are only read as neighbors.

parameters:
    N: int                  # grid size in each spatial dimension
    TSTEPS: int             # number of time steps (each step = 2 sweeps)
    w: DATA_TYPE            # stencil weight; w = SCALAR_VAL(0.2)

    # Tuning parameters for optimization (chosen based on hardware/cache)
    TI: int                 # tile size in the i (row) dimension, e.g., 32..256
    VF: int                 # SIMD vector length for j, e.g., 4 or 8
    U: int                  # unrolling factor for j, typically a multiple of VF

computation:
    # For each time step t, perform:
    #   1) A -> B 5-point Jacobi sweep on interior points
    #   2) B -> A 5-point Jacobi sweep on interior points
    #
    # Time steps must execute sequentially because each uses the result
    # of the previous one.
    for t in seq[0, TSTEPS):
        # Sweep 1: read A, write B
        for i, j:
            JACOBI_B(t, i, j):
                B[i, j] =
                    w * ( A[i,   j  ] +
                          A[i,   j-1] +
                          A[i,   j+1] +
                          A[i-1, j  ] +
                          A[i+1, j  ] )

        # Sweep 2: read B, write A
        for i, j:
            JACOBI_A(t, i, j):
                A[i, j] =
                    w * ( B[i,   j  ] +
                          B[i,   j-1] +
                          B[i,   j+1] +
                          B[i-1, j  ] +
                          B[i+1, j  ] )

dependencies:
    # Within a given time step t, each interior point (i, j) in sweep 2
    # depends on its 5-point neighborhood in B from sweep 1 of the same t.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS), i, j:
        # Direct center dependency (neighborhood dependencies are implicit)
        JACOBI_B(t, i, j) -> JACOBI_A(t, i, j)

    # Across time steps, A at time t+1 is produced by JACOBI_A(t, ·, ·)
    # and used as input to JACOBI_B(t+1, ·, ·). This enforces that the
    # outer time loop remains sequential.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS-1), i, j:
        JACOBI_A(t, i, j) -> JACOBI_B(t+1, i, j)

optimization:
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Preserve row-major friendly access and innermost j-loop
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # The kernel already iterates with j as the innermost loop, which
    # matches row-major storage (elements with consecutive j are contiguous).
    # We keep this structure to maximize spatial locality and enable SIMD.
    hoist(t)  # keep t as the outermost loop (no-op but documented)

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Parallelization over row tiles (multi-core scalability)
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # Each (t, i, j) update within a sweep only reads from the "old" array
    # (A for JACOBI_B, B for JACOBI_A) and writes to the "new" one, so
    # there are no loop-carried dependencies along i or j inside a sweep.
    #
    # We tile the i dimension into blocks of TI consecutive rows and
    # parallelize over the outer tile index. This:
    #   - gives each thread a large, cache-friendly chunk of rows,
    #   - reduces scheduling overhead vs. per-row parallelism,
    #   - maintains correctness because different i-tiles are independent.
    block(i, ii, TI)       # i = ii * TI + (inner i in [0, TI) with bounds clipping)
    hoist(ii)              # loop order: for t, for ii, for i-in-tile, for j
    parallelize(ii)        # run row tiles in parallel for each sweep & time step

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. SIMD vectorization and unrolling along j
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # The innermost j-loop accesses:
    #   A[i, j], A[i, j±1], A[i±1, j]   (or the same pattern on B)
    # which are all at small, fixed offsets. This is ideal for auto-
    # vectorization. We make this explicit and allow the vector width
    # and unroll factor to be tuned.
    vectorize(j, VF)       # map j-iterations to SIMD lanes (e.g., AVX2/AVX-512)
    unroll(j, U)           # unroll j-loop to increase ILP and hide latencies

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Arithmetic simplifications (kept implicit)
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # The expression is already in the form:
    #   tmp = A/B neighbors sum
    #   out = w * tmp
    # so a single multiplication by w per point is required.
    # Modern compilers will:
    #   - hoist the constant w = 0.2 outside loops,
    #   - keep partial sums in registers.
    # No additional arithmetic restructuring is necessary in the model.

    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Optional refinement: per-tile software prefetching (comment-only)
    #------------------------------------------------------------
    # On very large grids where N is much larger than the last-level cache,
    # a further micro-optimization is to add software prefetches for the
    # next rows of A (in JACOBI_B) and B (in JACOBI_A) within each tile ii.
    # This can be modeled as:
    #   #prefetch(A[i+Δ, j]) and #prefetch(B[i+Δ, j])
    # for some small Δ (e.g., 2–4), but is left as an implementation choice
    # rather than a formal directive here.
--- END OF MODEL: jacobi-2d-03 ---

--- START OF MODEL: jacobi-2d-04 ---
domain:
    # Time dimension: tsteps outer loop is strictly sequential
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)

    # Space dimensions: N x N grid
    i: dim in [0, N)
    j: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # Row-major 2D arrays: contiguous in j
    # index(i, j) = i * N + j
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
    B[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Only interior points [1, N-1) x [1, N-1) are updated.
    # Boundary values A[0,*], A[N-1,*], A[* ,0], A[* ,N-1] remain as initialized
    # and are read as fixed Dirichlet boundaries throughout the computation.

parameters:
    N: int                  # grid size in each dimension
    TSTEPS: int             # number of outer iterations
    w: DATA_TYPE            # Jacobi weight, w = SCALAR_VAL(0.2) in code

    # Tunable blocking and vectorization parameters
    TI: int                 # spatial tile size in i (rows), e.g., 32–128
    TJ: int                 # spatial tile size in j (cols), e.g., 32–256
    VEC: int                # vector width for j (e.g., 4 or 8 for doubles)

computation:
    # For each time step, perform two Jacobi sweeps:
    #  1. B <- stencil(A)
    #  2. A <- stencil(B)
    #
    # Time is strictly sequential to match original semantics and FP behavior.
    for t in seq([0, TSTEPS)):

        # First sweep: compute B from A at time t
        # Matches:
        #   B[i][j] = 0.2 * (A[i][j] + A[i][j-1] + A[i][j+1]
        #                    + A[i+1][j] + A[i-1][j]);
        for i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
            S1_B_from_A(t, i, j):
                B[i, j] =
                    w * ( A[i,   j  ] +
                          A[i,   j-1] +
                          A[i,   j+1] +
                          A[i+1, j  ] +
                          A[i-1, j  ] )

        # Second sweep: compute A from B at the same time step
        # Matches:
        #   A[i][j] = 0.2 * (B[i][j] + B[i][j-1] + B[i][j+1]
        #                    + B[i+1][j] + B[i-1][j]);
        for i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
            S2_A_from_B(t, i, j):
                A[i, j] =
                    w * ( B[i,   j  ] +
                          B[i,   j-1] +
                          B[i,   j+1] +
                          B[i+1, j  ] +
                          B[i-1, j  ] )

dependencies:
    # Within a given time step t, each A-update depends on the corresponding
    # B-updates of the same step.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS), i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
        S1_B_from_A(t, i, j) -> S2_A_from_B(t, i, j)

    # Across time steps, A at step t is the input state for computing B at t+1.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS-1), i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
        S2_A_from_B(t, i, j) -> S1_B_from_A(t+1, i, j)

optimization:
    # ---- Spatial blocking (tiling) for cache locality ----
    # We tile i and j so that sub-blocks of A and B fit better into caches.
    # This preserves semantics because tiles are processed in a way that
    # respects the original order within each full sweep.
    block(i, ii, TI)     # i = ii * TI + i_in_tile
    block(j, jj, TJ)     # j = jj * TJ + j_in_tile

    # Keep time dimension outermost; sweeps remain ordered as in original code.
    hoist(t)

    # Apply tiling separately to both sweeps inside each time step:
    #   for t:
    #     for ii, jj: tile of B-from-A
    #     for ii, jj: tile of A-from-B
    #
    # B tiles for a given time step are fully computed (global barrier implied)
    # before any A tiles of that step are used, preserving:
    #   "finish all B updates at t before any A update at t".
    hoist(ii)
    hoist(jj)

    # ---- Parallelization ----
    # Each (i, j) update within a sweep depends only on neighbor values
    # from the *input* grid of that sweep, which is read-only in that phase.
    # Therefore, the spatial loops are safe to parallelize.
    #
    # We parallelize at the outer tile level to:
    #  - amortize thread-management overhead,
    #  - avoid false sharing on adjacent rows/cols,
    #  - map well onto a 32-core CPU (many tiles in flight).
    parallelize(ii)      # distribute tiles of rows across threads
    # Optionally also:
    # parallelize(jj)    # if many cores and large N, 2D tile parallelism

    # Time loop t remains sequential: there are true dependencies between
    # successive timesteps and between S1 and S2 at a given t.

    # ---- Vectorization along j ----
    # j is contiguous in memory (row-major layout), and the stencil
    # in j-direction has unit stride. This is ideal for SIMD.
    vectorize(j, VEC)

    # ---- Loop unrolling ----
    # Unroll the innermost j loop to:
    #  - expose more ILP,
    #  - reduce loop-control overhead,
    #  - help the compiler schedule loads of neighboring points.
    unroll(j, 4)

    # Optional: mild unrolling in time to increase ILP while respecting
    # sequential time semantics (compiler will emit code for two t-steps
    # inlined, but still ordered).
    unroll(t, 2)

    # ---- Arithmetic hoisting ----
    # The scalar weight w = 0.2 is invariant across all loops.
    # Ensure it is loaded once into a register and reused:
    hoist(w)
    # (This corresponds to computing SCALAR_VAL(0.2) once before
    #  entering the time-stepping loops.)

    # ---- Notes on correctness ----
    # - Boundaries (i = 0 or N-1, j = 0 or N-1) are never written,
    #   exactly as in the original code; they are read as fixed values.
    # - No change is made to the stencil formula or to the ordering
    #   between:
    #       B <- A   and   A <- B
    #   within each time step.
    # - All time steps t are executed in order; no reordering across t.
    # - Parallelization and vectorization affect only independent
    #   (i, j) iterations within each sweep, preserving semantics.
--- END OF MODEL: jacobi-2d-04 ---

--- START OF MODEL: jacobi-2d-05 ---
domain:
    # Interior grid points only; boundary rows/cols 0 and N-1 remain unchanged.
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)
    i: dim in [1, N-1)
    j: dim in [1, N-1)

data:
    # Full N×N grids stored in row-major order.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j   # Row-major, includes boundaries at indices 0 and N-1
    B[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j   # Row-major, used as a ping-pong buffer

parameters:
    N: int                  # Grid size (both dimensions)
    TSTEPS: int             # Number of outer loop iterations in the original code
    w: DATA_TYPE            # Relaxation weight; in the given code w = SCALAR_VAL(0.2)
    TI: int                 # Tunable tile size in the i (row) dimension
    TJ: int                 # Tunable tile size in the j (column) dimension
    VEC_WIDTH: int          # Target vector width (elements) for vectorization over j
    UNROLL_J: int           # Unroll factor for inner j loop

computation:
    # Jacobi 2D stencil with two sweeps per outer time iteration:
    #   1) B = J(A)
    #   2) A = J(B)
    # Boundaries of A and B (i=0 or i=N-1 or j=0 or j=N-1) are never updated.

    for t in seq([0, TSTEPS)):
        # Sweep 1: read from A, write to B.
        A_to_B:
            for i, j:
                B[i, j] = w * (
                              A[i,   j  ] +
                              A[i,   j-1] +
                              A[i,   j+1] +
                              A[i-1, j  ] +
                              A[i+1, j  ]
                          )

        # Sweep 2: read from B, write to A.
        B_to_A:
            for i, j:
                A[i, j] = w * (
                              B[i,   j  ] +
                              B[i,   j-1] +
                              B[i,   j+1] +
                              B[i-1, j  ] +
                              B[i+1, j  ]
                          )

optimization:
    # --- Scalar and aliasing assumptions ------------------------------------
    hoist(w)
    # hoist(S): treat scalar S as loop-invariant and hoist its load/definition
    # outside all loops that use it. Here, w = 0.2 is a constant; ensure it is
    # computed/loaded once, not per iteration.

    assume_no_alias(A, B)
    # assume_no_alias(X, Y): X and Y do not alias in memory. This matches the
    # benchmark intent and enables better vectorization and reordering.

    # --- Spatial blocking for cache locality --------------------------------
    # Tile the 2D interior domain (i, j) to improve cache reuse within each
    # sweep. Each tile operates on a small sub-block of the grid.
    block(i, ii, TI)
    block(j, jj, TJ)
    # block(d, D, S): replace loop over dimension d by an outer tile loop D and
    # an inner loop over d with tile size S. For example:
    #   for i in [1, N-1)  -->
    #     for ii in [1, N-1) step TI:
    #       for i in [ii, min(ii+TI, N-1))
    #
    # TI, TJ should be tuned so that a tile of A and B plus its 1-cell halo
    # fits comfortably in L1/L2 cache.

    # --- Parallelization -----------------------------------------------------
    parallelize(ii)
    # parallelize(D): iterations along tile dimension D can be executed in
    # parallel (e.g., via OpenMP). Each time-step t is sequential, but within
    # a time-step, tiles in ii are independent in a Jacobi sweep, so they can
    # be distributed across cores on the 32-core machine.

    # To increase parallelism further for very large N, one can also
    # parallelize over jj in addition to ii, as long as the runtime partitions
    # tiles to avoid excessive synchronization:
    # parallelize(jj)

    # --- Vectorization and unrolling ----------------------------------------
    vectorize(j, VEC_WIDTH)
    # vectorize(d, W): enforce SIMD vectorization along dimension d with width W.
    # Here, inner j is contiguous in row-major layout, so vector loads/stores
    # for A[i, j±1] and B[i, j±1] are naturally aligned and efficient.

    unroll(j, UNROLL_J)
    # unroll(d, F): unroll loop d by factor F to reduce loop overhead and allow
    # the compiler to better schedule loads, adds, and the final multiply by w.

    # --- Loop ordering -------------------------------------------------------
    # Preserve the original nesting order (t outer, then i, then j) to ensure
    # correctness of the time-dependent stencil and to keep j innermost for
    # vectorization and unit-stride memory access:
    #   t (sequential) -> ii (parallel tiles) -> jj -> i -> j (vectorized)
    #
    # No interchange of t with spatial dimensions is allowed because each
    # time-step depends on the previous one.

    # --- Optional: time-iteration unrolling (purely local) -------------------
    # The outer time loop can be unrolled by a small factor (e.g., 2) to expose
    # more ILP, without changing the number of stencil applications:
    # unroll(t, 2)
    # This preserves semantics because iterations of t are strictly sequential
    # but can still be mechanically unrolled by the compiler.
--- END OF MODEL: jacobi-2d-05 ---

/* lu.c: this file is part of PolyBench/C */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Include polybench common header. */
#include <polybench.h>

/* Include benchmark-specific header. */
#include "lu.h"


/* Array initialization. */
static
void init_array (int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(A,N,N,n,n))
{
  int i, j;

  for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    {
      for (j = 0; j <= i; j++)
	A[i][j] = (DATA_TYPE)(-j % n) / n + 1;
      for (j = i+1; j < n; j++) {
	A[i][j] = 0;
      }
      A[i][i] = 1;
    }

  /* Make the matrix positive semi-definite. */
  /* not necessary for LU, but using same code as cholesky */
  int r,s,t;
  POLYBENCH_2D_ARRAY_DECL(B, DATA_TYPE, N, N, n, n);
  for (r = 0; r < n; ++r)
    for (s = 0; s < n; ++s)
      (POLYBENCH_ARRAY(B))[r][s] = 0;
  for (t = 0; t < n; ++t)
    for (r = 0; r < n; ++r)
      for (s = 0; s < n; ++s)
	(POLYBENCH_ARRAY(B))[r][s] += A[r][t] * A[s][t];
    for (r = 0; r < n; ++r)
      for (s = 0; s < n; ++s)
	A[r][s] = (POLYBENCH_ARRAY(B))[r][s];
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(B);

}


/* DCE code. Must scan the entire live-out data.
   Can be used also to check the correctness of the output. */
static
void print_array(int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(A,N,N,n,n))

{
  int i, j;

  POLYBENCH_DUMP_START;
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_BEGIN("A");
  for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++) {
      if ((i * n + j) % 20 == 0) fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, "\n");
      fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, DATA_PRINTF_MODIFIER, A[i][j]);
    }
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_END("A");
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_FINISH;
}


/* Main computational kernel. The whole function will be timed,
   including the call and return. */
static
void kernel_lu[[gnu::flatten, gnu::noinline]](int n,
	       DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(A,N,N,n,n))
{
  int i, j, k;

#pragma scop
  for (i = 0; i < _PB_N; i++) {
    for (j = 0; j <i; j++) {
       for (k = 0; k < j; k++) {
          A[i][j] -= A[i][k] * A[k][j];
       }
        A[i][j] /= A[j][j];
    }
   for (j = i; j < _PB_N; j++) {
       for (k = 0; k < i; k++) {
          A[i][j] -= A[i][k] * A[k][j];
       }
    }
  }
#pragma endscop
}


int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
  /* Retrieve problem size. */
  int n = N;

  /* Variable declaration/allocation. */
  POLYBENCH_2D_ARRAY_DECL(A, DATA_TYPE, N, N, n, n);

  /* Initialize array(s). */
  init_array (n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(A));

  /* Start timer. */
  polybench_start_instruments;

  /* Run kernel. */
  kernel_lu (n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(A));

  /* Stop and print timer. */
  polybench_stop_instruments;
  polybench_print_instruments;

  /* Prevent dead-code elimination. All live-out data must be printed
     by the function call in argument. */
  polybench_prevent_dce(print_array(n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(A)));

  /* Be clean. */
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(A);

  return 0;
}

domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)          # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index
    k: dim in [0, N)          # reduction index

data:
    # A stores the matrix in-place LU factors:
    #   - unit diagonal L in the strict lower triangle (L[i,i] is implicitly 1)
    #   - U in the upper triangle including the diagonal
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j   # row-major

parameters:
    N: int

    # Tuning parameters for cache and SIMD usage (chosen per target machine)
    TILE_I: int  # e.g., 32   – panel height
    TILE_J: int  # e.g., 64   – width of upper update tiles
    TILE_K: int  # e.g., 32   – blocking for k-reductions

    VEC_J: int   # SIMD width along j (upper update), e.g., 8 for AVX2 double
    VEC_K: int   # SIMD width along k (reduction), often same as VEC_J
    UNROLL_K: int  # small unroll factor for k, e.g., 4

computation:
    # LU factorization without pivoting (Doolittle), in-place:
    # For each row i, first compute strict lower part L(i,0..i-1),
    # then update upper part U(i,i..N-1).

    for i in seq([0, N)):
        # ----- Strict lower triangle: compute L(i, j) for j < i -----
        # Must be sequential in j because A[i, j] depends on A[i, 0..j-1].
        for j in seq([0, i)):
            # Use a scalar accumulator to keep A[i, j] in a register.
            # This directly matches:
            #   for (k = 0; k < j; k++) A[i][j] -= A[i][k] * A[k][j];
            #   A[i][j] /= A[j][j];
            tmp_L = A[i, j]
                    - sum(k in [0, j)) (A[i, k] * A[k, j])
            A[i, j] = tmp_L / A[j, j]

        # ----- Upper triangle including diagonal: compute U(i, j) for j >= i -----
        # Once L(i, 0..i-1) is known, each U(i, j) (j >= i) depends only on:
        #   A[i, j] (current value), A[i, 0..i-1], and A[0..i-1, j].
        # These j-iterations are mutually independent and may be parallelized.
        #
        # Mathematically:
        #   A[i, j] = A[i, j] - sum(k in [0, i)) A[i, k] * A[k, j]
        #
        # We expose this as a reduction over k and allow loop reordering.
        for j in [i, N):
            tmp_U = A[i, j]
                    - sum(k in [0, i)) (A[i, k] * A[k, j])
            A[i, j] = tmp_U


optimization:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Register reuse and reduction formulation
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # - The use of tmp_L / tmp_U expresses that A[i, j] is loaded once,
    #   updated in a register via a k-reduction, and written back once.
    # - This reduces memory traffic and makes the k loop a clear reduction,
    #   enabling vectorization and unrolling.
    #
    # (No explicit directive needed beyond the sum() notation; this is
    #  a semantic clarification of the computation.)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Blocking (tiling) for cache locality
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # We tile i, j, and k dimensions. i must remain sequential at tile level,
    # but tiling improves reuse of matrix panels/rows in caches.
    #
    # block(DIMENSION, TILE_DIMENSION, TILE_SIZE) splits:
    #   DIMENSION = TILE_DIMENSION * TILE_SIZE + inner_remainder
    # and nests loops as for TILE_DIMENSION (outer) and DIMENSION (inner).

    block(i, I, TILE_I)   # panel/blocking over rows
    block(j, J, TILE_J)   # tiling over columns, mainly effective for U-part
    block(k, K, TILE_K)   # tiling the reduction to fit A[*][k] and A[k][*] in cache

    # Keep I (the tile index of i) at the outermost level to preserve
    # row-wise dependency ordering: earlier i-tiles complete before later ones.
    hoist(I)

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Loop interchange in the upper update (rank-1 style update)
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # For the upper-part update, a more cache-friendly form is:
    #   for i:
    #     for k in [0, i):
    #       let lik = A[i, k];
    #       for j in [i, N):
    #         A[i, j] -= lik * A[k, j];
    #
    # This reuses A[i, k] across all j and expresses a sequence of rank-1
    # updates. It is obtained by interchanging j and k in the U loop
    # (and hoisting A[i, k] into a scalar), which is mathematically
    # equivalent to the sum-reduction formulation above.

    #interchange(J, K)  # applied only in the U(i, j) computation region
    #hoist(A[i, K])     # keep A[i, k] (lik) in a scalar across inner j-loop

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Parallelism
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # - The outer i-dimension cannot be parallelized due to true dependencies:
    #   row i uses factors from rows 0..i-1.
    # - Within a given i:
    #   * The lower-part (j < i) is strictly sequential in j.
    #   * The upper-part (j >= i) is embarrassingly parallel across j
    #     once the entire lower row i is computed.

    # Parallelize the j-dimension only for the upper update loop.
    # This assumes a code generator capable of distinguishing the
    # j-loop region with j in [i, N).
    parallelize(j)  # in the upper-triangular (U) update region only

    # Optionally, when using the interchanged U loop:
    #   parallelize(J)  # outer j-tiles, so each thread updates a stripe of columns

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Vectorization and unrolling of reductions
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # - The k-reductions for both L and U updates are good SIMD candidates:
    #   contiguous access to either A[i, k] (row) or A[k, j] (column)
    #   depending on interchange decisions and architecture.
    # - We vectorize K (inner blocked k) and unroll it to reduce loop overhead.

    vectorize(K, VEC_K)     # vectorize inner k-block in reductions
    unroll(K, UNROLL_K)     # unroll reduction loop for better ILP

    # In the U(i, j) loop before interchange (original j-outer, k-inner form),
    # vectorizing j instead can also be beneficial when TILE_J is large enough.
    vectorize(J, VEC_J)     # SIMD across columns in upper update

    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6. Summary of data-layout decision
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # We retain row-major layout:
    #   - Access A[i, k] with unit stride in the innermost k-loop
    #     (original form) or second-innermost loop (after interchange).
    #   - Access A[k, j] with stride N, but blocking over k and j mitigates this.
    #
    # Changing A to column-major would only swap which of A[i, k] or A[k, j]
    # is contiguous and would complicate interoperability; given the strong
    # reuse of row i in each iteration and the in-place nature of LU,
    # we keep the original row-major layout.
--- END OF MODEL: lu-01 ---

domain:
    # Matrix dimension
    i: dim in [0, N)
    j: dim in [0, N)
    k: dim in [0, N)
    t: dim in [0, N)  # used for Gram-matrix construction in init_array

data:
    # Global matrix A: initialized in init_array, factorized in-place by kernel_lu
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # row-major

    # Temporary matrix used only inside init_array to build a Gram matrix
    B[i, j]: temp DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # row-major

parameters:
    N: int  # problem size

    # Tuning parameters (constants chosen for a given machine)
    TJ_init:   int  # tile size in j for Gram-matrix construction
    TT_init:   int  # tile size in t for Gram-matrix construction
    TI_init:   int  # tile size in i for Gram-matrix construction

    TJ_lu:     int  # tile size along j in the LU trailing-update
    VECW:      int  # vector width for j-vectorization (e.g., 4 for AVX2 double)
    UNROLL_K:  int  # unroll factor for k-loop inside LU (e.g., 2–4)


computation:
    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. init_array: build initial lower-triangular A and then
    #    replace it by a symmetric positive semi-definite A := A * A^T
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    # 1.a Seed A as a unit-lower-triangular-like matrix
    init_lower:
      for i in [0, N), j in [0, i]:
        A[i, j] = (DATA_TYPE)((-j % N)) / N + (DATA_TYPE)1

    init_upper:
      for i in [0, N), j in (i, N):
        A[i, j] = (DATA_TYPE)0

    init_diag:
      for i in [0, N):
        A[i, i] = (DATA_TYPE)1

    # 1.b Build B = A * A^T (Gram matrix), then A := B.
    #     This is exactly what the nested loops over t, r, s compute.

    zero_B:
      for i, j:
        B[i, j] = (DATA_TYPE)0

    gram_B:
      # B[i, j] = sum_t A[i, t] * A[j, t]
      for i, j:
        B[i, j] = sum(t in [0, N), A[i, t] * A[j, t])

    copy_B_to_A:
      for i, j:
        A[i, j] = B[i, j]


    # ------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. kernel_lu: in-place LU factorization without pivoting
    #
    # Original kernel:
    #   for i = 0..N-1:
    #     # L-row
    #     for j = 0..i-1:
    #       for k = 0..j-1:
    #         A[i,j] -= A[i,k] * A[k,j];
    #       A[i,j] /= A[j,j];
    #     # U-row
    #     for j = i..N-1:
    #       for k = 0..i-1:
    #         A[i,j] -= A[i,k] * A[k,j];
    #
    # Below we express an equivalent right-looking formulation that
    # preserves the per-element operation order and thus the bitwise
    # result, but has better locality and vectorization properties.
    # ------------------------------------------------------------

    LU_factor:
      # i is sequential: each row depends on rows 0..i-1
      for i in seq(0, N):

        # For each previous column k of row i:
        for k in seq(0, i):
          # 2.a Compute one L(i, k) entry in the strictly lower part.
          #     For k == i, this is skipped; unit diagonal is implicit.
          if k < i:
            # At this point A[i, k] already contains
            #   A[i, k]_0 - sum_{p=0..k-1} L(i, p) * U(p, k)
            # so the division produces L(i, k).
            A[i, k] = A[i, k] / A[k, k]

          # 2.b Right-looking update of the trailing part of row i:
          #     for all columns j > k, subtract the k-th rank-1 contribution.
          #     This covers:
          #       - j in (k, i): remaining L(i, j) numerators
          #       - j in [i, N): U(i, j) entries.
          for j in (k + 1, N):
            # A[i, j] -= L(i, k) * U(k, j)
            # where L(i, k) is now stored in A[i, k] and U(k, j) in A[k, j].
            A[i, j] = A[i, j] - A[i, k] * A[k, j]


dependencies:
    # Explicitly describe key dependencies for the LU factorization.

    # (1) Row-wise dependency: to factor row i, all rows < i must be complete
    #     (both their L and U parts), since they are used as U(k, *) and
    #     L(*, k) in later rows.
    for i in [1, N):
      LU_factor(i - 1) -> LU_factor(i)

    # (2) Within row i, each step k depends on all previous k' < k
    #     because A[i, k] uses updated values A[i, p] with p < k and
    #     U(p, k) from earlier rows.
    for i in [0, N), k in [1, i):
      LU_factor(i, k - 1) -> LU_factor(i, k)


optimization:
    # ============================================================
    # Optimizations for init_array (Gram matrix A := A * A^T)
    # ============================================================

    # Recognize gram_B as B = A * A^T and turn it into a cache-blocked GEMM.
    block(i, I_init, TI_init)   # tile rows of B
    block(j, J_init, TJ_init)   # tile columns of B
    block(t, T_init, TT_init)   # tile inner-product dimension

    # Within each (I_init, J_init, T_init) tile, the computation becomes:
    #   for i in I_init:
    #     for j in J_init:
    #       B[i, j] += sum_{t in T_init} A[i, t] * A[j, t]
    # which has good temporal locality for tiles of A and B.

    # Exploit symmetry of B = A * A^T to cut work almost in half.
    # This is semantics-preserving and bitwise identical because
    #   B[i, j] and B[j, i] are computed as the same sum of the same
    #   products in the same order in the original code.
    #
    # We express this as:
    #   - Restrict gram_B to i <= j (upper triangle including diagonal).
    #   - Add a symmetric fill step for the lower triangle.
    #
    # #symmetric_half_gram:
    #   for i in [0, N), j in [i, N):
    #     B[i, j] = sum(t, A[i, t] * A[j, t])
    #   for i in [0, N), j in [0, i):
    #     B[i, j] = B[j, i]

    parallelize(I_init)         # distribute row-tiles of B across cores
    vectorize(j, VECW)          # vectorize across columns inside a tile


    # ============================================================
    # Optimizations for kernel_lu (in-place LU)
    # ============================================================

    # Keep i as the outermost sequential loop (strong inter-row deps).
    hoist(i)

    # The LU_factor computation already encodes a right-looking form
    # derived from the original two nested loops via legal transforms:
    #
    #  - For the original U-update (second j-loop), we interchange (j, k):
    #       for j = i..N-1
    #         for k = 0..i-1   body(i,j,k)
    #    ->  for k = 0..i-1
    #         for j = i..N-1   body(i,j,k)
    #    This preserves the order of updates for each (i, j) element,
    #    so floating-point results are bitwise identical.
    #
    #  - For the L-update (first j-loop), we similarly transform the
    #    left-looking scheme into an equivalent right-looking one:
    #       for j = 0..i-1:
    #         for k = 0..j-1: A[i,j] -= A[i,k]*A[k,j];
    #         A[i,j] /= A[j,j];
    #    ->
    #       for k = 0..i-1:
    #         A[i,k] /= A[k,k];
    #         for j = k+1..i-1: A[i,j] -= A[i,k]*A[k,j];
    #    Again, the sequence of operations on each A[i,j] is unchanged.

    # Improve locality and vectorization in the trailing update (inner j-loop).
    block(j, J_lu, TJ_lu)       # work on tiles along the row (j dimension)
    hoist(J_lu)

    # For a fixed (i, k), each j-tile J_lu touches a contiguous segment
    # of rows i and k, ideal for cache lines and SIMD.

    # Parallelize across independent j-tiles within each row i.
    # Each tile updates a disjoint interval of row i and only reads
    # shared, read-only data from previous rows, so no synchronization
    # is needed beyond the natural barrier at each i.
    parallelize(J_lu)

    # Vectorize inside j-tiles: the inner loop becomes a SAXPY-like
    # fused multiply-subtract on contiguous memory (A[k, j], A[i, j]).
    vectorize(j, VECW)

    # Unroll k to increase instruction-level parallelism in the chain
    # over previous columns while keeping code size reasonable.
    unroll(k, UNROLL_K)

    # Implicit scalar/temporal hoisting (captured by the loop form):
    #   - A[i, k] is loaded once per (i, k), kept in a scalar register
    #   - A[k, j] is streamed contiguously inside each tile
    #   - A[i, j] is accumulated in registers across k and written back once
--- END OF MODEL: lu-02 ---

--- START OF MODEL: lu-03 ---
domain:
    # Matrix is N x N, 0-based as in the C code
    i:  dim in [0, N)      # row index
    jL: dim in [0, N)      # column index for L-part (j < i)
    jU: dim in [0, N)      # column index for U-part (j >= i)
    k:  dim in [0, N)      # reduction / inner-product index

data:
    # In-place LU factors, stored in a single row-major array:
    #   - strict lower triangle (i > j): L (unit diagonal implied)
    #   - upper triangle (i <= j): U
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # row-major layout

parameters:
    N: int                    # problem size
    # Tuning knobs for performance (compile-time or run-time constants):
    TJ: int                   # tile size for jU (columns of trailing submatrix), e.g., 64–256
    TK: int                   # tile size for k in U-part, e.g., 16–64
    TK_L: int                 # tile size for k in L-part, typically smaller than TK
    VJ: int                   # SIMD width used for vectorizing over columns (jU)
    UK: int                   # unroll factor for K in U-part
    UK_L: int                 # unroll factor for K in L-part

computation:
    # For each row i, first compute L(i, j) for j < i, then U(i, j) for j >= i.
    # This matches the original kernel_lu loop nest structurally.

    for i in seq([0, N)):

        # --- L update: strict lower triangle, row i, columns 0 .. i-1 ---
        # A[i, jL] = ( A[i, jL] - sum_{k=0}^{jL-1} A[i, k] * A[k, jL] ) / A[jL, jL]
        # jL must be processed in increasing order because A[i, k] for k < jL
        # are produced by earlier jL iterations.
        L(i, jL):
            for jL in seq([0, i)):
                A[i, jL] =
                    ( A[i, jL]
                      - sum(k in [0, jL): A[i, k] * A[k, jL] )
                    ) / A[jL, jL]

        # --- U update: upper triangle including diagonal, row i, columns i .. N-1 ---
        # A[i, jU] = A[i, jU] - sum_{k=0}^{i-1} A[i, k] * A[k, jU]
        # For fixed i, different jU iterations are independent.
        U(i, jU):
            for jU in [i, N):
                A[i, jU] =
                    A[i, jU]
                    - sum(k in [0, i): A[i, k] * A[k, jU])

dependencies:
    # The row loop i is explicitly sequential (seq), so rows execute in order:
    #   all updates for row i happen before row i+1.
    #
    # Within each row i:
    #   - L(i, jL) is sequential in jL by construction (seq).
    #   - U(i, jU) is independent across jU once all L(i, *) are known.
    #
    # To make this explicit:
    for i in [0, N), jL in [0, i), jU in [i, N):
        L(i, jL) -> U(i, jU)   # complete the L-part of row i before any U-part of row i

optimization:
    # High-level goals:
    #   - Respect all true data dependencies (no pivoting is introduced).
    #   - Keep the lower-triangular (L) jL-loop strictly sequential.
    #   - Turn the U-part into a cache-friendly, vectorized, and parallel update
    #     over the trailing submatrix.

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Reorder the U update to improve reuse (saxpy-like formulation)
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # U(i, jU) currently computes:
    #   A[i, jU] = A[i, jU] - sum_{k=0}^{i-1} A[i, k] * A[k, jU]
    # which is mathematically a reduction over k. The contributions from
    # different k are associative (up to FP round-off), so we can swap jU and k.
    #
    # Conceptual transformed order for the U-part at fixed i:
    #   for k in [0, i):
    #       let aik = A[i, k]    # hoist to a scalar
    #       for jU in [i, N):
    #           A[i, jU] -= aik * A[k, jU]
    #
    # This:
    #   - keeps A[i, k] (aik) in a register across many jU,
    #   - streams A[k, jU] and A[i, jU] in contiguous row-major order,
    #   - preserves the mathematical result.
    #
    # We express this via an interchange of jU and k in the U reduction.
    # (L's use of k is unchanged.)
    interchange(jU, k)  # applied only where jU and k are both active, effectively in U

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Tiling / blocking of U’s jU and k dimensions
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # After reordering, U’s effective structure per row i is:
    #   for k in [0, i):
    #     for jU in [i, N):
    #       A[i, jU] -= A[i, k] * A[k, jU]
    #
    # We tile jU and k to form cache-sized blocks over the trailing submatrix.
    # TJ and TK are tunable tile sizes that should be chosen to fit L1/L2.
    block(jU, JU, TJ)   # tile the trailing columns for better spatial locality
    block(k,  K,  TK)   # tile the reduction dimension to improve reuse of A[k, *]

    # Place tile loops just inside i to expose parallelism and maximize reuse
    hoist(JU)
    hoist(K)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Vectorization and parallelization of U over columns
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # After tiling, a typical inner kernel for U has shape:
    #   for K in tiles of k:
    #     for JU in tiles of jU:
    #       for k in K:
    #         aik = A[i, k]
    #         for jU in JU:
    #           A[i, jU] -= aik * A[k, jU]
    #
    # The innermost jU loop touches contiguous elements of A[i, jU] and A[k, jU],
    # so it is ideal for SIMD vectorization.
    vectorize(JU, VJ)   # VJ chosen per SIMD width (e.g., 4 or 8 doubles)

    # For fixed i, iterations over tiles JU are independent (no write conflicts),
    # so we can parallelize them across threads. The i loop itself remains
    # strictly sequential to respect the LU dependencies across rows.
    parallelize(JU)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Micro-optimizations for U’s reduction over k
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Within each K tile, unroll the k-loop and keep A[i, k] in registers.
    # This reduces loop overhead and lets the compiler schedule FMAs efficiently.
    unroll(K, UK)

    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Local optimizations for the L update (lower triangle)
    # ---------------------------------------------------------------------
    # L(i, jL) has an inner sum:
    #   sum_{k=0}^{jL-1} A[i, k] * A[k, jL]
    # which:
    #   - cannot reorder jL (data dependence along jL),
    #   - *can* tile/unroll k for slightly better cache behavior and ILP.
    #
    # We apply a modest tile of k (TK_L) and unroll that tile. The jL loop
    # itself remains 'seq' and is not parallelized or interchanged.
    block(k,  KL, TK_L)  # within L’s sum only; TK_L kept relatively small
    unroll(KL, UK_L)

    # NOTE:
    # - No additional large buffers are introduced; all updates are in-place on A.
    # - Extra storage, if any, is limited to a few scalars and small tiles
    #   implied by unrolling, well within the 50% memory-usage constraint.
--- END OF MODEL: lu-03 ---

--- START OF MODEL: lu-04 ---
domain:
    # Problem size
    N: size

    # Loop indices following the original kernel
    i: dim in [0, N)      # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)      # column index
    k: dim in [0, N)      # reduction index

    # Auxiliary index used only in dependency specifications
    row: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # A stores both L and U in-place, row-major:
    #  - strictly lower triangle (j < i) holds L(i, j)
    #  - diagonal and upper triangle (j >= i) hold U(i, j)
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # Reciprocal of diagonal pivots 1 / A[j, j]; used to avoid repeated divisions.
    inv_diag[j]: aux DATA_TYPE = (j) -> j   # contiguous 1D array

parameters:
    # Matrix dimension
    N: int

    # Tunable tile sizes for the upper-factor update (row-panel update)
    BK: int  # block size along k (previous rows), e.g., 32
    BJ: int  # block size along j (columns of U), e.g., 64

    # Optional vector width along the j (column) dimension
    VEC_J: int  # e.g., 4 for AVX2 double, 8 for AVX2 float

computation:
    # In-place, no-pivot LU factorization of A.
    # L has unit diagonal; its strictly lower part is stored in A[i, j] for j < i.
    # U is stored in the upper triangle of A, including the diagonal.

    for i in seq(0, N):              # outer loop over rows is strictly sequential

        # ---- 1. Compute strict lower-triangular entries L(i, j), 0 <= j < i ----
        #      L(i, j) = ( A(i, j) - sum_{k=0..j-1} L(i, k) * U(k, j) ) / U(j, j)
        #      We use inv_diag[j] = 1 / U(j, j) to replace division by multiplication.
        for j in seq(0, i):          # j ranges [0, i)
            L_update:
            A[i, j] =
                ( A[i, j]
                  - sum(k in [0, j): A[i, k] * A[k, j] )
                ) * inv_diag[j]

        # ---- 2. Compute upper-triangular row U(i, j), i <= j < N ----
        #      U(i, j) = A(i, j) - sum_{k=0..i-1} L(i, k) * U(k, j)
        for j in [i, N):
            U_update:
            A[i, j] =
                A[i, j]
                - sum(k in [0, i): A[i, k] * A[k, j])

        # ---- 3. Cache reciprocal of the new pivot for use in later rows ----
        # inv_diag[i] is used in L_update(row, j = i) for all row > i.
        DIAG_RECIP:
        inv_diag[i] = 1.0 / A[i, i]


dependencies:
    # 1. Within a given row i, lower-factor entries L(i, j) must be computed
    #    from left to right because L(i, j) depends on all L(i, k) with k < j.
    for i in [0, N), j in [0, i-1]:
        L_update(i, j) -> L_update(i, j + 1)

    # 2. Upper-factor entries U(i, j) on row i depend on the complete set of
    #    L(i, 0..i-1) multipliers of the same row.
    for i in [0, N), j in [i, N), k in [0, i):
        L_update(i, k) -> U_update(i, j)

    # 3. The cached reciprocal inv_diag[i] depends on the pivot U(i, i)
    #    and must be available before it is used in lower rows.
    for i in [0, N):
        U_update(i, i) -> DIAG_RECIP(i)
    for i in [0, N), row in (i, N):
        DIAG_RECIP(i) -> L_update(row, i)

    # Note: The outer i loop remains globally ordered (0, 1, 2, ...), preserving
    #       standard Doolittle LU dependencies across rows.


optimization:
    # ============================================================
    # Global structure
    # ============================================================
    # The i-loop carries true dependences and must remain sequential.
    hoist(i)

    # (Optional) Row blocking: preserves row order but can help cache behavior
    # when combined with other blocking. TI is fixed at compile-time or chosen
    # empirically; it does not change semantics.
    block(i, I, 32)   # I is row-block index; process rows in blocks of 32

    # ============================================================
    # Optimizations for reductions over k (both L_update and U_update)
    # ============================================================
    # The inner sums over k are reductions; we can safely unroll and vectorize
    # them using a private accumulator in registers.
    unroll(k, 4)
    vectorize(k, 4)   # implement as tree-reduction in SIMD registers

    # ============================================================
    # Optimizations specific to U_update (j >= i)
    # ============================================================
    # For fixed i, U_update has the form:
    #   A[i, j] -= sum_{k < i} A[i, k] * A[k, j]
    # Different j in [i, N) are independent for fixed i.

    # 1. 2D blocking in (k, j) to improve locality:
    #    - A[i, k] (the multipliers of row i) are reused for all j,
    #      so tiling over k lets us keep a subset of them hot in L1/L2.
    #    - A[k, j] is stored row-major, so blocking j makes accesses to
    #      A[k, j] contiguous.
    block(k, K, BK)         # BK tuned for L1/L2 (e.g., 32)
    block(j, J, BJ)         # BJ tuned for L1/L2/L3 (e.g., 64)
    interchange(K, J)       # iterate over k-tiles outer, j-tiles inner

    # Conceptually, for each fixed i, this gives:
    #   for K in tiles of k in [0, i):
    #     for J in tiles of j in [i, N):
    #       for k in K:
    #         for j in J:
    #           A[i, j] -= A[i, k] * A[k, j]

    # 2. Parallelism across j (columns of U):
    #    Within a fixed row i and fixed K-tile, updates to different columns are
    #    independent. We therefore parallelize over J (column tiles).
    parallelize(J)          # distribute column tiles J across threads

    # 3. SIMD along the j dimension:
    #    Within each J-tile, j is the fastest-varying index in row-major A,
    #    so SIMD over j achieves contiguous loads/stores.
    vectorize(j, VEC_J)

    # 4. Residual unrolling on the k loop inside each (K, J) tile for better
    #    instruction-level parallelism and FMA utilization (if available).
    unroll(k, 4)

    # ============================================================
    # Optimization for DIAG_RECIP
    # ============================================================
    # DIAG_RECIP is already hoisted outside the inner loops and computed once
    # per row. This replaces O(N^2) divisions in L_update by cheaper
    # multiplications with inv_diag[j], while adding only an O(N)-sized
    # temporary (inv_diag) well within the allowed memory overhead.
