domain:
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)          # time step
    i: dim in [0, N)               # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)               # column index

data:
    # Single in-place grid including boundary cells at i,j = 0 and N-1.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # Row-major layout

    # Scalar temporaries used inside the (t,i)-loop to implement a sliding
    # 3-point window along j for rows i-1 and i+1.
    s_up:  tmp DATA_TYPE   # sum A[i-1, j-1] + A[i-1, j] + A[i-1, j+1]
    s_mid: tmp DATA_TYPE   # sum A[i,   j-1] + A[i,   j] + A[i,   j+1]
    s_dn:  tmp DATA_TYPE   # sum A[i+1, j-1] + A[i+1, j] + A[i+1, j+1]

parameters:
    N:       int           # grid dimension (N x N), includes boundary
    TSTEPS:  int           # number of time steps
    TI:      int           # tile size in the i (row) dimension; tuning knob
    inv9:    DATA_TYPE     # = SCALAR_VAL(1.0) / SCALAR_VAL(9.0)

computation:
    # 2D Gauss–Seidel over a 9-point stencil, performed in-place on A.
    # Boundaries (i=0 or N-1, j=0 or N-1) are left unchanged.
    update:
        for t in seq([0, TSTEPS)):
            for i in seq([1, N-1)):              # interior rows 1 .. N-2

                # --- Initialize sliding window at j = 1 --------------------
                # For j = 1, the 3-point horizontal windows are:
                #   columns 0,1,2 in rows i-1, i, i+1.
                s_up  = A[i-1, 0] + A[i-1, 1] + A[i-1, 2]
                s_mid = A[i,   0] + A[i,   1] + A[i,   2]
                s_dn  = A[i+1, 0] + A[i+1, 1] + A[i+1, 2]

                # First interior update in the row: j = 1.
                A[i, 1] = (s_up + s_mid + s_dn) * inv9

                # --- Main sweep: j = 2 .. N-2 -----------------------------
                # Note: j is strictly sequential because of the dependence
                # A[i, j-1] -> A[i, j].
                for j in seq([2, N-1)):          # interior cols 2 .. N-2

                    # Slide the 3-wide window one cell to the right in the
                    # rows above and below. Those rows are not modified
                    # inside this (t,i)-sweep, so their values are stable.
                    # New windows are:
                    #   [j-1, j, j+1] in rows i-1 and i+1.
                    s_up = s_up + A[i-1, j+1] - A[i-1, j-2]
                    s_dn = s_dn + A[i+1, j+1] - A[i+1, j-2]

                    # Central row window at current (t,i,j):
                    # - A[i, j-1] has already been updated at this time step.
                    # - A[i, j], A[i, j+1] are still from the previous state.
                    s_mid = A[i, j-1] + A[i, j] + A[i, j+1]

                    # 9-point Gauss–Seidel update using the three row sums.
                    A[i, j] = (s_up + s_mid + s_dn) * inv9


dependencies:
    # Intra-time-step Gauss–Seidel dependences:
    # Each interior update (t,i,j) depends on:
    #   - (t, i,   j-1)   : left neighbor (same row, previous column)
    #   - (t, i-1, j-1..j+1): three neighbors in the row above
    #
    # (Boundary conditions are excluded from the domains below.)

    # Left neighbor in same row.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS),
        i in [1, N-1),
        j in [2, N-1):               # j >= 2 so j-1 >= 1
        update(t, i, j-1) -> update(t, i, j)

    # Above-left neighbor.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS),
        i in [2, N-1),               # i-1 >= 1
        j in [2, N-1):               # j-1 >= 1
        update(t, i-1, j-1) -> update(t, i, j)

    # Above neighbor.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS),
        i in [2, N-1),
        j in [1, N-1):
        update(t, i-1, j) -> update(t, i, j)

    # Above-right neighbor.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS),
        i in [2, N-1),
        j in [1, N-2):               # j+1 <= N-2
        update(t, i-1, j+1) -> update(t, i, j)

    # Inter-time-step dependence: each point depends on its own value
    # from the previous time step.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS-1),
        i in [1, N-1),
        j in [1, N-1):
        update(t, i, j) -> update(t+1, i, j)


optimization:
    # 1. Cache-aware blocking in the i (row) dimension.
    #
    # block(i, I, TI) tiles i into outer tile index I and intra-tile index i,
    # preserving the original lexicographic order of (i,j):
    #
    #   for t
    #     for I in 1..N-2 step TI
    #       for i in I .. min(I+TI-1, N-2)
    #         for j in 1..N-2
    #
    # This keeps the execution order of all (i,j) identical to the original
    # code (just grouped into row-blocks), so all Gauss–Seidel dependences
    # remain valid.
    block(i, I, TI)
    # TI should be chosen so that three rows (i-1, i, i+1) of a tile and their
    # working set fit into L1/L2 cache. For double precision on a typical
    # 32 KiB L1, TI ≈ 64 is a reasonable starting value.

    # 2. Sliding-window reuse along j (already encoded in 'computation').
    #
    # The use of s_up and s_dn implements a 3-point sliding window along j
    # for rows i-1 and i+1. This reduces memory traffic from 9 loads per
    # grid point (naive 9-point stencil) to roughly 5, while keeping the
    # arithmetic structure essentially unchanged. The compiler can keep
    # s_up, s_mid, and s_dn in registers.

    # 3. Strength reduction: replace division by 9.0 with multiplication.
    #
    # The parameter 'inv9' is computed once (outside the kernel) as
    # SCALAR_VAL(1.0) / SCALAR_VAL(9.0), and the kernel uses multiplication
    # by inv9 instead of division by 9.0 inside the innermost loops.

    # 4. Inner-loop unrolling for instruction-level parallelism.
    #
    # Small-factor unrolling of the j-loop improves ILP while preserving
    # the dependence distance-1 in j, because the unrolled body still
    # evaluates j in strictly increasing order.
    unroll(j, 2)

    # 5. Parallelism considerations.
    #
    # Due to the Gauss–Seidel update order:
    #   - t has a dependence on t-1 (same cell),
    #   - i depends on i-1 (row above),
    #   - j depends on j-1 (left neighbor),
    # naive parallelization or vectorization in t, i, or j would violate
    # the specified dependences and change the numerical result.
    # Therefore no 'parallelize' or 'vectorize' directives are applied here.
--- END OF MODEL: seidel-2d-01 ---

--- START OF MODEL: seidel-2d-02 ---
domain:
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)          # time steps
    i: dim in [1, N-1)             # interior rows:  1 .. N-2
    j: dim in [1, N-1)             # interior cols:  1 .. N-2

data:
    # 2D grid including boundaries; backing storage is N×N row‑major.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j   # row-major, i,j ∈ [0, N)

parameters:
    N: int                          # grid extent in each dimension (including boundaries)
    TSTEPS: int                     # number of time steps
    inv9: DATA_TYPE                 # precomputed constant = 1.0 / 9.0

    # Tuning parameters for this kernel on the target x64 machine:
    TILE_I: int                     # tile size for i, e.g., 32 or 64; 1 ≤ TILE_I ≤ N-2
    UNROLL_J: int                   # unroll factor for j, e.g., 4 or 8; UNROLL_J | (N-2) preferred

computation:
    # In-place 2D Gauss–Seidel stencil:
    # for each time step t, sweep the interior of A in lexicographic (i,j) order,
    # updating each point to the average of its 3×3 neighborhood.
    update:
        for t in seq([0, TSTEPS)):
            for i in seq([1, N-1)):
                for j in seq([1, N-1)):
                    A[i, j] =
                        inv9 * (
                            A[i-1, j-1] + A[i-1, j] + A[i-1, j+1] +
                            A[i,   j-1] + A[i,   j] + A[i,   j+1] +
                            A[i+1, j-1] + A[i+1, j] + A[i+1, j+1]
                        )

dependencies:
    # Gauss–Seidel update order within each time step.
    # Each (t,i,j) must see already-updated values from:
    #   - its left neighbor on the same row
    #   - the three neighbors on the previous row
    #
    # This enforces the same lexicographic execution order as the original
    # triple loop (t outer, then i, then j).
    for t in [0, TSTEPS), i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
        update(t, i, j-1)   -> update(t, i, j)    # left   neighbor
        update(t, i-1, j-1) -> update(t, i, j)    # up-left neighbor
        update(t, i-1, j)   -> update(t, i, j)    # up     neighbor
        update(t, i-1, j+1) -> update(t, i, j)    # up-right neighbor

    # Time-stepping is inherently sequential: each step t+1 consumes the
    # state written by all iterations at step t. We therefore keep t
    # strictly sequential and do not parallelize or reorder it.
    # (Exact neighbor-level time dependences are omitted for brevity but
    # are fully enforced by the seq([0, TSTEPS)) annotation.)

optimization:
    # Strength reduction for the constant divisor:
    #   Original: A[i,j] = (sum of 9 neighbors) / 9.0
    #   Model:    A[i,j] = inv9 * (sum of 9 neighbors)
    #
    # inv9 is treated as a precomputed parameter equal to 1.0 / 9.0,
    # removing a costly division from the innermost loop and replacing
    # it with a multiplication.

    # 1) Cache-friendly 1D blocking along the outer spatial dimension i.
    #    This preserves the original lexicographic (i,j) order and all
    #    Gauss–Seidel dependences because tiling only along i does not
    #    change the relative order of any (i,j) pair.
    #
    #    Transformed loop nest shape (conceptually):
    #        for t:
    #          for I = 1 .. N-2 step TILE_I:
    #            for i = I .. min(I+TILE_I-1, N-2):
    #              for j = 1 .. N-2:
    #                update body
    #
    #    This groups consecutive rows into bands that fit better in cache/TLB
    #    when N is large, but does not introduce any illegal reordering.
    block(i, I, TILE_I)
    hoist(I)      # place the tile loop I directly inside the t loop

    # 2) Innermost-loop unrolling along j.
    #    Unrolling increases instruction-level parallelism and exposes more
    #    opportunities for the compiler to schedule loads/stores and FMAs.
    #    The unrolled iterations are still executed in the same j order, so
    #    the left-neighbor dependence A[i,j-1] → A[i,j] is preserved.
    #
    #    Example for UNROLL_J = 4 (conceptual):
    #        for j = 1; j <= N-2; j += 4:
    #            compute A[i,j]
    #            compute A[i,j+1]
    #            compute A[i,j+2]
    #            compute A[i,j+3]
    #
    #    This keeps the semantics identical to the original loop.
    unroll(j, UNROLL_J)

    # 3) No parallelize() and no 2D (i,j) blocking:
    #    - The Gauss–Seidel scheme has true dependences along both i and j
    #      and along diagonals (e.g., (i,j) → (i+1,j-1)), so naive DOALL
    #      parallelization or rectangular tiling over both i and j would
    #      violate these dependences.
    #    - Therefore we do not apply:
    #          parallelize(t), parallelize(i), parallelize(j),
    #          block(i, I, ..) combined with block(j, J, ..)
    #      or any loop interchange that would change the (i,j) sweep order.
--- END OF MODEL: seidel-2d-02 ---

--- START OF MODEL: seidel-2d-03 ---
# Optimized model for seidel-2d (in-place 2D Gauss–Seidel stencil)

domain:
    # Global index ranges (C indices 0..N-1, but the kernel updates the interior 1..N-2)
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)
    i: dim in [0, N)
    j: dim in [0, N)

data:
    # A is the only array, updated in-place.
    # Layout matches the C code: row-major, A[i][j] at offset i*N + j.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (compile-time / run-time equivalent to N and TSTEPS in C)
    N: int > 2
    TSTEPS: int > 0

    # Precompute reciprocal of 9.0 once, so inner loop does a multiplication
    # instead of a division. This is a standard strength-reduction optimization.
    inv9: DATA_TYPE  # = SCALAR_VAL(1.0) / SCALAR_VAL(9.0)

    # Tunable blocking/unrolling parameters
    TI: int  # tile size for i (e.g., 32, chosen s.t. 3*TI*N*sizeof(DATA_TYPE) fits in L2)
    UT: int  # unroll factor for time t  (e.g., 2 or 4)
    UI: int  # unroll factor for i       (e.g., 2 or 4)

computation:
    # Single Gauss–Seidel update of A over all time steps.
    # The order t → i → j is strictly sequential due to data dependencies.
    update:
        for t in seq[0, TSTEPS):
            # Spatial blocking in i only. This partitions rows into contiguous tiles
            # but DOES NOT change the global (i,j) lexicographic order: rows are
            # still visited in increasing i, and within each row, j is increasing.
            for I in seq[1, N-1) with step TI:
                for i in seq[I, min(I + TI, N-1)):
                    for j in seq[1, N-1):
                        # j ∈ [1, N-2], i ∈ [1, N-2] in the live iterations below
                        if i in [1, N-1) and j in [1, N-1):
                            # Reassociate the 9-point sum to exploit partial sums
                            # and allow the compiler to keep them in registers.
                            s0 = A[i-1, j-1] + A[i-1, j] + A[i-1, j+1]
                            s1 = A[i,   j-1] + A[i,   j] + A[i,   j+1]
                            s2 = A[i+1, j-1] + A[i+1, j] + A[i+1, j+1]
                            A[i, j] = inv9 * (s0 + s1 + s2)

dependencies:
    # Label shorthand: update(t, i, j) refers to the unique assignment to A[i,j]
    # at time step t in the 'update' computation above.

    # Intra-time-step flow dependencies (reads of UPDATED neighbors):
    # For interior points (i ∈ [1, N-2], j ∈ [1, N-2]):
    for t in [0, TSTEPS),
        i in [2, N-1),     # so i-1 ∈ [1, N-2]
        j in [2, N-1):     # so j-1 ∈ [1, N-2]
        # From three cells in the row above (new values at time t)
        update(t, i-1, j-1) -> update(t, i, j)
        update(t, i-1, j  ) -> update(t, i, j)
        update(t, i-1, j+1) -> update(t, i, j)   # j+1 is in [2, N-2]
        # From left neighbor in the same row (new value at time t)
        update(t, i,   j-1) -> update(t, i, j)

    # Intra-time-step anti-dependencies (reads of OLD values that must happen
    # before those locations are overwritten at the same time step):
    for t in [0, TSTEPS),
        i in [1, N-2],
        j in [1, N-2]:
        # We read A[i, j+1] before update(t, i, j+1) overwrites it
        if j+1 <= N-2:
            update(t, i, j) -> update(t, i, j+1)
        # We read A[i+1, j-1], A[i+1, j], A[i+1, j+1] before the corresponding writes
        if i+1 <= N-2 and j-1 >= 1:
            update(t, i, j) -> update(t, i+1, j-1)
        if i+1 <= N-2:
            update(t, i, j) -> update(t, i+1, j)
        if i+1 <= N-2 and j+1 <= N-2:
            update(t, i, j) -> update(t, i+1, j+1)

    # Inter-time-step dependence: each time step uses the values left by
    # the previous time step at every interior point.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS-1),
        i in [1, N-2],
        j in [1, N-2]:
        update(t,   i, j) -> update(t+1, i, j)

optimization:
    # Strength reduction: replace division by constant 9.0 with multiplication
    # by its precomputed reciprocal. Implemented via the 'inv9' parameter.
    # (No explicit directive needed beyond modelling inv9 as a parameter.)

    # Spatial blocking in i:
    block(i, I, TI)
        # I is the tile index (row block), i is the intra-tile row.
        # We only tile the i dimension and KEEP the i-loop outer and the
        # j-loop inner inside each tile. This preserves the original
        # lexicographic (i,j) execution order and thus all dependencies.
        #
        # Tile size TI is tuned (e.g., 32–128) so that the three rows
        # touched by the 9-point stencil for TI consecutive i-values
        # fit well in caches.

    # Time and i unrolling:
    unroll(t, UT)
        # Replicate the time-step loop body UT times in sequence.
        # UT is small (e.g., 2 or 4) so as not to blow up code size.
        # Order of time steps is unchanged, so semantics and dependencies
        # are preserved.

    unroll(i, UI)
        # Unroll the i-loop within each i-tile by UI (e.g., 2 or 4).
        # This preserves the sequential i-order (each unrolled instance
        # corresponds to a strictly increasing i) while exposing more
        # ILP and allowing the compiler to better schedule loads from
        # neighboring rows.

    # NOTE: We intentionally DO NOT parallelize or vectorize the i/j loops:
    # - Gauss–Seidel updates are strongly ordered: update(t, i, j) depends
    #   on updated values in row i-1 and at (i, j-1), and must execute
    #   before several neighbors that read its old value.
    # - These flow and anti-dependencies make naive parallelization or
    #   SIMD execution across i or j iterations illegal without changing
    #   the numerical scheme.
    #
    # If parallelism is required, a different algorithmic scheme (e.g.,
    # Jacobi with two arrays or multi-color Gauss–Seidel) must be used,
    # which would not preserve this kernel’s exact semantics.
--- END OF MODEL: seidel-2d-03 ---

--- START OF MODEL: seidel-2d-04 ---
domain:
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)        # time steps
    i: dim in [0, N)             # row index
    j: dim in [0, N)             # column index

data:
    # Single in-place grid. Full logical size is N×N, but only interior
    # points i,j ∈ [1, N-1) are updated; the boundary is fixed.
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
        # Row-major layout: row stride = N, j is the fastest-varying dim.

parameters:
    inv9: DATA_TYPE    # = SCALAR_VAL(1.0) / SCALAR_VAL(9.0)
                       # replaces division by 9.0 with a cheaper multiply
    TI: int            # tile size in i (e.g., 32), tunable for cache
    TJ: int            # tile size in j (e.g., 64), tunable for cache
    UI: int            # unroll factor in i inside each tile (e.g., 2 or 4)

computation:
    # In-place 2D Gauss–Seidel 9-point stencil.
    # Loops over t, i, j are all sequential to preserve exact update order.
    UPDATE:
      for t in seq([0, TSTEPS)):
        for i in seq([1, N-1)):        # i = 1 .. N-2
          for j in seq([1, N-1)):      # j = 1 .. N-2
            A[i, j] =
              inv9 * (
                  A[i-1, j-1] + A[i-1, j] + A[i-1, j+1] +
                  A[i,   j-1] + A[i,   j] + A[i,   j+1] +
                  A[i+1, j-1] + A[i+1, j] + A[i+1, j+1]
              )

dependencies:
    # Gauss–Seidel scheme uses freshly updated values along i and j within
    # the same time step, so spatial loops must remain sequential.
    #
    # For valid indices (t, i, j) with 0 ≤ t < TSTEPS, 1 ≤ i < N-1, 1 ≤ j < N-1:

    # 1. Row-wise dependence: A[i, j] uses A[i, j-1] at the same time step.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS), i in [1, N-1), j in [2, N-1):
        UPDATE(t, i, j-1) -> UPDATE(t, i, j)

    # 2. Inter-row dependences within a time step: A[i, j] uses updated row i-1.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS), i in [2, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
        UPDATE(t, i-1, j)   -> UPDATE(t, i, j)
    for t in [0, TSTEPS), i in [2, N-1), j in [2, N-1):
        UPDATE(t, i-1, j-1) -> UPDATE(t, i, j)
    for t in [0, TSTEPS), i in [2, N-1), j in [1, N-2):
        UPDATE(t, i-1, j+1) -> UPDATE(t, i, j)

    # 3. Temporal dependence: each time step uses results from the
    #    previous step (through the in-place array A).
    for t in [1, TSTEPS), i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
        UPDATE(t-1, i, j) -> UPDATE(t, i, j)

optimization:
    # --- Arithmetic optimization ------------------------------------------
    # Use multiplication by a precomputed constant instead of division
    # by 9.0.  This is captured by the 'inv9' parameter and the
    # expression "inv9 * ( ... )" above.  The compiler can keep 'inv9'
    # in a register and emit a single multiply per update.

    # --- Spatial blocking (tiling) for cache locality ---------------------
    # Tile the interior loops in i and j.  Tiling is done in a way that
    # preserves the original lexicographic order:
    #   original: for i = 1..N-2, for j = 1..N-2
    #   tiled:    for I, for J, for i in tile I, for j in tile J
    # With I advancing in increasing i and, inside each I, J advancing in
    # increasing j, every (i, j) is still executed in the same relative
    # order as in the original code.  Thus all Gauss–Seidel dependences
    # listed above remain satisfied.
    block(i, I, TI)   # i = I * TI + ii,   ii in [0, TI), clamped to [1, N-2]
    block(j, J, TJ)   # j = J * TJ + jj,   jj in [0, TJ), clamped to [1, N-2]

    # Hoist the tile loops directly under the time loop:
    # for t:
    #   for I:
    #     for J:
    #       for i in tile(I):
    #         for j in tile(J):
    #           UPDATE
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    # This improves spatial locality (each tile fits better in cache) and
    # gives some temporal locality across neighboring points within a tile.

    # --- Loop unrolling for ILP -------------------------------------------
    # Unroll the inner i-loop inside each (I, J) tile.  j remains the
    # innermost dimension and continues to carry the dependence on
    # A[i, j-1], so the sequential Gauss–Seidel ordering along j is
    # preserved.  Unrolling only replicates the body sequentially for
    # successive i values; it does not change the logical execution order.
    unroll(i, UI)

    # --- Parallelization notes (no directive applied) ---------------------
    # Due to the strong in-place Gauss–Seidel dependences:
    #   - along j: UPDATE(t, i, j-1) -> UPDATE(t, i, j)
    #   - along i: UPDATE(t, i-1, j±{0,1}) -> UPDATE(t, i, j)
    # and across time steps t,
    # naive parallelization of i, j, or t would violate correctness.
    # Therefore, no parallelize(...) directives are specified here.
--- END OF MODEL: seidel-2d-04 ---

--- START OF MODEL: seidel-2d-05 ---
domain:
    # Global problem sizes (compile-time constants in original code)
    N: size > 2
    TSTEPS: size > 0

    # Iteration dimensions
    t: dim in [0, TSTEPS)          # time steps (outermost loop)
    i: dim in [0, N)               # spatial row index
    j: dim in [0, N)               # spatial column index

    # Interior spatial domain actually updated by the kernel
    i_int: dim in [1, N-1)         # corresponds to 1 .. N-2 in C
    j_int: dim in [1, N-1)         # corresponds to 1 .. N-2 in C

data:
    # Single in-place 2D grid, row-major layout as in C (A[i][j])
    A[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (passed as runtime arguments in C, but equal to N,TSTEPS here)
    n: int = N
    tsteps: int = TSTEPS

    # Precomputed scalar to replace division by 9.0
    inv9: DATA_TYPE
        # Defined once before the timed kernel:
        #   inv9 = SCALAR_VAL(1.0) / SCALAR_VAL(9.0);
        # Using inv9 turns a division inside the stencil into a multiplication.

    # Tunable blocking and unrolling parameters
    BI: int                          # block size along i (rows), 1 <= BI <= n-2
    UJ: int                          # unroll factor for the inner j loop, UJ >= 1

computation:
    # Gauss–Seidel 2D stencil, in-place, time-major order.
    # The semantics must match the original exact (t, i, j) update order.

    for t in seq(0, tsteps):         # outermost time loop: t = 0 .. tsteps-1
        for i in seq(1, n-1):        # i = 1 .. n-2  (interior rows, sequential)
            for j in seq(1, n-1):    # j = 1 .. n-2  (interior cols, sequential)
                upd_A(t, i, j):
                    A[i, j] =
                        inv9 * (
                            A[i-1, j-1] + A[i-1, j]   + A[i-1, j+1] +
                            A[i,   j-1] + A[i,   j]   + A[i,   j+1] +
                            A[i+1, j-1] + A[i+1, j]   + A[i+1, j+1]
                        )

dependencies:
    # Gauss–Seidel uses A in-place: each update depends on some values that have
    # already been updated in the current time step (e.g., A[i-1,*], A[i,j-1])
    # and on some that are still "old" (e.g., A[i,j+1], A[i+1,*]).
    # To preserve the exact numerical behavior, we conservatively enforce the
    # original lexicographic (t, i, j) ordering.

    # 1. Time steps must execute sequentially.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS-1):
        # All updates at time t must complete before any update at time t+1.
        for i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
            upd_A(t, i, j) -> upd_A(t+1, i, j)

    # 2. Within each time step t, (i, j) updates must follow row-major order.
    for t in [0, TSTEPS), i in [1, N-1), j in [1, N-1):
        # Depend on the immediately previous point in the same row (west neighbor),
        # ensuring left-to-right Gauss–Seidel sweep:
        if j > 1:
            upd_A(t, i, j-1) -> upd_A(t, i, j)

        # Depend on the three points of the previous row that are used as inputs:
        if i > 1 and j > 1:
            upd_A(t, i-1, j-1) -> upd_A(t, i, j)
        if i > 1:
            upd_A(t, i-1, j)   -> upd_A(t, i, j)
        if i > 1 and j < N-2:
            upd_A(t, i-1, j+1) -> upd_A(t, i, j)

        # These constraints preserve the same "new vs. old" mixture of neighbors
        # as in the original nested loops.

optimization:
    #-----------------------------
    # 1. Strength reduction
    #-----------------------------
    # Replace division by 9.0 with multiplication by its reciprocal.
    # This is expressed by using 'inv9' in the computation section instead
    # of '/ SCALAR_VAL(9.0)'. The compiler can hoist the computation of inv9
    # out of the t/i/j loops.
    #   inv9 = SCALAR_VAL(1.0) / SCALAR_VAL(9.0)
    # Cost: 1 scalar division outside the kernel
    # Benefit: one division per grid point per time step becomes a multiply.

    #-----------------------------
    # 2. 1D blocking in the i (row) dimension
    #-----------------------------
    # We can safely strip-mine / block the i-loop only (keeping j as a simple
    # inner loop) without changing the global (i, j) lexicographic order. This
    # improves cache behavior for very large grids by operating on clusters of
    # consecutive rows while preserving Gauss–Seidel dependencies.

    block(i, ii, BI)
        # Semantics:
        #   for t in seq(0, tsteps):
        #     for ii in seq(1, n-1 step BI):             # tile start row
        #       for i in seq(ii, min(ii+BI, n-1)):       # original inner i
        #         for j in seq(1, n-1):
        #           upd_A(t, i, j)
        #
        # Because ii increases monotonically and i iterates from ii upward,
        # this is just a grouping of rows; the relative order of all (i, j)
        # pairs is identical to the original. Therefore all data dependencies
        # (including those to A[i-1,*] and A[i,*-1]) remain satisfied.

    hoist(ii)
        # Ensure the tile index ii is placed immediately inside the t loop
        # (i.e., loop nest: t -> ii -> i -> j), maximizing spatial locality
        # on three-row working sets over BI consecutive rows.

    #-----------------------------
    # 3. Unrolling of the inner j loop
    #-----------------------------
    # The inner j loop has loop-carried dependencies (on A[i, j-1]), so it cannot
    # be vectorized naively. However, it CAN be unrolled, because unrolling keeps
    # the iteration order (j, then j+1, ...) while reducing loop overhead and
    # enabling the compiler to better schedule loads and arithmetic.

    unroll(j, UJ)
        # Semantics for factor UJ (e.g., 4):
        #   for j in seq(1, n-1 step UJ):
        #     upd_A(t, i, j)
        #     upd_A(t, i, j+1)
        #     ...
        #     upd_A(t, i, j+UJ-1)
        #
        # Each unrolled group still executes j in strictly increasing order,
        # preserving the "left-to-right" Gauss–Seidel behavior while giving
        # the compiler more ILP within a row.

    #-----------------------------
    # 4. Deliberately NOT applied
    #-----------------------------
    # - block(j, JJ, BJ) or simultaneous 2D (i,j) tiling:
    #     Naive 2D tiling would reorder some (i,j) iterations (changing when
    #     A[i-1,j+1] is updated relative to A[i,j], for example), altering
    #     which neighbors are "new" vs. "old" within a time step. This would
    #     change the numerical behavior of the Gauss–Seidel scheme, so it is
    #     avoided here.
    #
    # - parallelize(i), parallelize(j), parallelize(t), vectorize(j):
    #     The in-place Gauss–Seidel update has strong data dependencies along
    #     both spatial dimensions and across time steps. Naively parallelizing
    #     or vectorizing these loops would violate those dependencies and change
    #     results. Advanced schemes (e.g., multi-coloring or wavefront) would
    #     change the update ordering and are therefore excluded to preserve
    #     the original kernel semantics exactly.
--- END OF MODEL: seidel-2d-05 ---

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Include polybench common header. */
#include <polybench.h>

/* Include benchmark-specific header. */
#include "symm.h"


/* Array initialization. */
static
void init_array(int m, int n,
		DATA_TYPE *alpha,
		DATA_TYPE *beta,
		DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(C,M,N,m,n),
		DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(A,M,M,m,m),
		DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(B,M,N,m,n))
{
  int i, j;

  *alpha = 1.5;
  *beta = 1.2;
  for (i = 0; i < m; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++) {
      C[i][j] = (DATA_TYPE) ((i+j) % 100) / m;
      B[i][j] = (DATA_TYPE) ((n+i-j) % 100) / m;
    }
  for (i = 0; i < m; i++) {
    for (j = 0; j <=i; j++)
      A[i][j] = (DATA_TYPE) ((i+j) % 100) / m;
    for (j = i+1; j < m; j++)
      A[i][j] = -999; //regions of arrays that should not be used
  }
}


/* DCE code. Must scan the entire live-out data.
   Can be used also to check the correctness of the output. */
static
void print_array(int m, int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(C,M,N,m,n))
{
  int i, j;

  POLYBENCH_DUMP_START;
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_BEGIN("C");
  for (i = 0; i < m; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++) {
	if ((i * m + j) % 20 == 0) fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, "\n");
	fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, DATA_PRINTF_MODIFIER, C[i][j]);
    }
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_END("C");
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_FINISH;
}


/* Main computational kernel. The whole function will be timed,
   including the call and return. */
static
void kernel_symm[[gnu::flatten, gnu::noinline]](int m, int n,
		 DATA_TYPE alpha,
		 DATA_TYPE beta,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(C,M,N,m,n),
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(A,M,M,m,m),
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(B,M,N,m,n))
{
  int i, j, k;
  DATA_TYPE temp2;

//BLAS PARAMS
//SIDE = 'L'
//UPLO = 'L'
// =>  Form  C := alpha*A*B + beta*C
// A is MxM
// B is MxN
// C is MxN
//note that due to Fortran array layout, the code below more closely resembles upper triangular case in BLAS
#pragma scop
   for (i = 0; i < _PB_M; i++)
      for (j = 0; j < _PB_N; j++ )
      {
        temp2 = 0;
        for (k = 0; k < i; k++) {
           C[k][j] += alpha*B[i][j] * A[i][k];
           temp2 += B[k][j] * A[i][k];
        }
        C[i][j] = beta * C[i][j] + alpha*B[i][j] * A[i][i] + alpha * temp2;
     }
#pragma endscop

}


int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
  /* Retrieve problem size. */
  int m = M;
  int n = N;

  /* Variable declaration/allocation. */
  DATA_TYPE alpha;
  DATA_TYPE beta;
  POLYBENCH_2D_ARRAY_DECL(C,DATA_TYPE,M,N,m,n);
  POLYBENCH_2D_ARRAY_DECL(A,DATA_TYPE,M,M,m,m);
  POLYBENCH_2D_ARRAY_DECL(B,DATA_TYPE,M,N,m,n);

  /* Initialize array(s). */
  init_array (m, n, &alpha, &beta,
	      POLYBENCH_ARRAY(C),
	      POLYBENCH_ARRAY(A),
	      POLYBENCH_ARRAY(B));

  /* Start timer. */
  polybench_start_instruments;

  /* Run kernel. */
  kernel_symm (m, n,
	       alpha, beta,
	       POLYBENCH_ARRAY(C),
	       POLYBENCH_ARRAY(A),
	       POLYBENCH_ARRAY(B));

  /* Stop and print timer. */
  polybench_stop_instruments;
  polybench_print_instruments;

  /* Prevent dead-code elimination. All live-out data must be printed
     by the function call in argument. */
  polybench_prevent_dce(print_array(m, n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(C)));

  /* Be clean. */
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(C);
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(A);
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(B);

  return 0;
}

domain:
    # Matrix dimensions follow the PolyBench symm kernel:
    #   A: M x M  (symmetric, lower triangle stored)
    #   B: M x N
    #   C: M x N
    i: dim in [0, M)
    j: dim in [0, N)
    k: dim in [0, M)

data:
    # A is stored in row-major order; only the lower triangle (i >= k)
    # is initialized and used. Logically we interpret A as symmetric:
    #   A_sym[i, k] = A[max(i, k), min(i, k)].
    A[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE =
        (i, k) -> i * M + k      # row-major, valid only for k <= i

    # B and C are full MxN row-major matrices.
    B[i, j]: in  DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j

    # 1D temporary buffers over j (columns). They are reused for each i and
    # do not change the mathematical result; they are introduced only in
    # the optimized schedule (see 'optimization' section).
    temp1[j]: tmp DATA_TYPE = (j) -> j   # holds alpha * B[i, j] for fixed i
    temp2[j]: tmp DATA_TYPE = (j) -> j   # holds sum_{k<i} A[i,k] * B[k, j]

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta:  DATA_TYPE

    # Tuning parameters (not part of the mathematical semantics):
    BM: int  # suggested block size in i (rows)  – can be left unused or 0
    BN: int  # block size in j (columns), e.g., 64–256 depending on cache
    VJ: int  # SIMD vector length in j, e.g., 4 or 8 for doubles
    UK: int  # unroll factor for k, e.g., 4

computation:
    # Logical BLAS SYMM semantics (SIDE = 'L', UPLO = 'L'):
    #   C_out = beta * C_in + alpha * Symm(A) * B,
    # where Symm(A) is the full symmetric matrix whose lower triangle is
    # stored in A:
    #   Symm(A)[i, k] = A[max(i, k), min(i, k)].
    #
    # Written explicitly to use only the stored lower triangle of A:
    #
    #   C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j]
    #             + alpha * (
    #                   A[i, i] * B[i, j]
    #                 + sum_{k=0..i-1}   A[i, k] * B[k, j]
    #                 + sum_{k=i+1..M-1} A[k, i] * B[k, j]
    #               )
    #
    # This exactly matches the PolyBench kernel, which accumulates the
    # k < i part directly for C[i, j] and the k > i part indirectly via
    # updates to C[k, j] at larger outer indices.
    for i, j:
        C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j] \
                  + alpha * (
                        A[i, i] * B[i, j]
                      + sum(k in [0, i),   A[i, k] * B[k, j])
                      + sum(k in [i+1, M), A[k, i] * B[k, j])
                  )

optimization:
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------
    # Custom optimization primitive:
    #   transform(NAME)
    # denotes an algorithmic transformation that is mathematically
    # equivalent to the 'computation' but changes loop structure and
    # introduces temporaries as described in the comments around it.
    # -----------------------------------------------------------------

    # 1. Hoist the beta scaling of C out of the main symmetric multiply.
    #
    # From:
    #   C[i,j] = beta*C[i,j] + alpha*F(i,j)
    # To:
    #   C[i,j] = beta*C[i,j]        # separate pass over C
    #   C[i,j] += alpha*F(i,j)      # main kernel no longer multiplies by beta
    #
    # This reduces work in the hot triangular kernel and exposes a
    # simple, easily vectorizable and parallelizable scaling pass.
    transform(scale_C_by_beta)

    # 2. Reorder the main kernel into an i–k–j loop nest with 1D
    #    temporary vectors to improve cache locality and reduce memory
    #    traffic. For each fixed row i:
    #
    #   # Precompute scaled row of B and zero accumulator.
    #   for j in [0, N):
    #       temp1[j] = alpha * B[i, j]
    #       temp2[j] = 0
    #
    #   # Handle contributions from the strictly lower part (k < i):
    #   for k in [0, i):                 # sequential in k, triangular
    #       a_ik = A[i, k]               # hoisted out of the j-loop
    #       for j in [0, N):             # innermost, contiguous in memory
    #           # C[k, j] gets alpha * A[i,k] * B[i,j]
    #           C[k, j] += a_ik * temp1[j]
    #           # temp2[j] accumulates A[i,k] * B[k,j]
    #           temp2[j] += a_ik * B[k, j]
    #
    #   # Finalize row i using the diagonal and the accumulated temp2.
    #   a_ii = A[i, i]
    #   for j in [0, N):
    #       C[i, j] += a_ii * temp1[j] + alpha * temp2[j]
    #
    # Together with the separate C *= beta pass above, this is
    # algebraically identical to the specification in 'computation':
    #   each A[i,k] (i>k) contributes once to C[k,*] and once to C[i,*],
    #   exactly matching Symm(A)*B, and no element of the upper triangle
    #   A[i,k] with k>i is ever read.
    #
    # Advantages:
    #   - Inner loops run over j, the contiguous dimension of row-major
    #     B and C, enabling efficient SIMD vectorization.
    #   - A[i,k] and alpha*B[i,j] are reused across many operations
    #     (rank-1 updates), reducing loads and multiplications.
    #   - temp1 and temp2 are length-N vectors; extra memory is O(N),
    #     well within the 50% overhead budget.
    transform(symm_rank1_update_with_temp_vectors)

    # 3. Block the column dimension j to improve cache locality for B
    #    and C and to provide a natural unit for parallel work.  After
    #    'block(j, Jb, BN)', Jb ranges over tiles and j ranges within
    #    each tile.
    block(j, Jb, BN)

    # 4. Expose parallelism over independent column tiles.
    #    - Different Jb tiles write to disjoint sets of C[*, j] and read
    #      disjoint columns of B, so they are free of data races.
    #    - The outer i loop remains sequential because rows C[k, *] are
    #      updated across multiple i values (reduction-like dependence).
    parallelize(Jb)

    # 5. Vectorize innermost j loops inside each tile.
    #    - With the i–k–j ordering from the transform above and row-
    #      major layout, the j-loop accesses B[i, j], B[k, j], C[k, j],
    #      C[i, j], temp1[j], and temp2[j] with unit stride.
    #    - VJ should match the SIMD width (e.g., 4 or 8 doubles).
    vectorize(j, VJ)

    # 6. Optionally unroll the k-loop to increase instruction-level
    #    parallelism and reduce loop control overhead within each
    #    (i, Jb) tile. The triangular bound (k < i) is preserved.
    unroll(k, UK)

    # 7. The outer i loop is kept sequential to respect the triangular
    #    dependency pattern on C:
    #      C[k, j] accumulates contributions from all i > k.
    #    We *do not* apply parallelize(i); any parallelization across i
    #    would require an explicit reduction scheme on C.

--- START OF MODEL: symm-02 ---
domain:
    # Matrix dimensions (PolyBench: M == m, N == n)
    i: dim in [0, M)          # row index of A and C
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index of B and C
    k: dim in [0, M)          # reduction index over rows of B / columns of A

data:
    # A is an MxM symmetric matrix stored in row-major *lower-triangular* form:
    #   A[i, k] is valid only for k <= i; elements with k > i are never read.
    A[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> i * M + k        # row-major, lower triangle used

    # B is an MxN dense matrix, row-major.
    B[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j        # row-major

    # C is an MxN dense matrix, row-major, updated in place.
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j     # row-major

    # Optional logical view (no extra storage):
    # S[i, k] = A[i, k]  if k <= i
    #         = A[k, i]  if k >  i
    # S is the full symmetric matrix implied by the stored lower triangle of A.
    # All computations below are expressed directly in terms of A to avoid
    # touching the unused upper triangle.
    #S[i, k]: virtual DATA_TYPE  # symmetric view over A (lower-triangular storage)

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta: DATA_TYPE
    M: int
    N: int

    # Tuning parameters for the optimized kernel (no semantic effect):
    TI: int    # tile size in i (rows of A,C)
    TJ: int    # tile size in j (cols of B,C)
    TK: int    # tile size in k (rows of B / columns of A)
    VJ: int    # vector width along j for SIMD
    UK: int    # unroll factor for the k-reduction inside a tile

computation:
    # High-level mathematical specification derived from the kernel:
    #   SIDE = 'L', UPLO = 'L'
    #   C := alpha * A_sym * B + beta * C
    # where A_sym is the symmetric matrix defined by A's lower triangle.
    #
    # For each output element C[i, j], the symmetric product can be written
    # without ever reading A's upper triangle as:
    #
    #   C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j]
    #             + alpha * [ sum_{k = 0..i}   A[i, k] * B[k, j]
    #                        + sum_{k = i+1..M-1} A[k, i] * B[k, j] ]
    #
    # The first sum uses row i of the stored lower triangle (including the
    # diagonal), the second sum uses column i of the strictly lower part.

    for i, j:
        C[i, j] =
            beta * C[i, j]
            + alpha * (
                  sum(k in [0, i+1),   A[i, k] * B[k, j])      # k <= i
                + sum(k in [i+1, M),   A[k, i] * B[k, j])      # k >  i
              )

dependencies:
    # Each (i, j) computes C[i, j] exactly once from the input values of
    # A, B, and the original C[i, j]. No C[i, j] depends on any other
    # C[i', j'] with (i', j') != (i, j).
    #
    # The only reductions are over k inside each (i, j), using a private
    # accumulator. Therefore:
    #   - All (i, j) iterations are mutually independent.
    #   - The k-reductions can be freely reordered or blocked, provided
    #     they remain associative and use a private accumulator per (i, j).

optimization:
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Cache-friendly 3D blocking (tiling)
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Tile the i (rows of A,C), j (cols of B,C), and k (rows of B)
    # dimensions. TK should be chosen so that a tile of B[Kk, Jj] and the
    # corresponding rows of C[i, Jj] fit in L1/L2 cache. TI and TJ tune
    # spatial locality for C and B.
    block(i, Ii, TI)     # Ii: tile index over rows of A,C
    block(j, Jj, TJ)     # Jj: tile index over columns of B,C
    block(k, Kk, TK)     # Kk: tile index over the reduction dimension

    # After blocking, the core computation conceptually becomes:
    #   for Ii, Jj, Kk:
    #     for i in tile(Ii), j in tile(Jj):
    #       C[i, j] += alpha * sum(k in tile(Kk) ∩ domain(i),
    #                              symmetric_A_times_B(i, k, j))
    # where domain(i) encodes the triangular constraint:
    #   k <= i   -> use A[i, k]
    #   k >  i   -> use A[k, i]

    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Loop reordering to reuse B and C (k-major, then i/j tiles)
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Hoist the k-tile loop Kk outward so that we process one band of rows
    # of B (B[Kk, :]) at a time, reusing it across many rows i and columns j
    # of C before moving to the next k-tile.
    #
    # Effective loop order (conceptually):
    #   for Kk:                         # outermost: k-tiles
    #     for Ii:                       # tiles over rows of A,C
    #       for Jj:                     # tiles over columns of B,C
    #         for i in tile(Ii):
    #           for j in tile(Jj):
    #             accumulate over k in tile(Kk) ∩ domain(i)
    hoist(Kk)

    # Hoist Ii and Jj above the point where the k-slice of B is fully
    # available; within a fixed Kk we then sweep C by tiles. This exposes
    # coarse-grain parallelism and improves temporal locality on C.
    hoist(Ii)
    hoist(Jj)

    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Exploit symmetry of A explicitly
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Within each (Kk, Ii) tile, split the k-iteration into the two affine
    # regions implied by the triangular structure of A:
    #
    #   for i in tile(Ii):
    #     # Part 1: k in [0, i] ∩ tile(Kk): use row i of A (A[i, k])
    #     for k in [0, i+1) ∩ tile(Kk):
    #       ... use A[i, k] * B[k, j] ...
    #
    #     # Part 2: k in [i+1, M) ∩ tile(Kk): use column i (A[k, i])
    #     for k in [i+1, M) ∩ tile(Kk):
    #       ... use A[k, i] * B[k, j] ...
    #
    # This guarantees that we never read A[i, k] with k > i (those entries
    # were initialized to a sentinel value and are semantically undefined).
    # It also allows the compiler/polyhedral optimizer to drop unreachable
    # parts of the iteration space and reduce conditionals in the innermost
    # loops.
    # (This is a semantic property, so we express it as a comment-level
    #  constraint on the reduced k-domain rather than as a new directive.)

    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Parallelization
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # All (i, j) iterations are independent, so we can parallelize
    # over outer tiles. On a 32-core/64-thread x64 machine, a 2D tiling
    # over Ii and Jj gives good load balance; a runtime can map the 2D
    # iteration space to threads.
    parallelize(Ii)      # distribute i-tiles across threads
    parallelize(Jj)      # optionally also distribute j-tiles (2D decomposition)

    # The k-tiles Kk are reductions; they execute sequentially with respect
    # to each (i, j), but different (i, j) tiles are independent.

    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Vectorization and unrolling
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # j is the unit-stride dimension in row-major storage for both B and C.
    # Make j the innermost loop inside each tile and vectorize it to exploit
    # SIMD (AVX/AVX2/AVX-512). VJ should match the hardware vector width.
    vectorize(j, VJ)

    # Unroll the k-loop within each tile to:
    #   - reduce loop overhead,
    #   - expose multiple independent FMA chains for better ILP.
    unroll(k, UK)

    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6. Scalar hoisting and reuse (micro-optimizations)
    #---------------------------------------------------------------
    # Within the innermost loops (after blocking/reordering), hoist:
    #   - alpha into a register,
    #   - a per-(i, k) scalar s = alpha * (A[i, k] or A[k, i]),
    # so that for a fixed (i, k) we compute s once and reuse it across the
    # inner j-loop:
    #
    #   s = alpha * (i >= k ? A[i, k] : A[k, i])
    #   for j in tile(Jj):
    #       C[i, j] += s * B[k, j]
    #
    # This eliminates redundant multiplications by alpha and reduces loads
    # from A inside the innermost FMA loop.
    #
    # (Expressed here as a comment-level guideline; it corresponds to
    #  common scalar replacement and strength-reduction performed by -O3.)
--- END OF MODEL: symm-02 ---

--- START OF MODEL: symm-03 ---
# Optimized model for symm.c
# (C := alpha * A * B + beta * C, with A symmetric and only its lower triangle stored)

domain:
    i: dim in [0, M)   # rows of A and C
    j: dim in [0, N)   # columns of B and C
    k: dim in [0, M)   # rows of B / columns of A

data:
    # A is conceptually symmetric. Only its lower triangle (k <= i) is initialized:
    #   A[i, k] is valid for 0 <= k <= i < M.
    # For k > i, A[i, k] holds a sentinel (-999) and must never be read.
    # We model it as a full MxM row-major array with a "lower_symmetric" access convention.
    A[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE  = (i, k) -> i * M + k   # row-major, valid for k <= i only

    # B and C are dense MxN row-major matrices.
    B[k, j]: in    DATA_TYPE   = (k, j) -> k * N + j   # row-major
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE   = (i, j) -> i * N + j   # row-major

    # Temporary buffer: a copy of B pre-scaled by alpha, to reduce multiplications
    # inside the main symmetric product.
    B_alpha[k, j]: temp DATA_TYPE = (k, j) -> k * N + j  # same layout as B

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta:  DATA_TYPE

    # Tunable blocking and SIMD parameters (hardware/caches dependent).
    Ti:  int  # tile size in i (rows of A, C), e.g., 64
    Tj:  int  # tile size in j (cols of B, C), e.g., 64
    Tk:  int  # tile size in k (rows of B / cols of A), e.g., 64
    VEC: int  # SIMD width along j, e.g., 4 (double) or 8 (float)
    UJ:  int  # unroll factor for innermost j-loop (multiple of VEC)

computation:
    # 1) Scale C by beta.
    # In the original kernel, each C[i, j] is multiplied by beta exactly once when i matches
    # the row index. Doing it here in a separate pass is mathematically equivalent and exposes
    # a simple, fully parallel loop.
    scale_C:
        for i, j:
            C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j]

    # 2) Pre-scale B by alpha once and reuse.
    # This trades one global M*N multiply for many per-(i, k, j) multiplications,
    # reducing arithmetic in the main kernel and allowing FMAs on (A * B_alpha).
    pre_scale_B:
        for k, j:
            B_alpha[k, j] = alpha * B[k, j]

    # 3) Symmetric matrix-matrix product:
    #    Conceptual symmetric matrix A_sym is defined by:
    #        A_sym[i, k] = A[i, k]  if k <= i
    #                    = A[k, i]  if k > i
    #    Only initialized entries of A (its lower triangle) are ever accessed.
    #
    #    Final result:
    #        C[i, j] = beta * C0[i, j] + alpha * sum_{k=0..M-1} A_sym[i, k] * B[k, j]
    #
    #    Using B_alpha (already multiplied by alpha) and the implicit A_sym:
    symm_main:
        for i, j:
            C[i, j] = C[i, j] +
                      sum(k,
                          (if k <= i
                           then A[i, k]
                           else A[k, i]) * B_alpha[k, j])

dependencies:
    # C must be fully scaled before symmetric contributions are accumulated.
    for i in [0, M), j in [0, N):
        scale_C(i, j) -> symm_main(i, j)

    # Each symm_main(i, j) uses B_alpha[k, j] for all k, so it depends on all
    # pre_scale_B(k, j) for that column j.
    for i in [0, M), j in [0, N), k in [0, M):
        pre_scale_B(k, j) -> symm_main(i, j)

optimization:
    # --- Cache blocking / tiling ---

    # Tile all three logical dimensions so that blocks of A, B_alpha, and C fit in cache.
    block(i, I, Ti)   # I indexes row tiles of A and C
    block(j, J, Tj)   # J indexes column tiles of B_alpha and C
    block(k, K, Tk)   # K indexes row tiles of B_alpha / column tiles of A

    # Execute tiles in the order (I, K, J) for better reuse of A and B_alpha:
    #   for I
    #     for K
    #       for J
    #         ... inner scalar loops over i, k, j inside the tiles ...
    hoist(I)
    hoist(K)
    hoist(J)

    # Inside each (I, K) tile, enforce the symmetric lower-triangular structure:
    # - Implement the k-sum of symm_main using only initialized entries of A:
    #       if k <= i then read A[i, k]
    #       else         read A[k, i]
    # - A code generator may choose equivalent implementations, e.g.:
    #     * Split the reduction over k into [0, i) and (i, M), or
    #     * Iterate only over the lower-triangular region (i >= k) and, for each
    #       (i, k), update both C[i, j] and C[k, j] in one pass:
    #           for i in [0, M)
    #             for k in [0, i]
    #               a = A[i, k]
    #               if i == k:
    #                 for j: C[i, j] += a * B_alpha[i, j]
    #               else:
    #                 for j:
    #                   C[i, j] += a * B_alpha[k, j]
    #                   C[k, j] += a * B_alpha[i, j]
    #   This variant matches the standard BLAS SYMM(L, L) algorithm and maximizes
    #   reuse of each A[i, k].

    # --- Parallelism ---

    # Different columns of C (different j) are completely independent:
    # C[:, j0] depends only on B_alpha[:, j0] and A.
    # Parallelize across column tiles to avoid write conflicts:
    parallelize(J)

    # With an implementation that privatizes or atomically updates tiles of C, additional
    # parallelism over I tiles can be exposed as well:
    # parallelize(I)

    # --- SIMD vectorization and unrolling ---

    # Ensure the innermost loop runs over j so that C[i, j] and B_alpha[k, j]
    # are accessed with unit stride (row-major layout).
    vectorize(j, VEC)
    unroll(j, UJ)

    # --- Optional layout optimization for A (packed lower triangle) ---
    # packed_lower(A, A_packed)
    #   # A_packed is a conceptual 1D buffer of length M*(M+1)/2 that stores the lower
    #   # triangle of A row by row:
    #   #   A_packed[offset(i, k)] = A[i, k]   for 0 <= k <= i < M
    #   #   offset(i, k) = i*(i+1)/2 + k
    #   #
    #   # All uses of:
    #   #   if k <= i then A[i, k] else A[k, i]
    #   # are implemented as:
    #   #   A_packed[offset(max(i, k), min(i, k))]
    #   #
    #   # This reduces the memory footprint and bandwidth for A, while never accessing
    #   # the sentinel region A[i, k] (k > i). Numerical results are unchanged.
--- END OF MODEL: symm-03 ---

domain:
    i: dim in [0, M)   # row index of A and C
    j: dim in [0, N)   # column index of B and C
    k: dim in [0, M)   # shared dimension (row of B / col or row of A)

data:
    # A is stored as an M×M row-major matrix, but only the lower triangle (k <= i)
    # contains valid data; the upper triangle is unused (filled with -999).
    A[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> i * M + k   # row-major, lower-triangular used

    # B and C are dense M×N row-major matrices.
    B[k, j]: in    DATA_TYPE = (k, j) -> k * N + j  # row-major
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # row-major

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    beta:  DATA_TYPE

    # Tuning parameters for cache blocking and SIMD; chosen to fit target cache sizes
    # and vector width on the x64 machine.
    TI: int > 0  # tile size for i (rows of A and C)
    TJ: int > 0  # tile size for j (columns of B and C)
    TK: int > 0  # tile size for k (rows of B / columns of A)

    VEC_WIDTH: int > 0  # SIMD width in elements for vectorization along j

computation:
    # High-level semantics:
    #   C := beta * C + alpha * A_sym * B
    # where A_sym is the symmetric matrix:
    #   A_sym[i, k] = A[i, k] if k <= i, else A[k, i]
    # Only the stored lower triangle of A is ever read.

    SCALE_C:
    for i, j:
        C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j]

    # Symmetric matrix-matrix multiply contribution.
    # Expanded to avoid any access to the unused upper part of A.
    UPDATE_C:
    for i, j:
        C[i, j] += alpha * (
            A[i, i] * B[i, j]                          # diagonal term
            + sum(k in [0, i))  A[i, k] * B[k, j]      # k < i: use A[i, k]
            + sum(k in (i, M)) A[k, i] * B[k, j]       # k > i: use A[k, i]
        )

dependencies:
    # The scaling of C must precede the symmetric update for each element.
    for i in [0, M), j in [0, N):
        SCALE_C(i, j) -> UPDATE_C(i, j)

    # Within UPDATE_C, for each fixed (i, j), the terms over k form a reduction.
    # There are no dependencies across different (i, j) pairs.
    # This permits reordering and parallelization over i and j, while k is a
    # pure reduction dimension.
    for i in [0, M), j in [0, N), k1 in [0, M), k2 in [0, M):
        if k1 < k2:
            UPDATE_C(i, j, k1) -> UPDATE_C(i, j, k2)

optimization:
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 1. Parallelize and vectorize the scaling of C (embarrassingly parallel).
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    parallelize(i)           # distribute rows of C across threads in SCALE_C
    vectorize(j, VEC_WIDTH)  # SIMD over contiguous columns of C in SCALE_C

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 2. Treat UPDATE_C as a GEMM-like kernel with a symmetric left matrix.
    #    Apply 3D tiling for cache locality.
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Tile the logical dimensions:
    block(i, I, TI)  # tiles of rows  of A and C
    block(k, K, TK)  # tiles of the shared dimension (rows of B / cols of A)
    block(j, J, TJ)  # tiles of columns of B and C

    # Choose a loop ordering that:
    #   - keeps j innermost for unit-stride access in B[k, j] and C[i, j];
    #   - reuses A[i, k] and A[k, i] across many j within a tile;
    #   - reuses B[k, j] across multiple i within a (K, J) tile.
    #
    # Target order inside UPDATE_C:
    #   for I in tiles(i):
    #     for K in tiles(k):
    #       for J in tiles(j):
    #         for i in I:
    #           for k in K:
    #             for j in J:  # innermost, unit-stride
    #               use A[i,k] or A[k,i], B[k,j], update C[i,j]
    interchange(K, J)  # make j-tiles (J) the innermost tile loop within each (I, K)

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 3. Exploit thread-level and data-parallelism in the tiled UPDATE_C.
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    parallelize(I)           # distribute independent row-tiles of C across cores
    vectorize(j, VEC_WIDTH)  # SIMD on the innermost j-loop in each (I, K, J) tile
    unroll(k, 4)             # modest unrolling of the k-loop inside each K-tile
                             # to increase ILP and register reuse

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 4. Algebraic hoisting of alpha out of the innermost loop.
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Conceptual transformation (no extra arrays required):
    #   For each (i, k) in a tile, compute once:
    #       a_ik = (k <= i ? A[i, k] : A[k, i])
    #       a_scaled = alpha * a_ik
    #   Then, for all j in the innermost loop:
    #       C[i, j] += a_scaled * B[k, j]
    #
    # This replaces a per-(i, k, j) multiplication by alpha with a per-(i, k)
    # multiplication, reducing arithmetic and enabling efficient FMA use.
    #scale_A_by_alpha(A)  # # conceptual optimization: hoist alpha*A into registers

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 5. Symmetry-aware access to A: avoid touching the unused upper triangle.
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Implement the A_sym access in UPDATE_C by always mapping to the lower
    # triangle of A:
    #   if k <= i: use A[i, k]
    #   else:      use A[k, i]
    #
    # This preserves the original semantics (never reading the sentinel -999
    # entries) while enabling symmetric reuse of each stored A[i, k].
    #symm_lower(A)  # # conceptual: enforce lower-triangular-only loads from A

    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # 6. (Optional) Per-thread or per-tile scratch buffers.
    # -------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # For large N, it can be beneficial to allocate a small temporary buffer per
    # (I, K) tile (on the stack or in thread-local storage) to hold a contiguous
    # block of B[K, J] or partial C[I, J], improving prefetching and alignment.
    # The total extra memory is O(TI * TJ + TK * TJ) per thread, which can be
    # kept well below 50% of the original footprint for reasonable tile sizes.
    #tile_local_buffers(B_tile[K, J], C_tile[I, J])  # conceptual tiling buffers

--- START OF MODEL: symm-05 ---
domain:
    i: dim in [0, M)      # row index of A and C
    j: dim in [0, N)      # column index of B and C
    k: dim in [0, M)      # row index of B / column index of A

data:
    # A stores only the lower triangular part of a logical symmetric matrix S:
    #   S[i, k] = A[i, k] if i >= k, else S[i, k] = A[k, i]
    # Entries A[i, k] with k > i are never used.
    A[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> i * M + k        # row-major M×M

    B[k, j]: in DATA_TYPE = (k, j) -> k * N + j        # row-major M×N
    C[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j     # row-major M×N

    alpha: scalar DATA_TYPE
    beta:  scalar DATA_TYPE

    # Loop-private temporaries (no extra asymptotic storage)
    s: scalar DATA_TYPE   # symmetric matrix element S(i,k)
    t: scalar DATA_TYPE   # alpha * s

parameters:
    # Tunable tile sizes (chosen for cache hierarchy of the target machine).
    TI: int   # tile size for i (rows of A,C), e.g., 32–64
    TK: int   # tile size for k (rows of B / cols of A), e.g., 32–64
    TJ: int   # tile size for j (columns of B,C), e.g., 64–256

    VEC: int  # SIMD width for vectorization along j (e.g., 4/8/16 depending on DATA_TYPE and ISA)

computation:
    # Mathematical semantics of the kernel:
    #   Let S(i,k) = A[i,k] if i >= k else A[k,i].
    #   Then for all i,j:
    #       C_out[i,j] = beta * C_in[i,j]
    #                    + alpha * sum_{k=0..M-1} S(i,k) * B[k,j]
    #
    # This is exactly the effect of the original kernel_symm, which implements
    # C := alpha * S * B + beta * C using only the stored lower triangle of S.

    # 1. Scale C by beta.
    SCALE:
      for i, j:
        C[i, j] = beta * C[i, j]

    # 2. Symmetric matrix–matrix product using only the stored lower triangle of A.
    #    The logical symmetric element is formed on the fly to avoid ever reading
    #    the A[i,k] entries with k > i that are marked as unused (-999).
    SYMM:
      for i, k:
        if i >= k:
          s = A[i, k]
        else:
          s = A[k, i]        # use symmetric counterpart from the lower triangle
        t = alpha * s        # invariant across j for this (i,k) pair

        for j:
          C[i, j] = C[i, j] + t * B[k, j]

dependencies:
    # Each C[i,j] must be scaled by SCALE before being updated by SYMM.
    for i in [0, M), j in [0, N):
        SCALE(i, j) -> SYMM(i, *, j)

optimization:
    # --- High-level algorithmic change --------------------------------------
    # The original code updates both C[i,j] and C[k,j] inside the same (i,k)
    # iteration to exploit symmetry and maintain triangular loop bounds.
    #
    # Here we instead use the *logical* symmetric matrix S derived from A and
    # compute the row-wise GEMM-like form
    #     C[i, :] = beta * C[i, :] + alpha * sum_k S(i,k) * B[k, :]
    #
    # This keeps all writes to C confined to a single row i at a time, which:
    #   - removes cross-row dependencies,
    #   - allows straightforward parallelization over i, and
    #   - enables contiguous access to both B[k, j] and C[i, j] in the inner loop.
    #
    # The mathematical result is identical to the original kernel in real
    # arithmetic (same symmetric matrix S and same linear operation).

    # --- Loop tiling (blocking) ---------------------------------------------
    # Tile all three dimensions to improve cache reuse:
    #   - i (rows of A,C): reuse C[i, :] across many k-blocks.
    #   - k (rows of B / cols of A): reuse B[k, :] and A[:,k] across j-blocks.
    #   - j (columns of B,C): operate on contiguous slices that fit in cache
    #     and map well to SIMD registers.
    block(i, I, TI)    # I: index of i-tiles of height TI
    block(k, K, TK)    # K: index of k-tiles of height TK
    block(j, J, TJ)    # J: index of j-tiles of width TJ

    # After blocking, the intended loop structure is (schematically):
    #   for I in 0..ceil(M/TI):
    #     for i in tile(I):
    #       # (Optionally SCALE fused here per row i, see 'fuse' below)
    #       for K in 0..ceil(M/TK):
    #         for k in tile(K):
    #           s = (i >= k ? A[i,k] : A[k,i])
    #           t = alpha * s
    #           for J in 0..ceil(N/TJ):
    #             for j in tile(J):
    #               C[i,j] += t * B[k,j]

    hoist(I)           # move I to the outermost position
    hoist(K)           # next outermost: tile over k
    hoist(J)           # outer tile over j, inner j remains innermost within each tile

    # --- Parallelization ----------------------------------------------------
    # Rows of C (i dimension) are now independent in SYMM.
    # Parallelizing over outer i-tiles balances load across cores and keeps
    # each thread working on contiguous rows of C.
    parallelize(I)

    # --- Vectorization and unrolling ---------------------------------------
    # The innermost loop iterates over j, which is contiguous in memory for
    # both B[k, j] and C[i, j], making it ideal for SIMD.
    vectorize(j, VEC)  # map inner j-loop to SIMD with hardware-appropriate width
    unroll(j, 4)       # moderate unrolling to hide FMA and load latency

    # --- Scalar hoisting / strength reduction -------------------------------
    # The product t = alpha * s is invariant over j for a fixed (i,k).
    # Compilers should hoist this out of the inner j-loop automatically, but
    # this model makes that explicit via the scalar 't' assigned before the j-loop.
    # No extra directive needed; this is encoded in the SYMM computation itself.

    # --- Optional loop fusion for better locality ---------------------------
    # Define a custom optimization:
    #   fuse(L1, L2, dim):
    #     Merge the loops labeled L1 and L2 along dimension 'dim' when they share
    #     the same bounds, preserving the original intra-iteration order of
    #     statements (all L1 body statements execute before L2's for each value
    #     of 'dim').
    #
    # Here we fuse SCALE and SYMM along dimension i so that each row of C is
    # scaled once and then immediately updated, improving temporal locality on C.
    fuse(SCALE, SYMM, i)   # # custom directive as described above

/**

 *

/* symm.c: this file is part of PolyBench/C */

#include <stdio.h>
#include <unistd.h>
#include <string.h>
#include <math.h>

/* Include polybench common header. */
#include <polybench.h>

/* Include benchmark-specific header. */
#include "symm.h"


/* Array initialization. */
static
void init_array(int m, int n,
		DATA_TYPE *alpha,
		DATA_TYPE *beta,
		DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(C,M,N,m,n),
		DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(A,M,M,m,m),
		DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(B,M,N,m,n))
{
  int i, j;

  *alpha = 1.5;
  *beta = 1.2;
  for (i = 0; i < m; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++) {
      C[i][j] = (DATA_TYPE) ((i+j) % 100) / m;
      B[i][j] = (DATA_TYPE) ((n+i-j) % 100) / m;
    }
  for (i = 0; i < m; i++) {
    for (j = 0; j <=i; j++)
      A[i][j] = (DATA_TYPE) ((i+j) % 100) / m;
    for (j = i+1; j < m; j++)
      A[i][j] = -999; //regions of arrays that should not be used
  }
}


/* DCE code. Must scan the entire live-out data.
   Can be used also to check the correctness of the output. */
static
void print_array(int m, int n,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(C,M,N,m,n))
{
  int i, j;

  POLYBENCH_DUMP_START;
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_BEGIN("C");
  for (i = 0; i < m; i++)
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++) {
	if ((i * m + j) % 20 == 0) fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, "\n");
	fprintf (POLYBENCH_DUMP_TARGET, DATA_PRINTF_MODIFIER, C[i][j]);
    }
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_END("C");
  POLYBENCH_DUMP_FINISH;
}


/* Main computational kernel. The whole function will be timed,
   including the call and return. */
static
void kernel_symm[[gnu::flatten, gnu::noinline]](int m, int n,
		 DATA_TYPE alpha,
		 DATA_TYPE beta,
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(C,M,N,m,n),
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(A,M,M,m,m),
		 DATA_TYPE POLYBENCH_2D(B,M,N,m,n))
{
  int i, j, k;
  DATA_TYPE temp2;

//BLAS PARAMS
//SIDE = 'L'
//UPLO = 'L'
// =>  Form  C := alpha*A*B + beta*C
// A is MxM
// B is MxN
// C is MxN
//note that due to Fortran array layout, the code below more closely resembles upper triangular case in BLAS
#pragma scop
   for (i = 0; i < _PB_M; i++)
      for (j = 0; j < _PB_N; j++ )
      {
        temp2 = 0;
        for (k = 0; k < i; k++) {
           C[k][j] += alpha*B[i][j] * A[i][k];
           temp2 += B[k][j] * A[i][k];
        }
        C[i][j] = beta * C[i][j] + alpha*B[i][j] * A[i][i] + alpha * temp2;
     }
#pragma endscop

}


int main(int argc, char** argv)
{
  /* Retrieve problem size. */
  int m = M;
  int n = N;

  /* Variable declaration/allocation. */
  DATA_TYPE alpha;
  DATA_TYPE beta;
  POLYBENCH_2D_ARRAY_DECL(C,DATA_TYPE,M,N,m,n);
  POLYBENCH_2D_ARRAY_DECL(A,DATA_TYPE,M,M,m,m);
  POLYBENCH_2D_ARRAY_DECL(B,DATA_TYPE,M,N,m,n);

  /* Initialize array(s). */
  init_array (m, n, &alpha, &beta,
	      POLYBENCH_ARRAY(C),
	      POLYBENCH_ARRAY(A),
	      POLYBENCH_ARRAY(B));

  /* Start timer. */
  polybench_start_instruments;

  /* Run kernel. */
  kernel_symm (m, n,
	       alpha, beta,
	       POLYBENCH_ARRAY(C),
	       POLYBENCH_ARRAY(A),
	       POLYBENCH_ARRAY(B));

  /* Stop and print timer. */
  polybench_stop_instruments;
  polybench_print_instruments;

  /* Prevent dead-code elimination. All live-out data must be printed
     by the function call in argument. */
  polybench_prevent_dce(print_array(m, n, POLYBENCH_ARRAY(C)));

  /* Be clean. */
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(C);
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(A);
  POLYBENCH_FREE_ARRAY(B);

  return 0;
}
